articles.title: Houthis hit Aden airport, Qatar says US-Iran talks progressing
articles.body:
Houthis announce that they have launched ballistic missiles against Yemen's Aden International Airport, meanwhile the Saudi-led coalition intercepted a separate Houthi missile north of Riyadh
US President Donald Trump says the Iran war will conclude through either "the nice way or the not-so-nice way". At the same time, Qatari officials have said that mediation efforts between the US and Iran are gradually progressing ahead
Oil prices climb above $101 a barrel
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon and southern Syria despite any agreements or alleged ceasefires
And so we continue our live coverage...
KSA launches air safety probe into flydubai incident
Saudi Arabia has launched an air accident probe following last week's cockpit stabbing on a flydubai jet, as experts examine any fallout for aviation safety alongside a separate UAE-led criminal investigation, Reuters reported- citing three people close to the matter.
Safety probes designed to keep flights safe are normal after accidents but are not mandatory when a deliberate act is involved, such as the suspected attempt by a co-pilot to bring down the Israel-bound flydubai jet on September 30.
Until now, it has remained unclear whether Saudi Arabia would go ahead with such a probe, which experts say could test a system of international co-operation designed to make recommendations for safety without attempting to assign blame.
The people close to the matter said Saudi Arabia had notified specialist aviation agencies abroad that it would carry out a safety investigation under international rules into flight FZ1073, which was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked the captain with an axe.
Saudi Arabia's National Transport Safety Center, which has responsibility for accident investigations, did not immediately comment following the Reuters report.
The Saudi government and the country's regulator also did not answer requests for comment.
The US National Transportation Safety Board, which would be closely involved in any probe because the Boeing 737 MAX jet that survived a steep plunge was designed and built in the United States, could not immediately be reached for comment.
Hezbollah has received $200 million from Iran to help Lebanese displaced by this year’s war with Israel, the first significant aid from the group to supporters who bore the brunt of the conflict- according to a new report by news agency Reuters.
Citing two people with direct knowledge of the transfer, Reuters reported that Hezbollah received the cash last month despite a tightening US economic chokehold on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, said the people.
Intermediaries who moved the money charged a 20% fee, reflecting the risks of dealing with the group, they said. One said this was four times the normal fee.
A Hezbollah official told Reuters that an amount had been secured and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the funds.
The Iranian foreign ministry, Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the US State Department and the Lebanese government did not publicly respond to the claims.
Israel’s bombardment and invasion of Lebanon uprooted hundreds of thousands of Hezbollah’s Shi’ite Muslim constituents after the group entered the regional war in support of Iran on March 2.
But those displaced have so far received little to no assistance from Hezbollah, an armed group founded by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards in 1982 which has suffered heavy Israeli blows in two wars since 2024 and is designated a terrorist group by Washington.
Attacks on tankers in Hormuz hit highest of any week
Attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest last week of any week since the Iran war began, according to maritime security sources tracking incidents, amid a bigger export push by Gulf producers.
Attacks, attempted attacks and harassment activity including drone overflights, surveillance and hailing using VHF radio by Iran's Revolutionary Guards have persisted in the strait, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said in a note on Sunday.
"These actions continue to demonstrate Iran’s intent to assert presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels," the JMIC said.
In the week of September 28-October 5, there had been at least 12 attacks on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the Strait of Hormuz, according to data from three maritime security sources who analysed incidents based on information received from the area.
That was the highest number of attacks in a single week since the US war with Iran began on February 28, the sources said.
Separate data collated by the UN's shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization (IMO), showed nine incidents involving vessels in the same week.
The UN body tends to take longer to verify and officially record incidents, maritime sources say.
The closest week in terms of comparable incidents was the week of July 13 when there were eight incidents, separate IMO data showed.
Israel army destroys memorials to Palestinians on October 7
Israel's military destroyed on Wednesday memorials across the West Bank to Palestinians, on the third anniversary of Hamas's October 7 attack, the army and local officials said.
Troops destroyed a stone monument and tore down commemorative posters in the northern region of Jenin, governorate spokeswoman Hala Abu Baker told news agency AFP.
"A memorial to the martyr Yasser Hamdouni was destroyed in the town of Yaabad, and photos of various martyrs were removed from several locations in the city of Jenin," Abu Baker said.
Israeli troops also raided the West Bank city of Nablus, "destroyed five memorials to martyrs in various parts of the city" and arrested scores of residents, deputy mayor Iyad Bakeer told AFP.
Israeli forces routinely demolish the homes of Palestinians accused of carrying out attacks.
Israel says it wants to deter attacks but rights groups accuse Israel of collectively punishing Palestinians' family members.
Violence has soared in the West Bank in the three years since the October 7 attack.
According to the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed 1,113 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war.
Secret CIA assessment warns Israel risks civil war
A secret CIA assessment has warned that Israel could face civil war or state collapse, according to a report by US investigative outlet Drop SiteNews.
The assessment, apparently prepared by the CIA's "Red Cell" unit, found that years of Israel's genocide on Gaza and wars in Lebanon and Iran had deepened political, economic and social divisions within the country.
Washington's "requests and ideas" about Iran's nuclear programme are at odds with Tehran's demands, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday when asked about US Vice President JD Vance's comment that Tehran must cut enrichment to end the war with Washington.
"Vance's comments are Washington's ideas and requests (...) Americans are free to make requests and have ideas, but they are at odds with Iran's demands," the senior Iranian official, who is directly involved in indirect negotiations with the United States, said.
The official added that no negotiations had taken place with the US about Iran's nuclear programme and that Washington must first meet Tehran's conditions before nuclear talks can start.
The official said US recognition of Iran's right to nuclear enrichment is Tehran's red line, which "it will not show flexibility on in any way. However, he added that details of enrichment can be discussed later."
Israeli settlers kill Palestinian in occupied West Bank
A Palestinian man was killed and nine people were injured during an Israeli settler attack followed by army intervention in an occupied West Bank village on Wednesday, according to the mayor and the Palestinian health ministry.
The Palestinian health ministry said 44-year-old Ali al-Bazzari died and nine others were injured "as a result of an assault by occupation forces and settlers" on the village of Burqa, north of Nablus in the northern occupied West Bank.
Who will govern Gaza? The battle over its post-war future
After three years of war, Gaza has no settled political future, with Palestinians sidelined, international efforts stalled, and Israel in full control, writes Mohamed Solaimane.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in Yemen began in recent weeks, according to data released on Wednesday by the United Nations' International Organization for Migration.
IOM described the crisis sparked by renewed fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi group and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen as alarming, with displacement figures surging from 76,000 in mid-September to more than 200,000 as of Wednesday - nearly all of whom fled since fighting began in early September.
Adviser to IRGC: 'illegal routes' in Hormuz to be blocked
Transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz deemed illegal by Iran will soon be closed, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards' Commander told semi-official Fars news agency on Wednesday.
Mohammadreza Naqdi said these few routes had been created by blasting and damaging some of the rocky passages in the strategic waterway and were used by small boats smuggling oil, challenging the dominant narrative that Gulf oil flows through the strait are regaining pre-war levels.
Iran military chief: 7 Oct 'accelerated' Israel's decline
The Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023 has accelerated Israel's decline, the chief of staff for Iran's armed forces said Wednesday, as Israelis marked its third anniversary.
"The Resistance Front turned its defensive strategy into an offensive strategy for the legitimate defence of the Palestinian people and their land, and accelerated the decline of the Zionist regime," Ali Abdollahi said in a statement.
Turkey sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia
Turkey is sending mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia to help it fight Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, two officials said on Wednesday, after the NATO member and Pakistan pledged to act on the collective defence commitment of their newly formed alliance.
Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member constituted an attack on all. They have been working to set the parameters of the new alliance and have held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.
On Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defence commitments and ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a robust defence industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh's technical military needs, and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.
A Turkish official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the support expected from Turkey was only in the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing, and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place as part of the alliance so far.
Israel carried out new strikes in Gaza on Wednesday as it marked the third anniversary of the 7 October Hamas-led attacks, with Palestinian officials reporting three people dead.
In Gaza City, Al-Shifa hospital reported two people killed in an Israeli strike overnight.
Gaza's civil defence identified one of the dead as Mohamed Tamous and said he was a volunteer for the agency, which serves as an emergency rescue service under Hamas.
In the southern city of Khan Yunis, Nasser Hospital said that a 60-year-old man, Hisham Ibrahim Abu Mustafa, was killed in an Israeli strike and that others were injured.
After years of Israeli genocide, Gazans are trapped in exile
Three years after Israel's genocidal war forced tens of thousands of Palestinians out of Gaza, many of those who left remain caught between two lives: one they were forced to abandon and another they never chose.
In Egypt, Turkey and elsewhere, Palestinians from Gaza have rented homes, found work and sent their children to school, slowly building a life in exile.
Iraq's central bank devalued the dinar currency against the dollar on Wednesday, with the country facing a deepening crisis brought on by the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Crude oil sales account for nearly 90 percent of Iraq's revenue but its exports have been hurt by the outbreak in February of the conflict between Iran and the United States, which choked off the Strait of Hormuz shipping route.
Consumer prices have also risen, while Iraq's foreign currency reserves have fallen by around $20 billion.
The central bank said in a statement late Tuesday that based on a government decision, "it had decided to adopt... a selling price of the US dollar to the public of 1,520 dinars".
The rate had been fixed at 1,320 dinars since February 2023.
The bank instructed financial institutions to "stop using the previous rate and adopt the new rate as of the start of the business day on October 7".
Iraq relies heavily on foreign currency generated by oil sales to finance imports, stabilise the dinar, and pay the salaries of public sector employees and retirees.
Iran has 'lost complete control' of Hormuz Strait: Rubio
Iran has "lost complete control" of the Strait of Hormuz, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday, adding that Tehran's economy was "in total and complete freefall".
"There's almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began. So they've lost complete control of the Straits," Rubio said during a visit to Athens.
The Houthis used ballistic and cruise missile drones to attack military facilities and airports in Saudi Arabia, the rebels’ military spokesman, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on social media on Wednesday. He didn’t provide evidence for the claim.
The attacks targeted King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh with missiles, he said.
Flights to and from the airport were disrupted, with planes holding away from the airfield, according to Flightradar24, a tracking platform.
Also attacked were Abha airport, military facilities in Khamis Mushait and other “critical sites” in the cities of Najran and Asir, Saree said.
Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, said they intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the rebels north of Riyadh.
Oil prices rose on Wednesday and stocks fell amid fresh concerns about Middle East supplies following a warning that Iran appeared to be stepping up attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.
The retreat came as investors brushed off another record day on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq and S&P 500 were boosted by a rush back into the AI trade that saw chip titan Nvidia push towards a $6 trillion market capitalisation.
Confidence has been given a boost this week as reports said that exports from the region, excluding Iran, were pushing back towards pre-war levels.
That helped push global benchmark Brent below $100 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate below $90, easing inflation concerns and giving central banks some room to hold off hiking interest rates.
However, both contracts rebounded on Tuesday and rose in early Asian trade, as figures showed Tehran had increased strikes on tankers in the crucial Strait of Hormuz.
UK Maritime Trade Operations said there had been nine attacks so far this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and Persian Gulf combined.
Qatari emir, Iranian interior minister discuss de-escalation
Qatar's emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani met Iran's interior minister Eskandar Momeni in Doha yesterday to discuss regional developments and efforts to de-escalate tensions in the region, the Gulf state's Amiri Diwan announced.
The visit comes amid continued Qatari mediation efforts to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Hezbollah leader: Israel must withdraw before talks
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said the group remains committed to armed resistance while Israeli forces occupies southern Lebanon, in a speech broadcast by the group's Al-Manar TV on Monday.
While commemorating former Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah, Qassem vowed that Israel would eventually be forced to leave southern Lebanon.
He rejected calls for concessions before any Israeli withdrawal, saying there was "nothing we can offer" while Lebanon was "under attack". He said discussions on the state's monopoly on weapons had to take place without "US interference".
IEA to meet over proposed release of oil, diesel reserves
The governing board of the International Energy Agency will hold an informal meeting at 1300 local time on Wednesday to discuss the proposed release of oil and diesel stocks, said two European Union diplomats.
The representatives of EU nations had already discussed this proposed release at a meeting on Wednesday morning, added the diplomats.
Under pressure from US President Donald Trump, the Group of Seven major economies agreed last week to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves and pledged to refrain from energy export restrictions.
However, there has been confusion among those in the oil and energy industry over how many barrels Europe and the US plan to make available to address shortages and record-high prices.
US VP Vance: Iran must cut nuclear enrichment to end war
US Vice President JD Vance said in an exclusive interview with Reuters that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries’ seven-month war, even as Washington was unsure how Tehran makes decisions in negotiations.
Vance, a longtime skeptic of US involvement in foreign wars, has taken a leading role in negotiating a settlement to the conflict and brokered a provisional peace agreement in June that quickly fell apart. The war has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for President Donald Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections.
Speaking on Monday after a campaign trip in Alaska, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns.
"If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance said.
What is 'Bibiwood' and its link with the flydubai incident?
The theories began circulating within hours of the incident aboard flight FZ1073 last Wednesday, ranging from claims that Israeli intelligence orchestrated the attack to suggestions that it never happened at all.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Aden International Airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones early on Wednesday, Yemen's Transport Ministry said, as fighting intensified across several fronts, while the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh.
One missile landed near the airport runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the ministry said. Authorities cancelled the landing and diverted the aircraft to Jeddah, while two planes on the runway were moved away from the area over fears of further strikes, it added. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control.

articles.title: Loyalty vs. Competence: Pete Hegseth’s policies have become the Pentagon's greatest threat
articles.body:
Despite the “strange war” Donald Trump is waging against Iran, the purges at the Pentagon have continued unabated in recent months. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has fired some generals without warning and blocked others from promotion, all while using the Pentagon’s civilian leadership to impose Donald Trump’s political and cultural agenda on the military. Meanwhile, the world’s most powerful fighting force is running short of ammunition, its personnel are exhausted, and its staffing levels have been depleted. Experts say Hegseth has created (or, at the very least, exacerbated) many of these problems himself — focusing more on political issues and the loyalty of his generals than on supplying the military and ensuring the competence of his subordinates.
The blitzkrieg drags on
Criticism of Pete Hegseth had been building for months before some Republicans in Congress finally began challenging the Trump administration’s agenda when it comes to military affairs. Finally, it was Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky who, on Sept. 15, introduced eight articles of impeachment against the defense secretary in the House of Representatives. Three accuse Hegseth of launching the war ing Iran without congressional authorization, while the others concern alleged abuses against civilians, the legality of military operations against drug traffickers and Yemeni Houthis, and the reprisals against Senator Mark Kelly after the Arizona Democrat called on service members to refuse to obey unlawful orders.
Other Republicans, however, secured enough votes to postpone consideration of Massie’s motion until November — after the midterm elections. Congress is likely to take the matter up in the future provided that Democrats gain control of the chamber (as polls currently suggest that they will).
There are ample grounds for criticism of Hegseth. The war launched by the United States and Israel in February was initially intended to swiftly decapitate the leadership in Tehran, resulting in a pro-Western shift. The allies achieved the first objective but not the second: after the old leadership was eliminated, power in Iran consolidated in the hands of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has not been afraid to escalate the conflict.
In September, the war shifted toward oil exports and maritime routes, with the U.S. beginning to strike Iranian oil tankers and Tehran responding with attacks on commercial vessels. Iranian missiles also began striking ever closer to American ships, and shortly after Saudi Arabia asked the United States for military assistance, Iranian attacks damaged a critical overland pipeline that had become an alternative to the waterborne route. Iran-backed Houthis also recently seized footholds in another part of the region’s maritime corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The U.S. administration is now being forced to plan for a long war. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly even warned Trump that Iran could continue resisting until the end of his term — meaning early 2029 — a message that is consistent with what Hegseth is hearing from his own generals. According to the Washington Post, as early as August the military’s top commanders told the Pentagon chief that the war could not continue indefinitely at its current pace given that U.S. Central Command, which oversees the Middle East, has kept more than 50,000 troops on heightened combat readiness for months.
As early as August, the military’s top commanders told Hegseth that the war in Iran could not continue indefinitely at its current pace
Generals are concerned that the operational tempo is increasing, service members are growing exhausted without relief, and rotations may not come until early 2027 (or even later). Meanwhile, stocks of precision-guided weapons are not being replenished.
When the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln recently pulled into port in Thailand after a 286-day deployment – one of the longest in the U.S. Navy's modern history – sailors complained about poor living conditions, a lack of variety in their food, and their deteriorating psychological state. Trump, however, responded that the carrier had been at sea for “not long enough.”
Chief of Naval Operations Daryl Caudle said outright that the Navy could not sustain the current level of operations against Iran with no end date in sight and sailors already stretched to their limits. Even U.S. convoys helping tankers pass through the Strait of Hormuz are now operating on a limited schedule and no longer providing 24-hour air-defense coverage. The United States is, of course, still capable of waging war against Iran, but its problems are mounting — and not only in the Middle East. As forces have been pulled in from other regions, deterrence of other potential U.S. adversaries, above all China and Russia, has weakened, generals warn.
Generals vs. the secretary
The resource shortage is compounded by strained relations between the secretary and the military leadership. For the past year and a half, Hegseth has systematically purged the top brass, removing officers he considers disloyal to his political agenda.
Although the U.S. military is subordinate to civilian political leaders, the armed forces have traditionally enjoyed considerable professional autonomy. The assessments of the Joint Chiefs of Staff have often differed from what politicians wanted to hear, and military leaders themselves handled operational planning and execution, assessed military risks, developed doctrine and standards, and made promotion recommendations.
Trump and Hegseth began “purging” the military leadership almost immediately after the current administration came into office. The president fired Joint Chiefs Chairman Charles Brown, while Hegseth ousted then-Chief of Naval Operations Lisa Franchetti and several other senior commanders — without making any allegations of misconduct against them. Brown later indirectly criticized the administration for politicizing military appointments.
More recently, Hegseth has shifted from firing officers to controlling who gets promoted. He has personally intervened in promotion lists drawn up by the military, removing many officers he considers unacceptable. According to media reports, participation in programs connecting with Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) was among the reasons some officers fell out of favor. In one instance, Hegseth removed all three women and two African American officers from a list of candidates for rear admiral. During the war with Iran, Hegseth also forced Army Chief of Staff Randy George to retire.
For the officers who remain, this inevitably raises the question of where the line now lies between professional assessments of their service and political loyalty. The upheaval in the Army continued when Army Secretary Dan Driscoll left his post in late August. The civilian head of the Army and one of its leading advocates for accelerated modernization, Driscoll was also Hegseth’s biggest rival for influence — and a potential successor as SecDef.
However, the personnel shakeups have not eliminated professional disagreements within the military leadership. As reported by U.S. media, in August the commanders of European Command, Indo-Pacific Command, and Southern Command, along with the Chief of Naval Operations, formally objected to extending the deployments of some forces stationed in their regions.
This was not a refusal to follow orders — which the generals and admirals were still required to carry them out. However, they still made clear that they considered the decision risky. Hegseth has yet to respond, and the dissenting commanders remain in their posts for now.
Where are the weapons, Hegseth?!
Personnel conflicts are only part of the problem. Even setting aside Hegseth’s relationship with the generals and its impact on military readiness, the armed forces simply lack sufficient ammunition and equipment. The U.S. is burning through its expensive weapons far faster than the American defense industry can replenish them. Meanwhile, cheap Iranian drones are creating a stark cost imbalance between offense and defense: Tehran can force the United States and its allies to spend many times more to intercept a drone than it costs to launch one.
According to The Washington Post, the U.S. has already expended 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles used against fortified targets, along with more than 1,000 missiles for Patriot air-defense systems and THAAD interceptors. In addition, CNN has reported that by August the United States had used about half of its prewar stockpile of Patriot missiles and roughly 80% of its THAAD interceptors. The U.S. also lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper heavy drones – about a quarter of its prewar fleet — as the slow, expensive UAVs proved relatively easy targets for Iran and its allies.
The United States has not only reduced its ability to strike, but also left its regional allies without adequate air defenses. They were willing to spend their oil revenues on American systems, but there are no longer enough of the systems to go around. It is hardly surprising that the Gulf monarchies are now turning to Ukraine for technology and expertise in countering cheap drones – the very experience Kyiv has gained through years of war with Russia.
The United States is learning the same lesson. The global drone market was already valued at $20 billion in 2025 and is expected to exceed $50 billion by 2034. The U.S. intends to take a leading position, albeit belatedly, with the Pentagon investing about $1 billion in the Drone Dominance initiative to produce up to 200,000 attack drones by 2027. Young people who until recently competed in drone racing are now winning half-billion-dollar Pentagon contracts to produce “killer drones” costing $5,000 apiece, and a whole new crop of companies is vying for billions of dollars being distributed by the Pentagon.
By 2034, the global drone market is expected to exceed $50 billion, and the United States wants to take a leading position
But once again, the key issue is Hegseth's arbitrary personnel shakeups, which could undermine combat readiness. After Randy George was forced out, the Army’s new leadership disbanded a 600-member experimental battalion that had spent nearly a year specializing in drone warfare — in part by absorbing lessons from Ukraine.
The Pentagon says a dedicated unit is no longer necessary and that drone skills should be spread throughout the Army. But lawmakers from both parties are demanding an explanation for why the experiment is being ended now, during a war in which cheap Iranian drones have become one of the main threats to U.S. forces.
Hegseth did not create the shortage, but he did arrive in the Pentagon promising to revive the defense industry, overhaul the procurement system, and speed up the adoption of new technologies. Instead, innovation is moving slowly — with any actual progress occurring almost in spite of a leadership that is disbanding specialized units. The military’s inability to replenish its losses is increasingly becoming a problem for which Hegseth bears primary responsibility.
Preparing for the last war
It is still too early to say that the personnel policies implemented by Hegseth and Trump have significantly weakened the U.S. armed forces. But warning signs are coming from all directions. The missile shortage, slow production, and strain on the Navy did not begin under Hegseth. As the old saying goes, U.S. generals prepared for the last war.
They were unprepared for a war of attrition against a major adversary like Iran. Hegseth, however, came to the Pentagon promising to “restore combat readiness” but is making the situation worse through personnel that appears to prioritize ideology over effectiveness. The U.S. military, for which Trump has requested a staggering $1.5 trillion defense budget for 2027, is working to address these shortcomings, with the Pentagon drawing up emergency plans to replenish its arsenal. Nevertheless, the political agenda pushed by Hegseth has already cost the military substantial resources and effort, and possibly lives as well.
The Secretary's politics are likely to remain the main obstacle to modernization programs and decisions. In other words, the Pentagon chief himself could become the U.S. military's biggest problem.

articles.title: Sweden Sends Patriot to Poland to Guard Ukraine Aid Hub
articles.body:
Sweden will deploy a Patriot air defense system and approximately 100 troops to southeastern Poland to protect a key NATO logistics hub supplying Ukraine, the Swedish government announced on Tuesday, Oct. 6.
The mission will begin in December and Sweden will deploy its Patriot system as part of a NATO operation, according to the Swedish Armed Forces.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Swedish unit will be stationed in Rzeszów, a major transit point for military equipment and civilian assistance headed to Ukraine. It will operate under NATO Air Command and contribute to the alliance’s Integrated Air and Missile Defense system.
“For the second time, Sweden is participating with Gripen fighter jets in support of NATO’s operation to protect NATO’s logistics hub in Poland. Sweden will also, starting December, provide the Patriot air defence system,” Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said.
“The purpose is to protect the logistics hub and thereby ensure that important materiel reaches Ukraine,” he added.
Sweden’s first NATO Patriot mission
The Patriot system will be operated by personnel from Sweden’s Air Defence Regiment, with support from the Blekinge Air Wing.
The Swedish Armed Forces said the unit would carry out the mission from the beginning of December through the end of 2026. Preparations are also underway to allow the deployment to continue during the first half of 2027.
“As Allies, we share responsibility for protecting and defending NATO territory. At the same time, supporting Ukraine remains a priority for Sweden,” Swedish Army Chief Johan Pekkari said.
How NATO Plans to Win: ‘Theory of Victory’ Against Russia to be Unveiled in Poland
Air Defence Regiment Commander Sofia Westermark said the unit was “well trained, well prepared” and had the personnel needed to complete the mission.
Sweden refers to its Patriot system as Air Defence System 103. It is designed to detect and intercept aircraft, cruise missiles, and certain ballistic missile threats.
Gripens already protecting Polish airspace
The Patriot deployment will reinforce a separate Swedish contribution involving Gripen fighter jets.
Beginning in October, Swedish Gripens joined NATO’s air and missile defense operations over Poland. Most of the aircraft are based in Sweden, while a smaller forward operating base has been established in Poland.
Stockholm said the aircraft would help protect NATO airspace and secure the continued flow of assistance to Ukraine amid repeated violations of allied airspace and other threats connected to Russia’s war.
Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said Russia’s recent attempts to disrupt support for Ukraine had increased the importance of protecting the Polish logistics hub.
“The purpose behind the Swedish contribution is to ensure that military and civilian support reaches Ukraine. This is simultaneously also part of our collective contribution to NATO’s deterrence and defence,” she said.
Poland moves its own Patriots east
Sweden’s announcement comes as Warsaw strengthens air defenses along Poland’s eastern frontier with deployment of its own Patriot batteries to the Lublin region near Ukraine.
The move is part of a broader military buildup that includes new ground units, drone forces, and aviation infrastructure. Polish authorities say the eastern regions face heightened risks because of Russia’s repeated strikes near the border and previous incidents involving missiles and drones entering or approaching Polish airspace.
The Swedish system in Rzeszów will have a more specific mission: shielding the NATO-operated supply route through which weapons, equipment, and humanitarian assistance continue to reach Ukraine.
