articles.title: 25-year-old Natalia, born in Russia, served in the Israeli army, returned to Ukraine during the full-scale invasion, and join the Armed Forces of Ukraine
articles.body:
Natalia is 25 years old and from Odesa. She has served in two armies—the Israeli and Ukrainian militaries. In the Armed Forces of Ukraine, she has, among other things, carried out missions as part of a UAV, FPV drone, and strike-wing crew on the Zaporizhzhia and Kupiansk fronts, NV reported on 5 October.
During the Russo-Ukrainian war, women in Ukraine have the right to voluntarily enlist in the military. As of March, more than 75,000 women were serving in the armed forces, more than 55,000 of them as service members, the commander-in-chief said, and their number has been growing every year. Recently, discussion around the mandatory mobilization of women has intensified. Keith Kellogg, former US Special Presidential Envoy for Ukraine under President Donald Trump, said that he considered mobilizing women in Ukraine appropriate. In response, Iryna Vereshchuk, Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, said she would rather see more missiles and more will from the United States than advice to mobilize women.
In Israel, Natalia served in a search-and-rescue brigade as a rescue soldier and in the engineering corps during a deployment along the northern border.
Natalia was born in Russia’s Saint Petersburg but does not remember her life there
The young woman was born in St. Petersburg, where her family lived at the time. When she was a year and a half old, her mother returned to Odesa with her and her older son. Natalia says she remembers her life exclusively in Ukraine.
She spent the first nearly two years studying at Lviv University, but later decided to leave the university and look for other educational opportunities. Natalia studied, among other places, in Denmark through a scholarship program. After completing it, she planned to enroll at a European university to study sound engineering, but the coronavirus pandemic began at that time.
She moved to Israel under a program for Jewish youth at the end of 2020. After the program ended, due to quarantine restrictions and closed airports, Natalia faced a choice: obtain a work visa or acquire citizenship under the Law of Return. She chose the latter—and with it, she also became obligated to perform military service.
In May 2022, Natalia joined the Israeli military and chose a combat unit.
“When the war started in Israel itself, I still had six months of mandatory service left. I was discharged and immediately transferred to reserve service. Once I managed to resolve all the bureaucratic issues so that this would not be considered desertion, I returned to Ukraine,” the young woman says.
Natalia returned to Ukraine in March 2025, and in August signed a contract with the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
“The army—both Israeli and Ukrainian—gives you a deeper understanding of what society is made of”
Among the advantages of the Ukrainian army, she highlights its ability to quickly adapt to circumstances. In particular, she mentions the use of drones, OSINT, and solving complex technological tasks with minimal resources.
“The West could learn from this situational agility. They often spend huge budgets on developments that should be cheap and mass-produced,” the veteran says.
However, such Ukrainian ingenuity is largely a consequence of a lack of funding, Natalia notes.
In the Israeli military, Natalia highlights society’s readiness for the constant threat of war and more systematic planning of military service.
“There, preparation for and perception of the army begin at school: by the age of 14–15, teenagers already understand where they want to go, what skills they need, and undergo selection for special or intelligence units,” the young woman says.
She then gives the opposite example of the situation in Ukraine.
This Ukrainian female soldier flies one of war’s heaviest drones. She turns down promotion twice to keep doing it
“In Ukraine, with very rare exceptions, people hide until they are mobilized, and suddenly face the reality of conscription without having any understanding of the system,” the veteran says.
Asked how adapted the Ukrainian army is to women, she answered: “In no way,” adding that the Israeli army is “also largely not fully adapted.”
In Ukraine, this is reflected, in particular, in the provision of clothing and equipment that often does not correspond to women’s sizes and physiology. She says she had to purchase her own anatomically fitted body armor. She cited the example of veteran Natalia Lishchyshyna, who had her breasts amputated due to prolonged wearing of body armor that was not adapted to the female anatomy.
In Israel, by contrast, there is a practice of reimbursing expenses for equipment that service members purchase at their own expense.
Serving in the military in both countries provides an opportunity to better understand what society is actually made of, the young woman says.
“The army—both Israeli and Ukrainian—gives you a deeper understanding of what society is made of. You encounter people you would never have crossed paths with in your civilian bubble because of differences in views or socioeconomic circumstances,” Natalia says.
She believes this makes it easier to accept mistakes, difficulties, and new challenges.
The Ukrainian army is not adapted to women in any way, Natalia says
In Natalia’s view, the problem is not only the living and working conditions but, above all, the lack of mechanisms necessary for the systematic mandatory mobilization of women. At the same time, she believes voluntary recruitment should be encouraged and expanded.
One of the problems is the lack of a legal procedure for temporary childcare in cases when both parents are simultaneously carrying out combat missions, Natalia says, stressing that she means the period of their service, rather than situations involving the death of one of the parents.
Another shortcoming is insufficient protection against sexual violence and harassment in the Ukrainian military.
“Here, any complaint goes through the direct chain of command. If the commander is not interested in resolving the problem or is involved in it themselves, the woman is left defenseless,” the veteran says.
In Israel, by contrast, there is a separate hotline and mechanisms for documenting such cases without directly approaching a commander.
Women in combat positions can also still be taken insufficiently seriously, denied participation in combat missions, or transferred to staff positions without their consent.
Natalia also emphasizes the lack of systematic military training for civilian women “at any level” and gives school education as an example.
“Even with the weak level of the school curriculum for the subject ‘Defense of Ukraine,’ boys had at least some basic knowledge. Girls were not involved in it at all,” the veteran says.
For now, Natalia believes that women’s military service should remain voluntary, as society as a whole is still not ready to fully accept women in the military.

articles.title: Europe is in revolt – its leaders are preparing for war
articles.body:
Europe is in revolt – its leaders are preparing for war
Europe’s leaders have grand plans – spend more on weapons, prepare for war, and tighten citizens’ belts. The people have more immediate concerns however, like finding somewhere to live, keeping their jobs, and getting an education. Across France, Germany, Spain, and other EU states, the widening rift has started to spill into the streets.
Recent weeks have seen housing marches across Spain, student riots and public-sector strikes in France, and demonstrations against military recruitment and industrial job cuts in Germany. Immigration has added to the anger over housing and overstretched services, while the prospect of conscription has young Germans asking whose wars they are expected to fight.
The demands differ, but a recurring complaint unites them – aside from those simply looking for an excuse to wreak havoc: governments aren’t listening. Instead of putting domestic problems first, European leaders are telling their constituents to accept less and sacrifice more, while committing billions to preparations for a suicidal war with Russia. That’s despite Moscow and even Europe’s own intelligence services repeatedly saying there is no imminent threat.
Spain: Priced out and fed up
Spain’s housing crisis has pushed tens of thousands into the streets. After years of soaring rents, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of 70 years in Madrid last month turned into a rallying point for those sick of being priced out of their homes and the government’s failure to tackle the housing affordability crisis.
The eviction sparked demonstrations across Spain, followed by mass marches and a continuing protest camp in central Madrid. Parliament’s subsequent rejection of emergency tenant protections added even more fuel to the fire, bringing tens of thousands into the streets in around 50 cities last weekend.
Rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade as immigration-driven population growth has continued to outstrip housing construction. The population, excluding migration, has meanwhile only continued to decline.
The pressure is even more visible in Ceuta, Spain’s North African enclave, where around 72,000 people crossed from Morocco in late July into a territory with roughly 84,000 inhabitants. Although most returned, thousands remained, overwhelming accommodation and straining public services.
Residents have taken to the streets demanding stronger border controls and faster deportations, accusing Madrid of abandoning them. Protests have escalated into clashes with police, while angry locals have torn down makeshift migrant camps.
Government promises to restore order have done little to quell the frustration of communities left to absorb the consequences.
France: School’s out
France has also been gripped by overlapping protests over wages, spending cuts, public services, and school conditions. Teachers, healthcare workers, firefighters and transport staff have joined numerous strikes in recent weeks, while a growing student movement has added school blockades to the disruption.
The school protests began in mid-September, with students demanding more teachers, smaller classes, repairs to neglected buildings, and lighter schedules. Thousands of teaching posts have been eliminated this year, with further cuts planned for next year.
Around 266,000 people joined demonstrations nationwide on Tuesday. More than 6,500 have been arrested over three weeks, while hundreds of students and police officers have been injured, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand to a police grenade and a 16-year-old who reportedly lost sight in one eye after being hit by a rubber bullet.
As the movement has grown, violent groups have joined the protests, torching buses, attacking emergency workers, and damaging schools. Across France, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked.
Similar demonstrations have spread to neighboring Belgium, where students have opposed education reforms, higher transport costs, and rising tuition fees. In Liege, school blockades have been accompanied by vandalism, fires and arrests.
France: The cuts keep coming
The student demonstrations came on the heels of wider protests that have gripped France for weeks, with public-sector workers protesting a squeeze on wages and services, compounded by soaring fuel prices.
Since 2017, public-sector pay has risen by 5%, while cumulative inflation has reached 24%. The government’s proposed €54 billion ($60.4 billion) budget package, which includes spending cuts and freezes affecting pensions and benefits, has only deepened the anger.
Other demonstrations have also challenged continued funding for Ukraine, with protesters arguing that the money should go toward hospitals, education, and lower fuel taxes.
Separate rallies in more than 20 cities have also opposed a bill that could give police shootings the presumption of legality, which critics say would make officers harder to hold accountable.
Germany: Factories shrink, the military grows
In Germany, workers and students have taken to the streets as Berlin pursues a frenzied military buildup in the midst of a deepening industrial crisis with hundreds of thousands losing their livelihoods and young men facing the prospect of being drafted.
Around 45,000 students joined protests in some 100 cities and towns in late September, carrying banners reading ‘We won’t fight in your wars’ and ‘Education instead of bombs’.
The government meanwhile is pressing ahead with plans to expand the armed forces to more than 260,000 active troops and 200,000 reservists by 2035 to align with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s fixation on creating “Europe’s strongest conventional army.”
Young men are already required to register for potential service, but politicians have been pushing for a return to conscription if voluntary recruitment fails to fill the ranks.
Aside from the thousands protesting such plans in the streets, resistance is also showing up in applications to avoid military service. More than 12,000 people sought conscientious objector status in the first eight months of this year – over three times the total for all of last year.
Tens of thousands of automotive workers have also protested sweeping job cuts and threats to factories. Volkswagen, for example, plans to shed 100,000 jobs across its brands, while other manufacturers are cutting production or moving it abroad.
Germany’s industrial woes have been further compounded by the loss of cheap Russian energy, which helped make its manufacturers competitive. Higher energy costs, US tariffs, and Chinese competition are now squeezing businesses and threatening jobs across the sector.
For arms manufacturers, however, Berlin’s priorities and its latest €108.2 billion defense budget have been good for business. While Volkswagen shares have fallen more than 75% from their 2021 peak, Rheinmetall’s have soared over 1,100% since early 2022. One Volkswagen factory is even set to shift toward producing military equipment for an Israeli arms company.
More guns and more fear
Even with streets burning and protesters demanding relief, European leaders have not let the turmoil distract them from their military ambitions.
In France, Macron marked Tuesday’s mass demonstrations by publicizing a nuclear missile test, posting a photograph of himself watching the launch with his back to the camera. While his constituents marched for better living conditions, his message was that France “must be feared to remain free.”
In Germany, Merz and NATO chief Mark Rutte smiled and waved through boos and chants of “murderers” and “blood on your hands” after the military bloc received the Westphalian Peace Prize last week. Inside the ceremony, officials praised military strength as the foundation of peace.
Those priorities are also taking shape in Brussels’ budget negotiations. Germany and five other EU states have demanded cuts to the bloc’s next budget, pushing to sacrifice funding for farmers and poorer regions in favor of ever-growing military spending.
The urgency is being justified by the supposed threat of a future Russian attack. However, Moscow has repeatedly denied any such plans, while even Finland’s president has admitted that his intelligence services see no imminent military threat.
Nevertheless, for European leaders, preparations for that hypothetical conflict, which they appear to almost count on, continue to take precedence over the mounting problems already bringing people out onto the streets.

articles.title: 5 Ballistic Missiles, 117 Drones: Ukraine Repels Massive Russian Overnight Attack
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Air Force said its forces intercepted or suppressed 161 Russian aerial targets during a massive overnight attack, including five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles, and 117 attack drones.
As per the report on Telegram, Russia launched the combined attack from 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 6, using ballistic, cruise, and anti-ship missiles, alongside 130 strike drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Among the ballistic weapons used were Russian Iskander-M, S-400 and North Korean KN-23 missiles, as well as Zircon and Onyx missiles.
Ukraine’s air defenses shot down or suppressed five ballistic missiles, marking a significant interception of weapons that are generally more difficult to counter than cruise missiles and drones.
The Air Force said it also intercepted 39 cruise missiles, including Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kalibr missiles. Information on another six cruise missiles was still being verified as of 9 a.m.
Ukrainian forces additionally shot down or suppressed 117 attack drones, including 38 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, as well as Gerbera and other unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
Russia launched the attack from multiple directions, including the Rostov, Bryansk, and Voronezh regions, the Caspian Sea, and occupied areas of the Donetsk region and Crimea. The primary targets were the Kyiv, Kharkiv, Poltava, and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
The attack involved Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare, and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups, the Air Force said.
UN Rights Council Extends Probe Into Russia’s Abuses Despite Moscow’s Opposition
Despite the reported interceptions, Russian missiles and attack drones struck 18 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at five locations.
The latest Air Force figures came as Ukrainian authorities reported casualties and damage in several regions following the overnight attack.
Russia launched a massive overnight missile and drone attack across Ukraine, killing at least 15 people as of 12:27 p.m. and damaging residential buildings and civilian infrastructure in several cities.
Kyiv was attacked with ballistic missiles in several waves, with the first salvo launched shortly after 3 a.m. Two people were killed in the capital, while impacts were recorded in four districts.
Kremenchuk in the Poltava region was also heavily hit, with Russian missiles striking a residential area and damaging apartment buildings and private homes. Two people were killed, according to preliminary information from the regional authorities. An industrial facility in the area was also struck.
In Pryluky, Chernihiv region, a Russian missile hit a five-story apartment building, severely damaging the structure and causing a large section to collapse. Emergency crews were searching the rubble for residents, with nine fatalities reported.
Strikes were also reported against industrial or civilian infrastructure in Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia, while Oleksandriia in the Kirovohrad region reported damage to critical infrastructure. Two people were killed in Oleksandriia, while contact was temporarily lost with two others, according to Mayor Serhiy Kuzmenko.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: What to use to shoot down jet-powered drones: experts explain how Ukraine is adapting weapons to new threats
articles.body:
What to use to shoot down jet-powered drones: experts explain how Ukraine is adapting weapons to new threats
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian defense companies are increasingly adapting weapons that have already been developed to new tasks instead of developing systems from scratch. Experts explained why the speed of such modifications is critical in the war against Russia.
Ukrainian defense companies operate in a low-profile mode and are in no hurry to say what weapons and modifications they are developing. New solutions often become known only at the testing or deployment stage. One such project could be a new configuration of the FP-1/FP-2, which Quantum WIY Industries presented as part of the cooperation between Quantum Systems and Fire Point. What this could offer Ukraine and why the ability to quickly modify existing weapons is critical in the technological race with russia was examined by UNN.
Details
Most Ukrainian defense companies operate under an extremely high level of secrecy. On the one hand, this is connected with the need not to provide information to the enemy so that it does not have time to develop countermeasures… Therefore, when information about a development that had never previously been publicly announced suddenly appears, this does not mean that it literally emerged yesterday. Companies often work in parallel on a large number of different projects, some of which never reach serial production
Concept of a possible FP-1/FP-2 modification with eight SPYS interceptor drones. Image taken from the Drone Wars X account.
In the case of the FP-1/FP-2 modification, the concept involves placing four SPYS interceptor drones under each wing of the unmanned aerial vehicle—eight in total. The main advantage of this configuration is the ability to launch the interceptors from the air.
Under the concept, the FP-1/FP-2 could deliver the SPYS drones to the required area and altitude without using up the interceptors’ own resources flying from a ground launch point. Aviation expert Valeriy Romanenko explains that this approach would expand the area in which the interceptors can be used.
As for the concept under which the FP-1 and FP-2 could serve as carriers for interceptor drones and launch up to eight interceptors against jet-powered drones, it is generally interesting. Why? First, because it sharply increases the operational range of such drones. They do not need to expend fuel climbing and flying over a fairly long distance. Essentially, the airborne platform lifts them to a considerable altitude
Interception of the "Geran-5"
It should be noted that during the presentation of the SPYS interceptor in July, WIY Drones stated that it was capable of hitting targets moving at speeds of up to 600 km/h. To this end, the company worked, among other things, on a head-on interception algorithm. In September, the first confirmed use of SPYS against the Russian jet-powered strike drone "Geran-5" emerged.
Interception of the Russian jet-powered UAV "Geran-5" by a SPYS drone. Video: WIY Drones.
This Russian jet-powered UAV has become a new threat to Ukrainian cities: it is significantly faster than earlier modifications of the "Geran," making it more difficult to intercept. The "Geran-5" has a tubular fuselage and, in terms of its characteristics, already more closely resembles a cheap cruise missile than a classic long-range drone, said Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Defence Research Establishment.
As a senior engineer at one of the defense companies told The Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, the "Geran-5" flies approximately 150 km/h faster than the jet-powered "Geran-4." This also changes the very logic of interception: instead of chasing the target from behind, the interceptor must be brought toward it head-on, which significantly complicates the task.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the "Geran-5" can carry a warhead weighing approximately 90 kg. The Chinese turbojet engine for such a drone is estimated to cost approximately $40,000, while the entire aircraft costs about $115,000. By comparison, older piston-powered modifications could cost around $30,000.
At the same time, Russia is rapidly scaling up its use of jet-powered drones. Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Air Force Command, notes that on some days, jet-powered drones may account for up to two-thirds of all drones launched by Russia. Production volumes are also growing—the enemy is already capable of producing around 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month.
The problem for Ukraine lies in the difficulty of intercepting them. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine is currently shooting down around 57% of jet-powered attack drones, calling this figure “significantly lower than necessary.” That is why finding new means of countering such targets is now becoming one of the key tasks for Ukraine’s defense industry.
“We are already seeing information that at least five manufacturers have proposed their solutions for countering jet-powered attack drones. At least 50 more Ukrainian companies are developing solutions to counter such targets. But if we are talking specifically about mass deployment, we will probably not see it any earlier than another three to four months from now. After the development stage, time is needed to scale up production, train personnel and, among other things, select appropriate tactics for their use,”
However, even after effective countermeasures against jet-powered drones emerge, the technological race will not stop: Ukraine will find a way to shoot them down, while Russia, in response, will try to improve its weapons once again.
“This means that, likewise, once interceptors have been developed and the percentage of jet-powered drones shot down reaches approximately 90–95%, we will see the enemy very quickly try to improve its solution. We are talking about several months. We will see the next stage in terms of speed. In other words, it will no longer be 400–650 km/h, but probably 750–800, perhaps even 900 km/h, which is, in principle, comparable to the speed of conventional cruise missiles,”
In fact, this concerns the ongoing evolution of systems that have already been created: a platform initially developed for one task can perform new functions as the adversary changes. In conditions where new means of attack and countermeasures against them emerge at intervals of several months, the ability to rapidly modernize existing weapons is a key condition for not losing the technological race to the enemy.
“I believe that Fire Point is demonstrating a very sound approach in this case—not simply creating a separate drone for each task, but using existing platforms and seeking new ways to employ them. This makes it possible to adapt more quickly to changes in the battlefield situation,”

articles.title: German radar already guarding Ukraine is picked to spot ballistic missiles. Its maker just signed a new deal with Kyiv
articles.body:
German radar maker Hensoldt has signed a memorandum with Ukraine's Defense Ministry for more large-scale radar deliveries, the company said on 5 October. Ukrainian defense outlet Defense Express reads it as a step toward fitting Hensoldt's TRML-4D, already in Ukrainian service, into FREYJA, a planned shield against ballistic missiles.
Ballistic missiles remain the hardest threat in Russia's air war. After Russia's overnight barrage on 7 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine is still searching daily for Patriot missiles. The only other system Ukraine can use against them is the Franco-Italian SAMP/T, which fires Aster 30 interceptors made in small numbers. That gap is why Fire Point is reworking its FP-7 missile into a Patriot-like interceptor. Such an interceptor still needs radars to find its target first.
A memorandum signed during Merz's visit
Hensoldt CEO Oliver Dörre signed the document on the sidelines of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's visit to Ukraine. Beyond deliveries, it covers further development of radar capabilities. The partners will also study options to deploy and jointly operate TRL-4D LR long-range radars. Hensoldt said this expands cooperation already agreed on in ballistic missile defense.
Russia’s air defenses can’t protect all its strategic sites once Ukraine’s ballistic missiles are ready, expert says
The TRL-4D LR is the land-based version of a long-range radar Hensoldt also builds for the German Navy, German outlet Sicherheit & Verteidigung reported. The outlet cited Germany's defense procurement office as giving the naval version a range of more than 400 km (250 miles) against air targets. That, it concluded, puts the range well beyond the TRML-4D's.
"The Ukrainian air defence forces urgently need our high-performance radars to help protect infrastructure such as bridges," Dörre said.
Defense Express, describing the same memorandum, tied both the mass deliveries and the joint-operation plan to the TRML-4D. Hensoldt's release names no model for the deliveries and links joint operation to the TRL-4D LR.
Eyes for FREYJA
Hensoldt and Fire Point signed a memorandum on FREYJA at the Eurosatory arms show in Paris in June, with the TRML-4D to play a key role, Hensoldt announced. Fire Point is set to act as prime contractor and hold design authority. Hensoldt is to produce, test, and deliver the radars.
Germany’s Hensoldt to supply Ukraine with six more TRML-4D radars to boost air defense capabilities
Defense Express expects any study of deployment options to focus on how well the radar detects ballistic missiles and relays that data. Hensoldt has its own unit in Ukraine to work closely with operators, the outlet noted. Earlier, the company began setting up a local hub so Ukraine can service and repair the TRML-4D itself.
Already on duty
Ukraine's military uses the TRML-4D both standalone and as the built-in radar of the IRIS-T SLM medium-range air defense system, Defense Express noted. Hensoldt lists an instrumented range of 250 km (155 miles) at altitudes up to 30 km (19 miles). Defense Express, citing the manufacturer, gives track ranges of more than 120 km (75 miles) for fighter jets and more than 60 km (37 miles) for supersonic missiles.
More radars give earlier warning of ballistic strikes, but they cannot stop them. Until the FP-7.X makes its first ballistic intercept, planned for mid-2027, that job stays with Patriot and SAMP/T missiles. Partners delivered three times fewer air defense missiles in the first half of 2026 than a year earlier, Zelenskyy said on 5 August.
Read also
- Turkey’s Korkut guns now shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine. Almost half of the jet-powered Shaheds still get through
- Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds: a small new missile named Nika, heading into testing
- Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January

articles.title: In war-torn Kyiv, Elkin-led Israeli delegation confronts familiar threats while marking Babyn Yar
articles.body:
To the Israeli delegation visiting the Ukrainian capital this week, the sound of sirens warning of incoming drones or missiles was familiar. But one important difference: Ukraine has no Iron Dome, no multilayered Israeli-style air defense system that can provide the same sense of protection as back home. When the alerts sound, people simply head underground and wait.
That was how Tuesday night unfolded for former minister Kharkiv-born Ze'ev Elkin and members of an Israeli delegation visiting Kyiv this week.
As ballistic missiles and drones targeted the Ukrainian capital, the delegation eventually spent the night together in a makeshift shelter arranged by the Israeli Embassy at their hotel, sleeping on beds placed side-by-side inside the protected room.
Elkin and the delegation had arrived in Ukraine for the 85th anniversary of the Babyn Yar massacre, when Nazi forces and their collaborators murdered tens of thousands of Jews in a ravine outside Kyiv in September 1941.
Ukraine today is fighting a war that has entered another dangerous and uncertain phase. Russian forces continue to attack Ukrainian cities, while Ukrainian forces have demonstrated an increasing ability to strike targets deep inside Russia.
The deterioration in the security situation prompted several international delegations expected to attend the Babyn Yar commemorations to cancel their visits. Among the senior-level delegations that did arrive were those from Israel and Germany.
Elkin was part of Israeli delegation, including Yad Vashem officials, to attend Babyn Yar memorial
The Israeli delegation included Elkin, Yad Vashem Chairman Dani Dayan, Yad Vashem representatives, and senior officials involved in Israel’s relations with Ukraine.
The symbolism was striking: a ceremony dedicated to remembering one of the darkest chapters in European history taking place while the same continent is once again experiencing a major war.
The most significant political meeting came unexpectedly. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky invited Elkin and the delegation to meet with him after learning that the Israeli minister was in Kyiv. The two discussed the war, the regional situation, and the strategic calculations surrounding Israel, Ukraine, and the United States.
Zelensky was particularly interested in Israel’s assessment of developments involving Iran and the broader Middle East.
Ultimately, both Israel and Ukraine understand that, as cooperation between Russia and Iran grows, what happens in Kyiv can eventually reach Jerusalem.
According to multiple reports, Iranian and Russian facilities are operating jointly inside Russia, where the two countries are upgrading their drones – with Iran receiving some of the drones.
Zelensky warned the Israeli delegation that the drones Iran is developing together with Russia today, combined with the operational experience the two countries are gaining, could eventually become a threat Israel will have to confront.
Beyond his meeting with Zelensky, Elkin met with senior Ukrainian government officials, including the speaker of the parliament and the minister responsible for rebuilding the country’s infrastructure following the war – a role that parallels Elkin’s own responsibilities for the reconstruction of Israel’s North and South.
Elkin, Israeli delegation held memorial for October 7 victims
Together with the Jewish community in Ukraine and the Israeli Embassy, Elkin and the delegation also held a memorial ceremony for the victims of the October 7 massacre.
The message from the Ukrainians in their meetings was clear: They want to see improved relations.
The central question hanging over Kyiv is whether the war is moving toward a negotiated settlement or another escalation.
Ukrainian attacks have increasingly reached targets inside Russian territory, changing a dynamic in which the fighting was largely concentrated inside Ukraine. At the same time, Russian forces have struggled to achieve rapid breakthroughs along the front.
That combination creates a dangerous incentive for Moscow to search for a new way to alter the balance.
The most difficult issue in any potential negotiations remains the Donbas.
Russia wants Ukraine to withdraw from the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in Donetsk Oblast, effectively demanding that Kyiv abandon positions that Ukrainian forces have defended since the war that began in 2014.
For Ukraine, the problem is not simply political.
The Donbas contains a defensive system built over more than a decade. Ukrainian forces have spent years constructing fortifications and positions there, and Russia’s slow progress demonstrates how difficult those defenses are to overcome.
Giving them up would mean more than surrendering territory. It would mean moving the defensive line westward and creating a new strategic vulnerability.
That is why the issue has become one of the hardest obstacles to any potential agreement.
Elkin's visit carried unavoidable symbolism.
At Babyn Yar, Elkin delivered his remarks in Ukrainian – a gesture that attracted attention in a country where language and identity have themselves become part of the struggle with Russia.
During their meeting, Zelensky highlighted Elkin’s command of Ukrainian, joking that his grammar and pronunciation were better than those of some Ukrainian ministers.
The Babyn Yar ceremony was intended to remember a catastrophe that took place 85 years ago. Yet in today’s Kyiv, remembrance and reality are impossible to separate.

articles.title: Oleksandr, Kyrylo and Serhii, all aged one, and eight-year-old Maksym were killed in Ukraine’s city by Russian strike on Putin’s birthday
articles.body:
Ukrainian rescuers are still pulling bodies from a collapsed apartment block in Pryluky. A Russian missile strike on the five-story residential building in the city of Chernihiv Oblast that borders both Russia and Belarus killed 19 people, including five children, and injured 55, Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported on 7 October.
Russia hit Kyiv and a dozen other regions overnight. Air defense downed five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles, and 117 drones, while missiles and drones hit 18 locations, the Air Force said. The nationwide strike killed at least 24 people, including four children.
Among the dead in Pryluky were three one-year-old boys, Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhii, and eight-year-old Maksym, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says. Seven of the injured are children. Some residents are still unreachable, and all emergency services are working at the site. Russia keeps using missiles against Ukrainian cities and civilians by deliberate choice, he states.
"My condolences to all the families and loved ones," Zelenskyy says.
The strike comes on Putin's birthday
The attack came on Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday on 7 October.
"Continuing to use missiles against Ukraine, against our people, our children, is an absolutely conscious choice of terror. This is what Moscow chooses despite all our efforts with partners to bring peace closer," Zelenskyy says.
He urges partners to increase pressure on Russia and bolster defense support for Ukraine, saying it is important that world leaders understand this and that the world not remain silent.
A pattern of strikes on Chernihiv Oblast
Pryluky, about 150 kilometers east of Kyiv, lies in a region Russia has hit repeatedly. The overnight barrage also damaged civilian and utility infrastructure across the Pryluky community, the city council said.
Ukraine had seen the attack. The day before, Zelenskyy warned that intelligence indicated a massive Russian strike was in preparation. Russia fired about 70 missiles overnight, killing two people each in the capital Kyiv and in the cities of Kremenchuk and Oleksandriia in addition to the Pryluky dead.
Read also
