- Ukraine’s drone pilot calls it his proudest strike: cheap FPV drone detonating over two tons of explosives packed inside Russian mine-clearer

articles.title: Syria weighs military aid for Saudi Arabia amid Yemen war, sources say
articles.body:
Syria weighs military aid for Saudi Arabia amid Yemen war, sources say
RIYADH, Oct 7 - Syria is carefully considering providing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia amid an escalating war against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, a US official and a Syrian military official briefed on the matter said.
Options being considered include defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis, the sources said.
The US official said Saudi Arabia had requested that Syria deploy forces to fight the Houthis.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's civil war.
"Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement.
The Saudi government media office and Yemen's information minister did not respond to requests for comment.
Saudi Arabia has been requesting assistance far and wide, from the US to Europe and the Middle East, for both defensive and offensive support in a renewed war against the group that follows weeks of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the kingdom.
The war is being led on the ground by a patchwork of Yemeni government forces with Saudi air support. They have made limited advances since the campaign was launched on Monday.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa made a public visit to Riyadh on Tuesday and met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, also known as MbS. He discussed potential Syrian military assistance for the kingdom, among other matters, the US official said.
Footage broadcast by Syrian state media showed that he was escorted back to his plane by Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, a brother of the crown prince who has overseen the Yemen file.
DEPLOYMENT COULD DEEPEN TENSIONS WITH NEIGHBOURS
Syrian fighters from opposition groups that battled former leader Bashar al-Assad in the country's civil war have in past years been recruited as mercenaries for other conflicts, notably Libya's internal conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war.
But for Damascus, any potential deployment carries risks.
The militias that made up the armed opposition are now under the nascent Syrian state, which has adopted a policy of avoiding engagement in conflict, including the Iran war, to focus on recovery from the 14-year Syrian civil war.
The state is still piecing together its army from the various militia groups from the former rebel coalition that toppled Assad, which included many hardline Sunni Islamist and foreign fighters, and trying to contain tensions with minorities including the Alawites, a Shi'ite offshoot to which Assad belonged.
A conflict between that army and the Houthis, who are also adherents of an offshoot of Shi'ite Islam, could have divisive religious undertones that the Syrian leadership and its Western partners want to avoid, the US official said.
It is for this reason that it previously rejected a US request to help fight Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Involvement in a battle against the Iran-backed Houthis could also be viewed as a hostile act by Iran and its allies Hezbollah in Lebanon and militias in Iraq, with which the Syrian rebels-turned-rulers have a history of conflict.
KEEN TO SHOW SUPPORT
At the same time, Sharaa is keen to show the country's support for Saudi Arabia and MbS, who played a decisive role helping the former jihadist gain international legitimacy, including by brokering a May 2025 meeting between Sharaa and US President Donald Trump.
Saudi Arabia has also provided financial assistance to Syria and a Syrian show of support could result in that increasing, the US official said.
"A new Syria sending defensive personnel of a very small number to the most holy places in the Islamic world, alongside technical support to neutralise incoming drones, would be tremendously and positively symbolic," said H.A. Hellyer, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London.
"But anything beyond, particularly in terms of Syrian boots on the ground, I think would be a wholly different proposition, and one I think Damascus would avoid, given the priorities they need to focus on in Syria," he said. REUTERS

articles.title: Three years since October 7: Israelis tell Meduza how the worst terrorist attack in their country’s history changed them and the world around them
articles.body:
Three years since October 7: Israelis tell Meduza how the worst terrorist attack in their country’s history changed them and the world around them
The Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, was one of the most horrific events in recent world history. Ahead of its third anniversary, Meduza spoke with residents of Israel, where the terrorist attack touched everyone. Eight people from cities across the country described what happened to them in those days and how they and the world around them have changed since.
Warning: This article contains profanity.
Exactly three years ago, on October 7, 2023, some 3,000 militants from the Palestinian terrorist movement Hamas attacked Israel and took 251 people hostage. About 1,200 other civilians, including 38 children, were killed; more than 350 of them were at the Nova music festival. Some were tortured, others burned alive. The militants also raped a large number of women — Israeli human rights advocates believe this was a deliberate Hamas strategy.
In response to October 7, Israel launched an operation in the Gaza Strip. Tens of thousands of people have died. Hamas has been defeated but still exists. The operation has drawn international criticism and has been accompanied by a rise in anti-Israel and antisemitic sentiment. During the operation, Israel freed 166 hostages. Another 85 died.
Yeva Broyde-Zaitsev, 37, ceramics shop owner and Hebrew teacher, Tel Aviv
In Russia, I worked in the archives of an art college and played in a band. I left Russia 10 years ago through the repatriation program. Russia had already seized Crimea, things were looking ominous, and I wasn’t expecting anything good.
At first, I didn’t think I’d stay in Israel: I planned to get Israeli citizenship and a darkon — an Israeli passport. Then I saw how much more people value human life here, how they respect individual freedom. My friends in Russia started scattering around the world, and in the end, I had no reason left to go back.
Throughout Israel’s history, there’s always been some fucked-up shit happening, terrorist attacks every year. But that happened in Moscow too. Whenever people asked whether I was scared of being blown up, I’d always say that if you’re going to get blown up, it might as well happen by the sea. So moving to Israel didn’t scare me. I think you face far more dangers every day in Moscow than you do in Israel. Here, I’m not afraid that someone passing by will give me grief about how I look or get aggressive. People are much friendlier here.
Before October 7, I didn’t have a feeling that something bad was going to happen. Or rather, this is the Middle East — you can have that feeling every day.
I was looking forward to my birthday on October 12. My friends and I were planning to fly to London and have a fucking amazing celebration. We ended up having to celebrate in a bomb shelter. Lots of people came, even though getting to my place was dangerous. We kept getting bombed, and we got horribly drunk because there was so much stress and terror, and we needed to let it out.
My husband serves in the military’s medical corps. When the siren went off early on October 7, he didn’t even wake up. That morning, I told him this whole nightmare had begun, and he reassured me that if things were really bad, he’d have been called up.
That happened the next day.
Several of my friends died at the Nova festival, where Hamas massacred people and took hostages. I spent the first few days with a friend. We just sobbed.
Whenever I was home alone, I’d sit there with a knife. I thought that if a terrorist broke in, of course I wouldn’t be able to fight him off. The knife was so I wouldn’t be taken captive: I was prepared to kill myself. That would have been much more peaceful than the endless suffering of being a hostage.
From the start of the attack, I also had this strange feeling… Relief, in a way. When Russia attacked Ukraine, I felt guilty because I’m from Russia, and my country had attacked another country. Here, we weren’t the ones attacking — we were being attacked. Finally, we weren’t the bad guys. But then [after the war in the Gaza Strip began], Israelis faced even more hatred than Russians.
In November, a friend in Berlin invited me and a mutual friend to stay with him. He said: Come over, just take a breather. Here, you won’t have to run to a bomb shelter 10 times a day.
We flew to Berlin, walked around the city a lot, and kept coming across pro-Palestinian flyers everywhere. The most progressive neighborhoods in Berlin were plastered with Free Palestine imagery. On one wall, there were photographs of Israeli hostages, and every one of them had nasty things written and drawn all over it.
How is that possible? To me, it’s just the usual barbaric attitude. “We’re so good and innocent, and those Israelis are killing Palestinian babies and deserve to have Hamas take them all captive.” “We can afford to forget that we do terrible things ourselves.” Meduza itself writes a lot whenever Israelis destroy something in Gaza, but not when Hamas destroys something in Israel and people are killed.
Anyway, my friend and I stayed in Berlin for a week and left because it was emotionally hard.
Since October 7, almost every time I meet people in other countries, I have to watch what I say. Because plenty of people take pleasure in hating Israelis. It’s easy to feel virtuous when you say you support everything good and oppose everything evil.
If someone near me starts talking about Palestine, I jump right into the conversation. I feel responsible because there’s so much people don’t know. They don’t know that Hamas literally governs Gaza, that it really is under Sharia law, or how extensive Hamas’s network of tunnels beneath civilian sites in Gaza is. Or that if Hamas had let ordinary Gazans shelter in those tunnels, there would have been far fewer casualties.
I feel I need to share my experience and tell people about Israel. I try to do that without downplaying Palestinians’ suffering.
We have to remember that we’re all human, and you can’t hate someone simply because they belong to a particular social group.
But I want the world to know that rockets landed near my home, that my friends no longer have a home, that people I loved were killed at a music festival — and in this war in general. And how many of us have suffered? All of us — every single one.
Tatyana Konev, 59, marketing specialist, Karmiel
I’ve been in Israel for 30 years — my husband and I came here in 1995. We were born and raised in Donetsk.
The war after October 7 isn’t our first war in Israel. There was the Second Lebanon War in 2006. It was very frightening because we had two small children, and my husband kept getting called up for military training, though he wasn’t sent to the front.
On October 8, this new war reached the next generation: My son got a call-up notice. It came while he was at work, and I packed his backpack while he was on his way home. Then my husband drove him to his military unit.
A couple of hours later, they came back. It turned out that 20% more people had reported for duty than the unit needed because some had shown up without call-up notices. They let my son go because they didn’t need that many people, and he worked at an important medical equipment manufacturer.
I don’t know what would have happened if my son had stayed with the unit. Its soldiers cleared mines from tunnels in Gaza. So many of them died.
In Israel, war is always close by. There’s an old saying here that our children won’t have to fight. Meaning that any day now, the wars will end. But children and grandchildren have been fighting for generations.
October 7 was Shabbat and the holiday of Simchat Torah — “Rejoicing in the Torah.” Religious families had their phones and televisions, all their means of communication, switched off that day. They didn’t know what had happened. October 2023 also marked 50 years since the start of the Yom Kippur War. I kept saying that Israel’s enemies would want to mark the occasion.
I know a family whose kibbutz was invaded by militants. The family hid in a bomb shelter and stayed there for 28 hours. The militants took over their house. The Israeli army came to liberate the kibbutz, and the militants fired back from inside the family’s house. When the family came out of the bomb shelter, their house was covered in blood.
That day turned many Israelis’ worldview upside down. People in the kibbutzim in the south were mostly very left-wing. I often argued with them about left-wing ideas and told them about my life in the Soviet Union. Left-wing people here couldn’t believe things like that could happen under socialism — to them, it was the ideal.
A lot of people on the left thought that if we helped the people of Gaza, they’d warm to us. October 7 showed how badly that idea failed. A colleague of mine called herself a “proud leftist,” and after October 7, she wrote that she’d lost faith in her ideals.
Some people moved further right, others turned to religion. Israelis generally started looking at life differently. So many times before bed, I’ve thought: “Here I am, going to sleep in my own bed. Tomorrow I’ll get up and have coffee. What’s it like to be a hostage underground? To spend a year or two like that, with almost no food or water, under constant threat of violence?”
One of my colleagues served in the army in a role we call the “knock on the door.” When a soldier’s death is confirmed, someone assigned to that task goes to their family to tell them what happened. For two years after the war began, my colleague was hardly ever in the office. She had so many doors to knock on.
And even after all the hostages were released, my colleague was still making lots of visits to people’s homes. We asked her why. She said not all hostages and soldiers are mentally well when they return to civilian life. People can’t cope with what happened and take their own lives.
For example, last year, a young man whose girlfriend had been killed right in front of him at the Nova music festival took his own life.
Another colleague of mine lost his daughter. I’d drawn cards for her bat mitzvah, and then the girl was gone, killed in combat on October 7 or 8.
Now, every morning, I thank God that my house hasn’t been bombed and my children are alive.
Boris Voitsekhovsky, 53, artist, cook, and former journalist, Haifa
In November 2022, my wife and I moved from Moscow to Haifa through the repatriation program because of the mobilization. We’d never been to Israel before. When I left, I had a remote job as the managing editor of Moslenta, but I quit after moving. Now I write children’s books, cook food to order, and paint — a whole range of things.
There was a blizzard in Moscow that November. We were freezing at the airport, and then we arrived in Haifa: warmth, sunshine, palm trees. Beautiful. It was a strange contrast. For the first year, it felt like some kind of extended vacation. There was a forest near our apartment, and we could get to the sea in 20 minutes by bus. We really relaxed and didn’t feel any danger.
That’s pretty much how the whole year before October 7 went: meeting friends, grilling kebabs, drinking wine by the sea. In time, I realized Haifa reminded me of Sukhumi, the largest city in Abkhazia, where I used to spend vacations as a child. Even the smells are the same — the same flowers grow there.
Of course, we understood that terrorist attacks happen regularly in Israel: Someone shoots at a car somewhere, someone gets stabbed. But we saw them all as isolated incidents. There was no sense that trouble was brewing.
On October 7, I was alone in Haifa. My wife had flown to Moscow to see her parents. I was planning to go to a friend’s birthday party. I woke up and read the news. At first, I thought: All sorts of things happen in Israel. Give it a day or two, and it’ll be over. Then reports started coming in that huge numbers of people had been killed, both at the festival and in the kibbutzim…
It seemed like it wouldn’t affect us because Haifa is in northern Israel, and the main events happened in the south, on the border with Gaza. So I went to the birthday party, and my wife flew back the next day.
Toward nightfall, we started hearing explosions. It wasn’t clear exactly what was happening, but it was clearly nothing good.
We started getting daily warnings about the risk of rocket attacks. A special app sent us instructions on what to do if an alarm went off. First, you’re supposed to go into a mamad — a reinforced room in your apartment. But our building is old, and we don’t have one. The instructions say that if you don’t have a room like that, go to the basement; if there’s no basement, go to the stairwell; if there’s no stairwell, stay in a room without windows. We don’t have a basement. We live on the second floor of a two-story building, and the stairs lead straight from the street into our apartment. We even have windows in the bathroom. Basically, as unsafe as it gets.
So every time, my wife and I ran to the stairwell of the building next door. You get an alert, and you have a couple of minutes to get there. But when ballistic missiles started coming from Iran, it got harder because then you only have about a minute.
In 2024, my wife and I spent nights in a bomb shelter at a school. If an attack happens at night, it’s hard to get to the building next door in time. But being in the school’s bomb shelter was great. You get an alert, and you don’t have to go anywhere — you’re already there. We slept on a camping mat. We brought blankets and pillows from home. The concrete floors were cold, and the air was stuffy. My back hurt afterward — it was a concrete floor, after all.
I couldn’t count how many warnings we got, but Haifa itself wasn’t hit all that often. There were deaths, though: In the first few months, for example, a rocket hit an oil refinery outside the city, killing workers.
Some people in Israel are, let’s say, bloodthirsty. They say all of Gaza should be paved over because they’re all scum there. I don’t understand that. Just as I can’t accept the idea that all Russians are assholes because Russia attacked Ukraine. I know plenty of good people in Russia. My parents live there, after all.
But there are fewer bloodthirsty people now — that’s how it seems to me. Because people are exhausted. When the war began, it seemed like it would end quickly, and now it’s been going on for years. People want to make plans and live in peace.
It was impossible not to follow what was happening with the hostages. Everyone was writing and talking about it, and there were constant street protests. I didn’t take part because, of course, the hostages need to be brought back, but I don’t know how rallies could help with that. Is the army going to do more, or what?
But I cooked for soldiers. Jews came to Israel from all over the world to fight. People helped however they could: putting them up in their homes, feeding them, raising money for equipment and footwear.
I don’t know if you could say I have PTSD, but sudden noises bother me. When a car suddenly starts honking, for example, or a tire bursts. Or that bang-bang when a motorcycle goes by. A motorcycle sounds just like a drone. Exactly the same.
When we first arrived in Israel, people had so many plans: They were opening shops, galleries. Now it’s impossible to know how to make plans at all. What’s going to happen tomorrow? Maybe another war? Should we buy property here, start a business? Or maybe move to another country before the kids get called up?
Larisa Zimina, 52, HR specialist, Netanya
In August 2023, there was a hot-air balloon festival at the very spot where the music festival took place, or somewhere very close by. I went with my children. There were several thousand big Israeli families there, with very young children, tents, and dogs. There’s only one road in. It still terrifies me to think that we wouldn’t have gotten out if the attack had happened that day. If I’d felt there was a threat [of a terrorist attack], I wouldn’t have gone.
On the morning of October 7, I was talking to a friend in America. Her son was in Israel and wasn’t answering her calls. She said he’d gone to some event. I said: It’s seven in the morning. He’s been dancing and drinking and partying all night. He’s probably asleep, and maybe his phone’s dead. We joked that trees don’t have power outlets. The guy’s 23, he’s finished his military service. Why keep calling him?
Then I started reading the news and realized things were looking bad. My mother called from Beersheba and said the sirens were going off there. I also remember religious [Jews] stopping me in the street. They couldn’t read the news [on Shabbat] and were asking what was happening.
The boy whose mother I’d been talking to was killed. That boy used to babysit my child. His brother was my son’s best friend. His mother flew in from Chicago right away — on October 9, we were at the missing-persons center that had been set up near Ben Gurion Airport. People were sobbing, screaming, wailing.
October 7 profoundly changed how safe I feel in Israel. It always used to be a short war, a long break, then another, and another. Suddenly, the war turned out not to be short. The odds of losing our “lottery” got much higher.
[Before,] there were knife attacks and suicide bombings, but they didn’t stop me from working, taking buses, going to parties, or just living my life. I used to work in news in Russia, and I know that the chance of dying of any cause in Russia is much higher than the chance of being killed by a terrorist in Israel.
I live my life as I always have — but if I had a house, I’d build a bomb shelter. Many of my friends have gotten gun permits. Now I’d think twice about renting an apartment in Kfar Saba.
October 7 was an astonishing combination of a fuckup and Israel’s usual laid-back attitude. I used to spend a lot of time working on this conflict, working with left-wing organizations that support two states for two peoples. And I understand how complicated it all is — how nobody’s hands are clean. How many stupid things and mistakes both sides have made, Israel included…
But I’m Israeli, and I’m on the Israelis’ side. And it always matters who started it — with the attack from Gaza, that’s obvious.
Really, everyone should be ready for anything. You can start with the basics: stock up on food, water, portable gas stoves, and blankets at home. Be ready for everything to suddenly shut down and another endless war to begin. I teach my children to steer clear of crowds and watch who’s walking behind them.
And you’ve got to keep yourself sane any way you can: exercise, sex, sleep.
Grigory Nedayev, 31, software developer, Tel Aviv
I moved from Moscow to Israel in March 2022, shortly after [Russia invaded Ukraine]. I knew where I was going, so the possibility that one of Israel’s neighbors might fire a rocket at it, or that a terrorist attack might happen somewhere, didn’t surprise me. So I was prepared — and before October 7, I felt safe.
The Hamas attack happened the day after my wife and I got back from a vacation in France. We flew into Israel on October 6 — lovely weather, warm, peaceful. Around 6:30 a.m. the next day, an outdoor warning siren went off. I woke up and thought: Something’s happening.
But something’s always happening here. I went up to the roof of our building. The sky was clear, no rockets or explosions, just the siren. So I went back to sleep. I really underestimated the danger.
That morning, my wife and I started reading the news and realized it was serious. There wasn’t any panic, though. I’m not an anxious person. I thought: There were Hamas attacks in 2019 and 2021 too. And the Gaza Strip is 80 kilometers [about 50 miles] from us. That’s a ridiculously short distance by Russian standards, of course, but it’s still not right on our doorstep. It seemed like it would last a couple of days, so the next day I didn’t even read the news.
I work on Sundays, and at the morning meeting I saw how tense my colleagues were. We didn’t discuss work, just what was happening. Over the next few days, I followed the news closely. Rockets were coming toward Tel Aviv, and the Israeli army was intercepting them. I’d never seen anything like that before — at most, some smoke in the distance from an intercepted rocket. Now it was frightening: Things were exploding right over your head.
I’m pretty resilient, but even I struggled with all the reports of people being burned and brutally killed. You read it and absorb all that horror. You get depressed.
After the hostage deal fell through and Hamas killed six hostages, I was so shaken that I went to a rally. I wanted to, how do I put it, express my opinion.
Then I came across a post looking for volunteers in a Russian-language Telegram chat. I signed up — I wanted to help however I could. They took us somewhere, something like a military base, and we spent the whole day packing food, canned goods, and all sorts of little things for soldiers.
About a year ago, all the hostages came home. There was almost jubilation in the streets. People weren’t exactly walking around shouting “hooray!” but you could see from their faces that they were happy. I felt a kind of happiness too, real relief. Because that horror had dragged on for so long, deals kept falling through, politicians did nothing but argue — you just wanted it to end.
Over these years, I’ve started questioning whether I want to live in Israel, and I’ve become more pessimistic about the future. Even though none of this has affected me personally. I live in a building with a reinforced room — my bedroom is a bomb shelter, so I don’t have to run anywhere. A couple of months after the war began, our company switched to remote work, so I just sat and worked in that room to the sound of rockets exploding. In theory, if a rocket hit the wall of that room, I’d be stunned by the blast, but it wouldn’t kill me.
I haven’t changed. But I think the country has. This war has pretty much killed the idea of peaceful coexistence with Palestine. My impression is that many people who used to be left-wing or centrist have shifted to the right.
Zina Kapitovskaya, 74, retiree, Haifa
When I learned what was happening on October 7, I was overcome with horror, fear, hatred. And sorrow, like any normal person, over the deaths of completely innocent people, including children.
We knew about the balloons they sent from Gaza. We knew they hated us. But we never thought it could turn into such a horrific massacre.
Years ago, I happened to miss a bus that later exploded. For a while afterward, I couldn’t get on buses. Israel is a country where something can happen at any moment. But a massacre like October 7 was unimaginable.
I didn’t see a therapist after October 7: It turns out I’m pretty resilient, and I can cope on my own. Probably partly because October 7 didn’t affect anyone close to me. My grandchildren were in the army at the time, but they didn’t get caught up in that meat grinder. If they had, I’d probably have been losing my mind just like other parents and grandparents in that situation.
I can’t say my everyday routine has changed since October 7. My sense of safety hasn’t changed either. Nor has my attitude toward the Arabs who live near us: I’m not afraid of them.
The worst thing is that no state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attack has been set up. There’s a law specifying how a state commission of inquiry must be formed and who must sit on it. Commissions like that were set up after several wars. Three years have passed, and no one has been held responsible. Only a few people acknowledged responsibility and resigned on their own. Elections are coming up in Israel, and setting up a state commission of inquiry is at the top of the sensible parties’ platforms.
My attitude toward the government changed enormously [after the events of October 7]. I think they bear a lot of the blame, and they absolutely need to be replaced. [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu says one thing, but who knows what he really thinks.
Of course, the problem didn’t start on October 7. This has all been going on for a very long time. I’m not a politician. I don’t know how to fix it, but I’m sure war isn’t necessarily the answer.
Gavriel Feldman, 49, editor of Mir Torah (World of Torah), a publication about Judaism, Jerusalem
October 7 was Simchat Torah. I went to the synagogue for the very first minyan [communal prayer service]. Most people go to the other, longer minyan: They sing for hours, dance with the Torah scrolls, and socialize. I went to the first minyan because it’s very short, so I could get home to the children and take them back [to the synagogue] for the main celebration and dancing without rushing.
Large floor-standing air conditioners had been set up in the room for the dancing. They were humming, and we couldn’t hear the sirens. I realized something was happening when I got home during a lull in the sirens.
Then rockets started hitting. We had to decide whether to take the children [to the synagogue]. Something was clearly happening, but we didn’t know what. We decided to go for a little while. The lower hall in our synagogue doubles as a bomb shelter. When we arrived, it was clear that the dancing was winding down.
Rumors started circulating because people in our community were being called up to fight. Secular neighbors told us a few things. We knew militants had broken through and hostages had been taken. A picture was beginning to emerge, but nobody understood the scale of it, how many people had been killed or abducted.
Turning on a phone or television is a direct violation of Shabbat. You can do it if there’s an immediate threat to life, but there wasn’t one. Rocket attacks are fairly routine in Israel.
This [observing Shabbat] is a difficult issue: It’s a holiday, Simchat Torah. There are stories about our great teachers who, even in moments of immense personal grief, set it aside when a holiday began and fulfilled the commandments. After the holiday, a person like that returns to their deep mourning, but during the holiday they rejoice, and it isn’t an act.
But we’re ordinary people… [For us,] that’s quite difficult. The children and I left the synagogue and went home fairly quickly. After that, we started going to bomb shelters…
The next day, once Shabbat and the holiday were over, people started collecting supplies for soldiers. Because it had become clear that the state wasn’t prepared for anything. The army couldn’t provide reservists with what they needed. On the morning of October 8, I bought the most urgently requested items and took bags of them somewhere.
Not long before that, our son had been born, and he had some [health] complications. He was our sixth child. Even as experienced parents, we had to learn a lot of things all over again. We were really tied down [caring for the baby], while the war was going on in the background.
I coped with it fairly easily. It was harder for my wife. Anxiety, not knowing what would happen next, no sense of certainty or safety.
For many people in Israel, October 7 shattered their understanding of the world. For me, it didn’t. If you start from the belief that the Almighty governs the world, while the world’s progressives are trying to take it in the wrong direction, then you understand that stability and tranquility are something of an illusion, a way of fooling yourself. If everything’s okay for you today, you shouldn’t assume it necessarily always will be.
October 7 woke a great many people up. In that sense, some good came out of this horrific tragedy. For a while, you could see the unity in Israel that everyone loves to talk about.
Then, of course, that unity fell apart — turning to “mold and linden honey,” as the Russian song goes. But at least we knew unity was possible.
Vitaly Starov, 44, programmer, Acre
My wife and I left Russia because repression was growing, and we suspected I might be jailed. We understood that we were moving to a country where terrorist attacks could happen, a country that’s constantly at war.
We arrived in Israel about three months before October 7. Luckily, we managed to get all our paperwork done except for my driver’s license. We got identity cards, bus and commuter train passes, and joined a health insurance fund. After October 7, everything closed, then opened only intermittently. It took me six months to get my license.
On October 7, I woke up with an inflamed ear, apparently because I’d walked barefoot on the tile [in our apartment] the day before. My ear hurt, and the pain spread to a tooth. I thought I should probably see a doctor, but then I started reading the news and felt even worse.
The Hamas attack was shocking: a brutal massacre with large numbers of civilian casualties. The videos of hostages being dragged through crowds in Gaza, beaten and spat on, really hit me hard.
That same day, checkpoints were set up at the northern entrances to Acre, and armored vehicles with men carrying automatic weapons were brought in. The Lebanese border is 10 to 15 kilometers [about six to nine miles] north of the city. The thinking was that Hezbollah might break through the border and make it as far as Acre. But it limited itself to rocket attacks. There were fears that unrest would break out among Israeli Arabs, but that didn’t happen.
Hezbollah launched its first attacks from Lebanon a day or two later, and after that, there were air-raid sirens on many days. Almost all the rockets were shot down. Only a few got through. The bomb shelters in Acre, like those in many cities in northern Israel, were full of junk and partly flooded. I went to help clear them out as a volunteer.
My attitude toward Israel hasn’t changed since October 7, but my attitude toward the current Israeli government has. For the worse: They haven’t solved a single problem, only compounded them. No state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7 has been set up. The goals of the war Israel has become embroiled in are unclear, and there are serious questions about how it’s being fought.
I wouldn’t say I have PTSD, and I probably don’t need to see a therapist. But naturally, there’s nothing good about air-raid sirens either. Now, wherever you go, you automatically look around for the nearest bomb shelter. Still, I don’t feel threatened by Arabs — and there are a lot of them in Acre.
After October 7, it became much clearer why so many Israelis carry guns in public. It doesn’t surprise me to see people carrying automatic military rifles while buying groceries in a supermarket. And overall, the Israeli army and security services showed their strength and proved they could regroup even after a huge failure.
Acre is a small city, and we didn’t really have rallies calling for the hostages’ release. But my wife and I went to roadside protests with signs several times, handed out ribbons, and put up banners around the city. Relatives of hostages came to Acre, and we met with them. The main demand was for the government to agree to a deal to free the hostages.
We did all this with local Hebrew speakers. There were no Russian speakers there. There was very little information in Russian about the movement supporting the hostages. I posted in Acre’s Russian-language chats a few times, but nobody came to the protests.
Israel is a small country. Almost everyone who’s lived here a long time has relatives or acquaintances who were harmed [in the terrorist attack] — or at least knows someone who does. Most Israelis think their country upholds European standards. Seeing that brutality [during the terrorist attack] convinced them that barbarians had attacked, people they couldn’t negotiate with. That’s where all those statements come from about there being no innocent people in Gaza, about building a parking lot in its place. Those statements cast Israel in the worst possible light.
I definitely don’t want to go back to Moscow. Sometimes it all gets too much, and I want to move somewhere else [to a third country]. But we’re citizens here, and in another country we’d have to go through all the bureaucracy again. Learn another language, unless it’s English.
Israel’s actually not a bad country to live in. Apart from the wars and the rocket attacks.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Russia hits Ukraine with drones and missiles, killing at least eight
articles.body:
Russia hits Ukraine with drones and missiles, killing at least eight
KYIV, Oct 7 - Russia launched a barrage of drones and missiles at Ukraine on Wednesday, killing at least eight people and damaging residential buildings, industrial facilities and infrastructure, Ukrainian officials said.
Two people were killed in the capital Kyiv, four in the northern city of Pryluki and two in the central Poltava region, authorities said.
"Ukraine has once again been hit by Russian missiles throughout the night," Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said on the Telegram app.
'ANOTHER SLEEPLESS NIGHT'
"Another sleepless night, another act of terror, after which people still have to plan their working day despite everything," he added.
Russia launched 130 drones, 48 cruise missiles and also ballistic missiles to attack Ukraine, the Ukrainian air force said. Air defence units downed 161 targets, it said on Telegram.
Kyiv and Poltava in central Ukraine, the southeastern region of Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv in the northeast were the focus of the Russian attacks, the Ukrainian air force said.
Russia's defence ministry said its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea- and air-launched weapons, as well as drones.
It said the targets included sites where Ukrainian defence company Fire Point manufactures and stores its Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv as well as regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkiv.
Last week, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Ukraine had fired its first domestically made ballistic missile in combat, produced by Fire Point.
In an interview with Reuters last week, Zelenskiy said he expected the company to have a longer-range FP-9 missile ready by the autumn, which the company has said will be capable of reaching Moscow.
MISSILE HITS APARTMENT BLOCK
In Pryluki in the northern Chernihiv region, a Russian missile slammed into a five-storey residential building, regional authorities said. At least four people were killed on the spot and 20 more were wounded, while more residents could be buried under the rubble, local authorities said.
Video images showed rescuers pulling people from beneath the wreckage.
Many Kyiv residents took shelter in the city's deep underground metro stations as warnings of the upcoming attacks were shared by Ukrainian officials and military intelligence.
Several loud explosions reverberated through the capital during the night, Reuters witnesses said.
"The metro is better, because we live on the 9th floor of a high-rise, and it's really scary when you're on the 9th floor and missiles are flying at you," Lesia, a 49-year-old Kyiv resident, told Reuters.
Ukrainian officials said Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in addition to the drones.
For months, Ukraine suffered from a critical lack of air defences, prompting Zelenskiy and other officials to repeatedly plead for help and more supplies.
Overnight air strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro damaged an industrial facility, transport infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and apartment buildings in Kremenchuk, regional officials said on the Telegram messaging app. REUTERS

articles.title: Kremlin outraged by France's ballistic missile launch from nuclear submarine
articles.body:
Kremlin outraged by France's ballistic missile launch from nuclear submarine
The Kremlin has stated that it views France's launch of an M51.3 ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine on 6 October as a "loud and clear message".
Source: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, as cited by Russian news agency Interfax; European Pravda
Details: According to Peskov, Moscow believes that "any problems should be resolved through dialogue rather than demonstrative missile launches".
The spokesman for Putin, the leader of an aggressor state, once again expressed outrage that the European Union is building up its military capabilities "with the aim of turning into a military-political bloc".
Quote from Peskov: "This is bad because they are building their identity in the field of defence and security on the basis of confrontation with the Russian Federation. This is a dead end. As history shows, this leads to nothing good."
At the same time, he claimed that Russia is "monitoring all such plans and actions".
Background:
- The day before, France conducted a test launch of a new ballistic missile from the nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine Le Vigilant. French President Emmanuel Macron observed the test.
- In March, Macron delivered a speech on France's nuclear weapons doctrine, introducing the concept of "preventive deterrence", which provides for the deployment of French nuclear assets on the territory of allied countries.
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: Ukraine says Russia bombed apartment block as birthday gift for Putin
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia’s military of deliberately killing civilians and bombing residential buildings as a macabre gift for Vladimir Putin, who celebrates his 74th birthday on Wednesday.
Ukraine’s president described Russia’s overnight drone and missiles strikes, which killed at least 24 people, as “despicable”. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” he said.
Video showed a ballistic missile slamming into a five-storey apartment block in the town of Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The concrete building collapsed, entombing those inside. Eighteen people died, including four children, officials said.
Zelenskyy identified them as Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhii, who was one year old, as well as eight-year-old Maksym. He said five children were among about 50 people who were injured. Rescuers continued to pick through the rubble, with several residents not yet accounted for, he added.
“Today, on Putin’s birthday, the Russian army ‘presented’ him with the destruction of a residential block in Pryluky,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. “The Russians know very well that they are striking ordinary cities, ordinary life. It is an absolutely deliberate choice of terror.”
He acknowledged Ukraine was struggling to shoot down enemy ballistic missiles, and appealed to allies to provide US-manufactured Patriot interceptors. “Air defence packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” he said.
The bombardment featured 70 ballistic missiles, as well as 46 jet-powered drones, which in recent weeks have been terrorising Ukrainians on a daily basis. Ukraine’s air force said it managed to down more than 80% of the fast-moving drones – an improvement on the previous average of 50% to 60%.
Eleven regions were hit. Two people were killed in Kyiv, with other deadly strikes in the central cities of Kremenchuk and Oleksandriia, where four civilians died. There was also extensive damage in Dnipro.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said Russian generals had given Putin his favourite birthday present: “war crimes”. Moscow’s grim strategy of bombarding the country’s population so it capitulated would not work, he said.
“The Ukrainian people are not going to give up, because it’s about Ukraine’s survival as a nation and as a state,” he said. The “ultimate” present would be a dock in The Hague, home to the international criminal court, where the Russian president would stand trial, Sybiha said.
One resident in Kremenchuk said the attack happened early on Wednesday. The woman told Ukrainian media: “We were making tea in the morning. My husband was getting ready for work. And that was it. I found myself on the floor. What can I say? It was very scary.”
Local people in Dnipro said a blast wave affected 16 buildings, blowing out doors and windows. One woman, Iryna, said her auto parts workshop had been hit for the sixth time. The ceiling collapsed in Wednesday’s strike, she said, with toilets, sinks and equipment damaged.
“The explosion happened around three in the morning. We were sleeping at home. Everyone was scared, probably the whole city heard it. We will restore the shop and continue to work,” she told the Suspline channel.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had carried out its own long-range strikes on economic and military sites inside Russia. They included two oil complexes and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions. “These are justified Ukrainian responses to all Russian attacks on our people,” he said.
The president posted dramatic video of a burning oil tanker close to the southern resort city of Sochi. Russian officials said naval drones had hit the Liberian-flagged ship, adding that “crude oil was burning openly on the Black Sea”. Its Indian crew of 23 was rescued, they said.
Both sides have heavily targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since Putin’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In recent weeks Russia has picked off vessels carrying Ukrainian grain, paralysing maritime traffic from Ukraine’s southern ports including Odesa.
This week, a civilian cargo ship sank after a suspected attack by Russian drones in the Black Sea. Its crew is still missing. A second vessel carrying grain was also hit while sailing in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, said the Bulgarian prime minister, Rumen Radev. The search for survivors was called off on Wednesday, according to V Adm Rumen Nikolov of the Maritime Administration executive agency. “There are no traces of the sailors from the first ship, and there will be none,” he said.

articles.title: Sybiha calls on partners to give Putin "real gifts" that help him choose diplomacy over war
articles.body:
Following a massive Russian attack, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha urged international partners to step up sanctions against Russia and increase military support for Ukraine to force the Kremlin to choose a diplomatic path instead of continuing the war.
"On Putin’s birthday, Russian generals brought him his favorite present: war crimes. A massive attack with hundreds of missiles and drones hit residential buildings and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhia, Kremenchuk, and Pryluky. At least two people were killed in the capital and four more accross the country," he wrote on X.
According to Sybiha, Russian generals are not telling Putin that he is not winning this war and never will.
"He has lost 1.6 million troops killed and injured without achieving a single strategic goal of his invasion. His slow advances have stalled and Ukraine started to liberate more land than he manages to occupy. His economy is in decline and his influence around the world is waning. All of this because he refuses to end this war," the minister wrote.
He urged not to leave Russia's terror unanswered: " Following this attack, I urge all partners to give Putin real presents that will help him finally choose diplomacy over war."
According to him, this includes tightening sanctions against the Russian military-industrial complex—including facilities that manufacture ballistic missiles and the "Rassvet" satellite system—as well as boosting support for Ukraine, specifically with air defense assets and energy assistance ahead of winter.
"But his ultimate present will be a dock in The Hague. We are preparing the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression Against Ukraine for practical launch already next year. Putin and his friends should know that accountability is inevitable," Sybiha stated.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: 25 people killed on Wed as result of massive Russian strike
articles.body:
The death toll from the massive Russian strike on Ukraine has risen to 25, with 100 people wounded, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.
"In total, the death toll following this massive strike on Ukraine stands at 25 people. One hundred people were wounded. The strike was a combination of various weapons: a lot of ballistic missiles, a lot of cruise missiles, and Shahed UAVs. This is the 'gift' Putin gave himself for his birthday: the killing of children, the killing of people. During the day, there were new strikes with Shahed UAVs and aerial bombs," Zelenskyy said in an evening address on Wednesday.
The president said Russia will move toward escalation.
"The sanctions regime has been significantly weakened, and signals about lifting sanctions on oligarchs are, in fact, signals that the war is normalizing. Unfortunately," he added.
According to him, Putin can still sell oil and "calculate the situation in dollars and euros in a way that remains profitable for him."
Zelenskyy said it is in Putin's interest to wage war, since war is his nature and ideology.
"And this is not just Ukraine's problem, not just ours, not just that of our people and our children. It is a problem for everyone in Europe and the Western world," Zelenskyy said.
He emphasized the need for additional measures to support Ukraine, as well as the need for air defense systems.
"We are counting heavily on prompt deliveries from our partners and on sufficient production. We are in constant contact with everyone involved in these decisions. The delivery schedule must be ensured," he said.

articles.title: “Putin’s Favorite Gift—War Crimes”: Sybiha Responds to Massive Russian Attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category

“Putin’s Favorite Gift—War Crimes”: Sybiha Responds to Massive Russian Attack on Ukraine
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called on international partners to strengthen sanctions against Russia’s military-industrial complex and increase air defense and energy support for Ukraine following a large-scale Russian missile and drone attack.
Sybiha said hundreds of missiles and drones struck residential buildings and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Kremenchuk, and Pryluky.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“On Putin’s birthday, Russian generals presented him with his favorite gift—war crimes,” Sybiha said.
The foreign minister said Russian military leaders were failing to tell Putin that Russia was not winning the war and would not achieve victory. According to Sybiha, Russia has lost 1.6 million troops killed and wounded without achieving any of the strategic objectives of its invasion.
He also said Russia’s advances had stalled, while Ukraine had begun liberating more territory than Russian forces were able to capture. Sybiha further pointed to what he described as Russia’s declining economy and weakening international influence, attributing these developments to Putin’s refusal to end the war.
Sybiha acknowledged that Ukraine was also facing significant difficulties but stressed that Ukrainians had no intention of surrendering, as the war concerned the survival of Ukraine as both a nation and a state.
Following the attack, the minister urged Ukraine’s partners to respond by tightening sanctions against Russia’s military-industrial complex, including enterprises involved in producing ballistic missiles and the Rassvet satellite system.
He also called for stronger support for Ukraine, including the provision of all necessary air defense capabilities and energy assistance ahead of winter.

This means strengthening sanctions against his military-industrial complex, particularly enterprises producing ballistic missiles and the Rassvet satellite system, as well as increasing support for Ukraine, including the provision of all necessary air defense capabilities and energy assistance ahead of winter,” the statement read.

articles.title: Air Force: Ukraine downs 161 Russian targets, including 44 missiles, 5 ballistic
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces neutralized 161 Russian air targets overnight Wednesday, including 44 missiles, five of which were ballistic, while missile and strike UAV hits were recorded at 18 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense shot down/suppressed 161 targets: 5 Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Zircon/Onyx ballistic missiles; 39 Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kalibr cruise missiles (information regarding another 6 cruise missiles is being clarified); 117 Russian Shahed-type UAVs (38 of them jet-powered), Gerbera, and other types of drones," the report says.
Overall, on the night of October 7 (from 18:00 on October 6), Russia attacked with: Zircon/Onyx anti-ship missiles from Russia's Rostov region; Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles from Russia's Bryansk and Voronezh regions; 48 air-, ground-, and sea-launched Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kalibr cruise missiles from the Vologda and Kursk regions and the Caspian Sea, respectively; and 130 Shahed-type strike UAVs (46 of them jet-powered), Gerbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the directions of Oryol and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, and temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare (EW) and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Meanwhile, Russian missile and strike UAV hits were recorded at 18 locations, and the fall of intercepted debris was recorded at 5 locations.
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine informed that the main directions of the attack were Kyiv region, Kharkiv region, Poltava region, and Dnipropetrovsk region.

articles.title: Russia hits Ukraine with wave of attacks on Putin’s birthday
articles.body:
KYIV – Russian strikes killed at least 12 people and injured over 40 across Ukraine on Wednesday — the same day that Russian President Vladimir Putin celebrates his 74th birthday.
“As a birthday ‘gift’ to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region. It was an ordinary five-story apartment building,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday morning, adding that there may be more victims trapped under the rubble.
The Ukrainian air force reported it had shot down most of the 130 killer drones and cruise missiles but only five of about 20 ballistic missiles. Pryluky was the worst-hit area, with five people killed and 26 injured, including five children, according to Zelenskyy. One missile landed in a densely populated Kyiv residential district and did not detonate.
Advertisement
Local authorities also reported destruction in Kyiv, where two people were killed, as well as in Dnipro, Kremenchuk, Zaporizhzhia and other regions. Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s energy system was one of the key targets of the latest attack.
Ukraine’s energy ministry said it had to schedule power cutsin some parts of the country to save energy, while residents in at least five regions were still without electricity on Wednesday morning.
“The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes. Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. And air defense packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” Zelenskyy added.
“Mr. Putin, is this what you wanted for your birthday? People killed in their sleep, injured children, shattered homes?” EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová wrote on Facebook.
In the past 24 hours, Ukraine has also burned a Russian oil tanker in the Black Sea, struck two oil facilities and a military training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions. The Russian defense ministry reported shooting down 311 drones over 16 Russian regions and the Black Sea.

articles.title: FACTBOX: Russian forces hit enterprises producing Flamingo missiles in Ukraine
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. Russian forces delivered a massive strike overnight, hitting industrial sites producing Flamingo missiles and drones in Kiev and six regions in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry said on Wednesday.
TASS has compiled the main details on the strikes.
Defense Ministry’s statement
- Russian forces delivered a massive strike by ground-, sea-and air-launched precision-guided weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), hitting Ukrainian targets, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, as a result of the strike, Ukrainian military industrial sites involved in the production and storage of Flamingo cruise missiles and long-and medium-range UAVs for the Fire Point company in the city of Kiev and the Kiev, Chernigov, Kirovograd, Dnepropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkov Regions were hit.
- In addition, Russian forces struck port and ship-repair infrastructure in the Odessa Region and vessels used by the Ukrainian army.
- Russian troops hit a dry cargo ship with supplies for Ukrainian forces at the port of Yuzhny in the Odessa Region, using Geran-4 Seeker drones, the Defense Ministry said, releasing footage of the strike.
- Russian forces also struck a storage facility for fuel and lubricants at the Chernomorsk port in the Odessa Region, using Geran drones.
Targets hit
- The Defense Ministry later stated that Russian forces struck the Smart Ammunition industrial facility for the assembly and storage of FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, FP-9 tactical missiles and their components in the city of Kiev.
- Russian troops also struck the Kiev Cardboard and Paper Mill plant that served as a production and storage facility for FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles and their components in the settlement of Obukhov in the Kiev Region.
- In addition, the Trading House Plastmas-Priluki industrial enterprise, which produced and stored components for FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, was hit in the town of Priluki in the Chernigov Region.
- A workshop belonging to the Alexandria Group of industrial enterprises that manufactured components for long-and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles, including fixed-wing drones, was hit in the settlement of Alexandria in the Kirovograd Region.
- Russian forces also struck a rocket and space industry facility of the State Enterprise Production Association Yuzhny Machine-Building Plant named after O.M. Makarov, which produced, stored and supplied FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles to the Ukrainian army, along with FP-1 and FP-2 long-and medium-range drones, in the city of Dnepr in the Dnepropetrovsk Region.
- In addition, the AvtoKrAZ factory, where transporter erector launchers for FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles were produced and stored, was hit in the city of Kremenchug in the Poltava Region.
- Russian forces also struck the JTI Ukraine tobacco factory in the city of Kremenchug, where the production lines were being used to manufacture small arms ammunition for the Ukrainian army.
- Moreover, the Russian army hit a mechanical plant in the settlement of Lozovaya in the Kharkov Region, where FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles and their components were assembled and stored.
- The Danube Ship Repair plant at the Izmail port in the Odessa Region that manufactured and stored uncrewed boats and their components was also hit.
- In addition, Russian forces struck a dry cargo ship carrying military supplies and dual-use goods for the Ukrainian army at the port of Odessa.
Situation in Ukraine
- Non-residential buildings in Kiev’s Obolonsky District and warehouse facilities in the Podolsky District were damaged, Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said on his Telegram channel.
- Later he said that debris caught fire in an open area in the Darnitsky District and fragments hit non-residential buildings in the Shevchenkovsky District.
- An industrial enterprise was damaged in Dnepropetrovsk, the RBC-Ukraine news agency reported.
- No details have been provided.
- Explosions damaged a warehouse and energy facilities in the city of Kiev and in the Kiev Region, the Strana news outlet reported.
- The outlet did not specify where the damaged sites are located.
- However, the publication posted on its Telegram channel footage of large-scale fires at the sites of explosions.
- Explosions damaged the Tripolskaya thermal power plant in the Kiev Region, Strana later reported.
- The publication provided no further details, only noting that the authorities said nothing about it.
- Trams on several routes stopped after explosions disrupted power in the overhead contact system in Kiev, the city administration said.
- A transport infrastructure facility was damaged in the Kiev-controlled city of Zaporozhye, acting head of the regional military administration, appointed by Ukraine, Mikhail Semikin said.
- No details have been provided.
- According to Semikin, temporary traffic restrictions are possible on some road sectors.
- Over a thousand residents have been left without power in the town of Izyum in the Kharkov Region after infrastructure was damaged, the district military administration reported.
- Head of the Kharkov Region administration Oleg Sinegubov said that railway infrastructure and warehouse facilities were damaged in the Izyumsky District.

articles.title: Bulgaria to Add Five Air Defense Missile Systems Following Black Sea Drone Attack
articles.body:
Bulgaria Falls to 90th in World Football Rankings
Bulgaria has fallen five places to 90th in the latest FIFA world rankings, with the decline following a poor start to the Nations League campaign
Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the government will approve an investment expenditure plan for five additional air defense missile systems, while warning that developing capabilities against unmanned systems in the air and maritime domains requires time, funding and a systematic approach.
Radev made the remarks before the regular Council of Ministers meeting, hours before the Consultative Council for National Security (CCNS) convenes following drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
He thanked the crew of the Bulgarian ship DIOSCURIA, as well as rescue teams from the Navy and Air Force, Border Police and medical teams, for their professional response in helping people in distress after two vessels were attacked.
"Once again, we have demonstrated that human life is a supreme value for us and that Bulgaria possesses emergency rescue capabilities within its Exclusive Economic Zone, in accordance with international conventions," Radev said.
The Prime Minister said the CCNS should not become a venue for political campaigning and called for restraint in the wake of the attacks.
"The CCNS must not turn into a stage for pre-election demagoguery. There is no room for hysteria. Composure and sober judgment are required," Radev stated.
He said establishing the necessary capabilities to counter unmanned systems at sea and in the air is a complicated process that cannot be completed quickly.
"It requires time and funding," Radev said.
The Prime Minister recalled that plans had been initiated in 2023, during a caretaker government he had appointed, to purchase high-end unmanned aerial systems capable of monitoring Bulgaria's entire Exclusive Economic Zone. He said the initiative had not progressed since then.
"Many governments have come and gone since then. Absolutely nothing. Zero," Radev said.
He added that the Defense Minister had now prepared the required documentation and that a procurement procedure had been launched, including a Request for Information sent to leading global companies.
Radev also recalled that Bulgaria joined the European Sky Shield Initiative in 2022, again at the initiative of the Defense Minister of his caretaker government.
He said a contract had already been signed for one IRIS-T air defense system and that the government would approve an investment expenditure project for five more systems.
"Today, following all the work carried out by our government, we adopting an investment expenditure project to purchase five additional air defense missile systems. I expect us to have a contract within weeks," the Prime Minister stated.
Radev said the objective was to protect Bulgarian territory while strengthening the country's contribution to NATO's collective defense capabilities.
He also reiterated his call for diplomatic efforts to end the war.
"Pouring money into this war and endless rearmament is far costlier than diplomatic efforts and finding a lasting solution for peace. Our government will continue to work in this direction," Radev said.
A day after two ships were sunk in drone attacks inside Bulgaria's Exclusive Economic Zone in the Black Sea, Radev again did not identify who owned the drones.
Meanwhile, MPs rejected a Democratic Bulgaria (DB) proposal that would have required Radev and senior security officials to appear before Parliament over the October 6 attacks on commercial vessels. The proposed hearing also included Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev, Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov, Transport and Communications Minister Georgi Peev, State Agency for National Security (SANS) Chairman Plamen Tonchev, State Intelligence Agency Chairman Antoan Gechev and Military Intelligence Service Director Brigadier General Venelin Venev.
Instead, Radev focused on the operation in Plovdiv targeting abuses involving clinical pathways, hospital activities and high-cost medications, as well as the siphoning of funds from the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF).
He praised officials from the Ministry of Health, Ministry of Interior, Prosecutor's Office and SANS who took part in the operation and said cross-checks would continue throughout the country.
"Cross-checks are continuing across the country. We are preparing amendments to the Public Procurement Act to curb the siphoning of funds from the NHIF," Radev stated.
The Prime Minister also said the government was working to accelerate the professional advancement of young doctors and that the 2027 budget would provide for higher salaries for them.
"We are planning a salary increase for them in the 2027 budget," he said.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un Calls Russia’s War in Ukraine ‘Sacred’ in Putin Birthday Message
articles.body:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un pledged his “invariable support” for Russia and praised Moscow’s war against Ukraine as a “sacred war of justice” in a birthday message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, underscoring the deepening military alliance between Pyongyang and the Kremlin.
The message was published Wednesday, Oct. 7 – Putin’s 74th birthday – by North Korea’s state-run Korean Central News Agency.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I am pleased to have good friendship with you and open up a new chapter for the development of the relations between our two countries,” Kim wrote, according to KCNA.
He said strengthening the “comprehensive strategic partnership and alliance” with Russia remained a firm policy of the North Korean government and pledged continued backing for Putin and the Russian Federation.
Kim also said he was convinced that what he called the Russian people’s “sacred war of justice” would end in victory – language Pyongyang has repeatedly used to justify its military support for Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
From political support to troops on the battlefield
Relations between Moscow and Pyongyang have moved far beyond diplomatic declarations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The two countries signed a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement during Putin’s visit to Pyongyang in June 2024, including a mutual defense clause that significantly expanded military cooperation.
Zelensky Warns of Massive Russian Strike as 3 Tu-160 Bombers Take Off
North Korea later deployed thousands of soldiers to Russia, particularly to the Kursk region, where they fought alongside Russian forces.
South Korea’s National Intelligence Service estimated earlier this year that about 6,000 North Korean troops had been killed or wounded in the war. It also estimated that roughly 10,000 North Korean combat troops and another 1,000 engineering personnel were deployed in Russia’s Kursk region.
Separate estimates have put the total number of North Korean soldiers sent to Russia since 2024 at roughly 14,000 to 15,000.
In return, Western and South Korean officials have said Moscow has provided Pyongyang with economic assistance, military technology and battlefield experience.
Kim stresses personal alliance with Putin
Kim’s birthday letter also highlighted the increasingly personal nature of his relationship with Putin.
He addressed the Russian leader as his “dearest friend” and closed the message by saying he warmly embraced his “dear comrade,” according to North Korean state media.
The wording reflects a relationship that has grown steadily closer as both governments face international sanctions and political isolation from Western states.
Kim’s latest message made clear that Pyongyang sees that partnership as long-term rather than temporary.

articles.title: ‘War Is His Nature’: Zelensky Says Putin’s Birthday ‘Gift’ Killed 25 Ukrainians
articles.body:
28 people were killed across Ukraine in Russian attacks on Oct. 7, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said, raising an earlier nationwide death toll of 25 reported by President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The heaviest loss of life was reported in the northern city of Pryluky, where a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile struck a five-story apartment building.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky said 19 people were killed there, including five children, while Chernihiv Regional State Administration Head Viacheslav Chaus later put the death toll at 20.
Vyhivskyi later confirmed that 20 people were killed in Pryluky, including five children – three of them just one year old.
Images from the scene showed a large section of the residential building collapsed as rescuers searched the rubble for survivors. Emergency crews continued clearing the destroyed structure throughout the day.
The attack was part of a wider Russian barrage targeting several Ukrainian cities. Residential buildings and civilian infrastructure were damaged in Kyiv, Kremenchuk and Pryluky.
In Kyiv, Russian ballistic missiles struck the capital in several waves, with the first salvo launched shortly after 3 a.m. Two people were killed and several sites were damaged across the city, according to Ukrainian authorities.
In Kremenchuk, Russian missiles and drones damaged apartment buildings and private homes. Two people were killed and seven injured, according to the Poltava Regional Military Administration.
Ukraine Working on 5 Ceasefire Tracks With Partners, Foreign Ministry Says
Vyhivskyi said the day’s Russian attacks on Pryluky, Kremenchuk, Oleksandriia and Kyiv had killed 28 people in total. Emergency workers and police rescued or evacuated 29 people from damaged buildings and dangerous areas, most of them in Pryluky.
Zelensky said Russia used a combination of ballistic and cruise missiles and Shahed drones in the overnight attack, and continued striking Ukraine with drones and aerial bombs during the day.
“Such a ‘gift’ Putin gave himself for his birthday. The killing of children, the killing of people,” Zelensky said in his evening address, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin turning 74 on Oct. 7.
He said the attack demonstrated that Moscow intends to continue escalating its war against Ukraine despite international efforts to end the conflict.
“It is important that there is no silence from leaders over what happened, over what happens every day, and, most importantly, over the fact that Russia intends to continue moving in this direction: toward escalation, killings and shelling,” Zelensky said.
“This is exactly what Moscow chooses despite all our efforts with our partners to bring peace closer,” he said, calling for greater pressure on Russia and additional military assistance for Ukraine.
Zelensky also criticized what he described as weakening sanctions pressure on Moscow, saying that discussions about lifting sanctions on Russian oligarchs risk normalizing the war.
“Putin still does not feel that this is creating real problems for him,” he said. “It is in his interest to wage war. War is his nature, his ideology.”
He added that Russia’s continued ability to sell oil and conduct international transactions meant the pressure on Moscow remained insufficient.
“And this is not only Ukraine’s problem, not only our problem, and not only the problem of our people and our children. It is a problem for everyone in Europe and the Western world,” Zelensky said.
