articles.title: Middle East live: Houthis target airport in Yemen as Israel marks October 7 anniversary
articles.body:
French FM denounces 'poison' of anti-Semitism as Israel marks October 7 attacks anniversary
Israelis on Wednesday took part in commemorations for the victims of Hamas's October 7, 2023 attacks, which killed 1,200 people and saw 251 hostages taken. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot denounced the "poison of anti-Semitism" as he attended a memorial ceremony at the site of the Nova music festival massacre. Read about the day’s events as they unfolded on our liveblog.
(This live page is no longer being updated.)
UN peacekeeping force says shots fired at post on Israel-Lebanon border
The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon says one of its posts was targeted earlier today near the border with Israel by small-arms fire, but there were no casualties.
"This morning, several rounds of small arms fire impacted a UNIFIL position near Kfar Shouba along the Blue Line in Sector East," the UN force said in a statement, referring to the de facto border between Israel and Lebanon.
The blue helmets described the shooting as "unacceptable".
"Such deliberate attacks gravely endanger the lives of peacekeepers," it said, adding that it was investigating the incident.
Death toll in Gaza strikes rises to five
The death toll from today's strikes in Gaza has risen to five, according to hospital sources.
Al-Shifa Hospital, located in Gaza City, reported two deaths at dawn following an Israeli strike in Jabalia, in the north of the territory.
The Gaza Civil Defence, a first-aid organisation, identified one of the victims as one of its volunteers, aged 23.
In Khan Younis, in the south of the territory, Nasser Hospital reported three further deaths in Israeli strikes carried out in several parts of the city.
How is Israel's economy faring after three years of war?
Israel’s tech sector – specifically its defence startups – has played a big part in spurring economic growth in the country after a small dip in the wake of the October 7 attacks three years ago.
But challenges, notably demographic ones, are on the horizon.
France rejects 'poison' of anti-Semitism, says French FM at Nova site
Speaking at the site of Nova music festival massacre, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said France rejects "anti-Semitism and hatred of others".
"At a time when our societies are facing the resurgence of unchecked anti-Semitism, we will not allow this poison to spread within the Republic. For everything in the very soul of France rejects anti-Semitism and hatred of others," the minister said in Re’im, in southern Israel.
He described the October 7 attack as an "abominable assault", which "wounded the Israeli people and all Jews to the core" and caused "a trauma that must not be downplayed".
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi Arabia
Earlier today, Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed new attacks on airports and military facilities in neighbouring Saudi Arabia, pulling the kingdom deeper into the latest front in the Iran war,.
As the Saudi capital is targeted again, new cage-like fences have been erected this week around fuel tanks and other equipment of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company near the Riyadh airport, AP reports.
The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said on social media that the rebels launched ballistic missiles and drones against King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
Flights were briefly disrupted, according to Flightradar24.
Tears, silence and techno music at Nova festival site
At the site of the Nova music festival, where Hamas militants in trucks and paragliders opened fire around dawn on October 7, 2023, family members bowed their heads quietly -- although at least one instead put on techno music in tribute to the fallen.
Katia Zohar, whose daughter Bar Zohar was killed at age 23, called the start of the attack at 6:29 am (0329 GMT) "the minute that changed our lives forever".
"Sadly I remember everything," Zohar said. "The moment she called for me to come and pick her up because there were missiles in the air. Then the second time when she called from the road, screaming that they were shooting at her."
Anna Davitashvili, 53, paid tribute to her eldest son Shaun, who was killed at 25 at Nova alongside friends, by playing the last track of techno music that the partygoers were dancing to when the attack began.
"I feel him here. I'm terribly sorry that I couldn't save him, I couldn't help him get out of this massacre," she said, tears filling her eyes.
Lebanon's Hezbollah gets $200 million from Iran to help displaced, sources say
Hezbollah has received $200 million from Iran to help Lebanese displaced by this year’s war with Israel, two people with direct knowledge of the transfer have told Reuters.
Hezbollah received the cash last month despite a tightening US economic chokehold on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, the sources said.
Intermediaries who moved the money charged a 20% fee, reflecting the risks of dealing with the group, they said. One said this was four times the normal fee.
Asked for comment, a Hezbollah official said an amount had been secured and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the funds.
Questions remain over what Netanyahu knew ahead of Hamas attacks
After a string of resignations by top security officials, Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu is the only senior figure from October 7 still in office, making the country's upcoming election in many ways a referendum on his leadership, AP reports.
His opponents — from across the political spectrum — call his outgoing coalition "the massacre government". Netanyahu says he has led a "war of redemption".
Netanyahu has repeatedly rejected calls for a commission of inquiry while trying to shift the blame to security officials. He recently accused the then-head of the Shin Bet security service, Ronen Bar, of withholding information ahead of the attack — prompting Bar to threaten a defamation lawsuit.
Netanyahu has meanwhile denied reports in American media outlets that the United Arab Emirates and Egypt warned him ahead of October 7.
Protesters arrested at pro-Palestine march in London
Police in London have arrested five people during a pro-Palestine student demonstration, the PA news agency reports.
Despite calls to ban the demonstration or postpone it to another date, around a hundred people marched in central London, chanting “Freedom, freedom for Palestine” and “Freedom for the people, freedom for the land”.
Credit: Reuters
One group held up a banner reading, “Descendants of Holocaust survivors against the genocide in Gaza”.
Police said the five protesters were arrested on suspicion of incitement to racial hatred.
📷 Berlin ceremony marks anniversary of October 7 attacks
A person carries an Israeli flag bearing the message ‘Don’t forget’ in Berlin, on October 7, 2026. Credit: Fabrizio Bensch, Reuters
A symbolic installation depicting a destroyed living room on display in Berlin. Credit: Fabrizio Bensch, Reuters
'Time doesn't heal': Parents of October 7 attacks victim Aner Shapira
22-year-old Aner Shapira managed to throw seven grenades back towards Hamas fighters during the October 7 attacks, before an eighth one exploded in his hands, killing him.
Three years on, his bereaved parents tell FRANCE 24 they can still feel his presence.
Shira and Moshe Shapira say that time doesn't heal, but they are learning how to live with their loss.
Click on the link below for the full story.
Israel strikes Gaza on October 7 anniversary, killing three
Israel has carried out new strikes in Gaza, with Palestinian officials reporting three people dead.
Loud bangs across the border in Gaza were audible from the site of the Nova music festival just as family members gathered at dawn to mourn the more than 300 revellers killed three years earlier.
In Gaza City, Al-Shifa hospital reported two people killed in an Israeli strike overnight.
Palestinian children walk amid the rubble of buildings in Gaza City on October 7, 2026.
Gaza's civil defence identified one of the dead as Mohamed Tamous and said he was a volunteer for the agency, which serves as an emergency rescue service under Hamas.
In the southern city of Khan Yunis, Nasser Hospital said that a 60-year-old man, Hisham Ibrahim Abu Mustafa, was killed in an Israeli strike and that others were injured.
🎥Houthis attack Aden airport as fighting intensifies in Yemen
Yemen's Houthis attacked Aden's international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones on Wednesday, the country's Transport Ministry said, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed government forces intensified.
Fighting has been focused in recent days on areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
📸 Commemorative installation on Tel Aviv beach
@Jack Guez, AFP
@Jack Guez, AFP
More than 200,000 people displaced since fighting in Yemen began, says UN agency
More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in Yemen began in recent weeks, according to data released on Wednesday by the United Nations' International Organization for Migration.
IOM described the crisis sparked by renewed fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi group and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen as alarming, with displacement figures surging from 76,000 in mid-September to more than 200,000 as of Wednesday – nearly all of whom fled since fighting began in early September.
🎥What did Netanyahu know before Hamas' October 7 attacks?
Accusations that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu failed to stop Hamas's October 7 attack have threatened to poison his campaign, particularly since reports emerged suggesting the United Arab Emirates and Egypt had warned him of the imminent danger.
FRANCE 24's International Affairs Editor Kethevane Gorjestani tells us more.
'Illegal routes' in Strait of Hormuz to soon be blocked, Iran state media reports
Transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz deemed illegal by Iran will soon be closed, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards' Commander told semi-official Fars news agency on Wednesday.
Mohammadreza Naqdi said these few routes had been created by blasting and damaging some of the rocky passages in the strategic waterway and were used by small boats smuggling oil, challenging the dominant narrative that Gulf oil flows through the strait are regaining pre-war levels.
Palestinian man killed, nine others injured in West Bank clash
The Palestinian health ministry said 44-year-old Ali al-Bazzari had died and nine others were injured "as a result of an assault by occupation forces and settlers" on the village of Burqa, north of Nablus in the northern West Bank.
Israel's military told AFP it was looking into the incident.
Al-Bazzari was a member of the Palestinian National Security Forces, according to an obituary that it published on Wednesday.
Wednesday's attack took place as farmers from Burqa were picking olives on land between the cities of Nablus and Tulkarem, according to village mayor Ammar Salah.
"Clashes broke out between young men from the village and settlers before the (Israeli) occupation forces intervened and opened live fire at the Palestinians, killing the young man Al-Bazzari and injuring others," Salah told AFP.
Iran's military chief of staff says October 7 hastened 'decline' of Israel
The Hamas attack of October 7, 2023 has accelerated Israel's decline, the chief of staff for Iran's armed forces said Wednesday, as Israelis marked the third anniversary of the deadliest day in their country's history.
"The Resistance Front turned its defensive strategy into an offensive strategy for the legitimate defence of the Palestinian people and their land, and accelerated the decline of the Zionist regime," Ali Abdollahi said in a statement.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters, AP and AFP)

articles.title: Taliban and North Korea rubbed shoulders at Russia’s war games—one fuels Moscow’s war, the other needs its help
articles.body:
Defense officials from Taliban-controlled Afghanistan spoke with North Korean representatives at Russia's Center-2026 strategic exercises, Afghanistan's Defense Ministry reported. So far, neither Moscow nor Pyongyang has confirmed any meeting, and Kabul disclosed no details of the talks or any agreement.
Since invading Ukraine, Russia has gathered a circle of sanctioned governments it both leans on for its war and props up in return—a trade that runs in opposite directions depending on the partner. Each new tie leaves one more isolated state with a stake in the war grinding on.
Observers among dozens
The exercises ran from 28 September to 3 October in Russia's Chelyabinsk Oblast. The Taliban attended as observers for the first time since it retook power in 2021, Militarnyi reported, one of dozens of foreign delegations present.
Mawlawi Nasibullah Madani, commander of the Abdullah bin Masoud Joint Combat Training Command, led the Taliban delegation. The ministry said its officers held discussions with North Korea's military attaché and with officials from China, India, Vietnam, and other countries on bilateral ties and military cooperation. The delegation also toured an exhibition featuring heavy weapons, drones, long-range missiles, and robotic systems.
Moscow's expanding military network
On 27 May 2026, Russia and the Taliban signed a military-technical cooperation agreement. Russia's special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, claimed the deal is a practical framework focused on repairing Soviet- and Russian-made equipment the Taliban already holds. Russia remains the only country to formally recognize the Taliban government, a step it took in July 2025.
North Korea signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty with Russia in June 2024 that includes a mutual defense clause. Pyongyang has since sent an estimated 14,000 troops to Russia's Kursk Oblast. In April, Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War put North Korea's losses at 7,058, including 2,251 killed.

articles.title: Kremlin says France's test nuclear launch is part of 'dead end' anti-Russia strategy
articles.body:
Kremlin says France's test nuclear launch is part of 'dead end' anti-Russia strategy
MOSCOW, Oct 7 - The Kremlin said on Wednesday that France's test launch of a nuclear-capable missile showed that Europe was building its defence identity around confrontation with Russia, describing the strategy as a "dead end".
On Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron hailed the test of the submarine-launched ballistic missile off the coast of Brittany as a message "sent loud and clear for wherever it must be received", without mentioning Russia directly.
The launch came amid heightened tensions over the war in Ukraine, European security, and nuclear deterrence. Russia has recently renewed warnings that it could use nuclear weapons to defend itself and the exclave of Kaliningrad.
Asked about the test launch, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia had received France's message and said it was an example of what he called Europe's obsession with militarisation.
"They are building their identity in the field of defence and security on the basis of confrontation with the Russian Federation. This is a dead end path. As history shows, it leads to nothing good," he said.
He said Russia remained on alert, but open to dialogue. "We believe that any problems should be resolved not through demonstrative missile launches, but through dialogue," he said. REUTERS

articles.title: Zelensky on Russian attack: Infrastructure in Kyiv and 12 regions hit, energy sector key target
articles.body:
Zelensky on Russian attack: Infrastructure in Kyiv and 12 regions hit, energy sector key target
According to Ukrinform, the head of state announced this in a Facebook post.
"One of the key targets was our energy infrastructure. The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes: 70 missiles in total, many of them ballistic, as well as 'shaheds.' Unfortunately, only some of them were shot down. Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge," Zelensky said.
According to him, air defense packages are now a vital necessity. "That is why every day we are looking for missiles for Patriot systems that can and must actually protect people's lives here, in Ukrainian skies," Zelensky said.
He also noted that the attack took place on the birthday of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin.
"Today, as a birthday 'gift' to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region. It was an ordinary five-story apartment building. Tragically, as of now, five people have been reported killed and 26 injured, including five children. There may still be people under the rubble. First responders are working nonstop at the site – doing everything possible to find every person," Zelensky said.
According to him, another five apartment buildings in Dnipro were damaged by Russian missile strikes, while four apartment buildings in Kremenchuk were damaged, with two people killed and eight injured. An apartment building in Zaporizhzhia was damaged by a drone. Two people were killed in Kyiv by Russian forces. Another two people were killed in Oleksandriia, Kirovohrad region.
"My condolences to all the families and loved ones of those killed. Overall, infrastructure in Kyiv and 12 regions came under attack last night," Zelensky said.
As reported, Ukraine's air defense forces neutralized five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles and 117 drones used by Russian forces to attack Ukraine since the evening of October 6.

articles.title: Ukraine squeezes more defense out of Soviet-era stock, pairing Kub launcher and American RIM-7 interceptors to catch Russia’s jet-powered drones
articles.body:
Kyiv is bolting two Soviet-era missile systems together to knock down Russia's fastest Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones. Ukraine's 156th Maksym Kryvonis Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment has downed about 20 air targets using a Kub launcher firing under the radar and fire control of a Buk unit.
Russia has switched to jet-powered Gerans, faster drones that Ukraine's cheap interceptors struggle to catch, so more of them reach their targets. The damage from Russian strikes is set to reach up to $10 billion this year, according to Ukraine's Economy Ministry.
Meanwhile, Western resupply has thinned too. Deliveries of air defense missiles from partners fell threefold in the first half of 2026 against 2025, even though those partners hold the missiles, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says.
So crews stretch what they have. In the Kub-Buk hybrid, a Kub launcher cannot aim on its own, lacking a radar to light up a target for its missile, according to Militarnyi. A Buk has that radar, so the two fire together, the Kub sending its 3M9 missile where the Buk points. The pairing is possible because both come from the same Soviet design line.
Western missiles in Soviet launchers
The same regiment reaches for a second workaround as Buk missiles run short. Its crews have rewired launchers to fire American RIM-7 interceptors, a Soviet-Western mongrel that troops nicknamed Frankenstein and the US calls FrankenSAM.
The patchwork earns its keep. One crew commander said some of these machines have more than 34 air kills each, and a single launcher has sent up RIM-7s 131 times, Ukrainian troops said.
A layered answer
The hybrids are one thread in a wider web. Ukraine is stitching together a layered defense against the jet-powered Gerans, leaning on electronic jamming, fighter jets, and a new class of homegrown interceptor drones. Each tool has limits, and the newest interceptors still bring down only the occasional jet drone.
The bet now is on numbers. Ukraine aims to build up to 400 interceptor drones a month by the end of October to chase the faster Gerans, Zelenskyy said on 2 October. Until that scale arrives, improvised launchers like the 156th Regiment keep filling the gap.

articles.title: Russian strike on Pryluky in Ukraine’s Chernihiv Region kills at least 19, including five children, in deadliest attack of the past month
articles.body:
The death toll from an Kh-101 Russian missile strike on the Ukrainian city of Pryluky on Oct. 7 has risen to 19 people, according to a report by President Volodymyr Zelensky. The strike occurred at around 6 a.m. local time, hitting a five-story residential building. Rescue workers recovered the bodies of five children from the rubble.
On the morning of Oct. 7, police in the Chernihiv Region reported that Russian forces had carried out a missile strike on Pryluky. Local authorities said three sites had been hit: a multistory residential building, a children and youth creativity center, and an unidentified business. Police immediately reported deaths and injuries.
Chernihiv regional governor Vyacheslav Chaus announced:
“A missile strike on Pryluky. One of the hits was directly on a residential apartment building. In the morning, while people were still asleep.”
Chaus later said at least nine people had been killed in Pryluky, including three children. About an hour later, he updated the toll to 13 dead, including four children. Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said the youngest victim was 8 years old. President Zelensky released the latest updated count, which brought the death toll to 19, in a post on Telegram at 8 p.m. Kyiv time.
Chaus said rescue crews were continuing to clear the rubble of the five-story building, meaning the number of dead and injured could still rise. Over 50 people were known to be wounded, with three of them hospitalized in serious condition.
The strike is already the deadliest Russian attack on Ukraine in a month. The Kyiv Independent previously reported that overnight and morning strikes had killed 15 people nationwide, and after the death toll in Pryluky rose from nine to 19, the updated figure brought the national toll to 25. President Zelensky confirmed the figures:
“The total death toll from this massive strike on Ukraine stands at 25 people. One hundred people were wounded. It was a combined strike involving numerous ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and Shahed drones. This was the ‘gift’ Putin gave himself for his birthday: the murder of children, the murder of people. During the day, there were new strikes with Shahed drones and aerial bombs.”
In a previous post, Zelensky said that three of the children who died in the strike were only one year old:
“Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhiy, who were only one year old, and eight-year-old Maksym. My condolences to all their families and loved ones.”
On Sept. 27, Russian attacks killed 14 people across Ukraine, while strikes on Oct. 6 killed 13. No single location had recorded as many deaths over the past month as Pryluky did on Oct. 7.

articles.title: First time since 2018: NATO’s top military body went to Kyiv to study the war it may one day face
articles.body:
NATO's Military Committee, the Alliance's highest military body, visited Kyiv on 6 October to reaffirm support for Ukraine, its chair, Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, said. It was the committee's first official visit to Ukraine's capital in eight years. The officers came to hear how Ukraine is fighting Russia and to draw lessons for NATO's own defense, and Dragone used the visit to warn Moscow.
Russia's war no longer stays inside Ukraine: its drones, saboteurs, and pressure campaigns increasingly reach NATO members. That turns Ukraine, the only European army facing Russia in combat, from a country the Alliance helps into one it learns from.
All 32 allies at the table
Dragone brought the military representatives of all 32 member states to hear the latest battlefield assessment directly from Ukraine's commander-in-chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, and his staff. They also came to learn what more NATO can do to support Ukraine, he said in an address recorded in Kyiv.
"After eight years, the NATO Military Committee comes back to Kyiv for an official visit. But while we were not physically present here, Ukraine is in our thoughts, in our discussions, in our decisions and following action every single day," Dragone said.
The visit fulfilled a promise he made to Drapatyi during their last conversation in August, the admiral said. It also follows a June visit to Kyiv by the North Atlantic Council, NATO's main political decision-making body. "We are here in full strength with a clear message. The bond between NATO and Ukraine is stronger and stronger," he said.
Lessons from Ukraine's commanders
The talks with Drapatyi focused on Ukraine's military priorities and lessons learned to strengthen Allied preparedness for current and future threats, Dragone wrote on X. The delegation also paid respects at the Wall of Remembrance of the Fallen for Ukraine in Kyiv.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
In his address, Dragone said Ukraine's courageous and resilient spirit remains unbreakable and serves as an example to other nations.
"An example that combines with all the lessons we can learn from your commanders, from their experience, which will ultimately help our Alliance too to better face today's and tomorrow's threats," he said.
To Russia: "You are failing"
Dragone also addressed Russia directly. NATO stands unwavering with Ukraine in the face of Russia's continued aggression and its reckless hybrid activities in member countries, he said.
"To those who think that by perpetrating acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, and violation of the airspace in national NATO territory they will undermine this support and our resolve, I will respond: You are failing. NATO support for Ukraine continues to grow, and our unity is stronger than ever."
Russia bears full responsibility for such dangerous and unacceptable behavior, and allies will keep sharpening their tools and strengthening deterrence and defense, the admiral added.
Drapatyi became Ukraine's commander-in-chief in July, when President Volodymyr Zelenskyy replaced Oleksandr Syrskyi after a week of political turmoil.
Kyiv under fire, Russian troops pushed back near Lyman
The day after the visit, Russia struck Kyiv and 12 oblasts with about 70 missiles. In recent weeks, Russian attacks have cratered the capital's bridges and hit a school, a café, and warehouses, as well as a maternity hospital. Ukrainian troops also retook ground near Lyman in the Vivaldi counteroffensive.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy condemns ‘vile’ attacks from Russia that killed 20 in one apartment
articles.body:
- The death toll from Russia’s latest attack on Ukraine has climbed to 28, its interior minister, Ivan Vyhivskyi, has said. Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones on Wednesday. The heaviest losses were in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile obliterated a five-storey residential building. Twenty people died in the attack, including five children, said Pryluky’s regional governor, Vyacheslav Chaus. On Wednesday evening, prosecutors in Kyiv said falling debris from a drone killed two people in a suburb of the capital.
- In Pryluky, an excavator and dozens of rescuers with shovels sifted through rubble at the site where several sections of the apartment block had collapsed. Emergency workers used ladders to get to the upper floors of what remained of the building, and as they worked their way down brought out 15 survivors. About 55 people were wounded in the town, regional officials said.
- Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the Pryluky attack one of Russia’s “most vile”. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” the Ukrainian president said. “This was one of the most vile strikes.”
- Russia’s defence ministry has said its forces struck a vessel heading to the Ukrainian Black seaport of Odesa with cargo for the Ukrainian military. The statement on Telegram on Wednesday gave no further details of the strike. The ministry also said Russian drones had hit infrastructure in Ukrainian ports, without elaborating.
- Bulgarian president Iliana Yotova blamed Russia’s war in Ukraine for worsening security in the Black Sea on Wednesday. Early on Tuesday, two ships were hit in a drone attack in Bulgaria’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone, with one sinking and the other damaged. The crew of the damaged ship were rescued but the crew of the sunken one remain missing. Yotova did not directly blame Russia, but said on Wednesday that the war had led to “a significant deterioration” in security for commercial vessels in the region. Bulgaria has halted its search for the missing crew.
- European Union envoys approved 1,646 new designations under the bloc’s sanctions regime for Russia, with most focused on the country’s military industrial complex, three EU diplomats said on Wednesday. More than half of the newly added entities and individuals are involved in the chain of production of Russia’s ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Ukraine finds US-made navigation sensor inside Russia’s new jet-powered drone
articles.body:
Ukraine has found the US component in a Russian jet-powered drone targeting civilians, supermarkets, medical warehouses, and bridges. According to its Defense Intelligence, the new weapon contains a PNI5GA magneto-inductive sensor made by the US company PNI Sensor.
The US-made navigation component adds to evidence that Western technology continues to appear in Russia's strike drones. HUR had already identified US-made chips in the Geran-4 in May, but the newly reported PNI5GA is a navigation sensor in a modified version of the drone that Institute for the Study of War (ISW) says Russia may seek to field ahead of winter.
A Russian engine replaces the Chinese one
Russia has also replaced the drone's Chinese-made Telefly turbojet engine with a Russian-made equivalent produced in Alabuga. Russia is using the Alabuga zone to bring more of its drone production home rather than importing Iranian or Chinese parts, according to the ISW.
"The remaining electronic units and components are unchanged and identical to those used in previous Geran UAVs," HUR said.
What the warhead is built to cut
The modified drone also carries a specialized KRSN warhead designed to cut through bridge structures and power-line supports. Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov described the warhead on 30 September, saying it consists of a 40-kilogram main charge and four strike modules. Its warhead is meant to destroy hardened targets made of steel and concrete and to damage cable-stayed bridges.
Russia has stepped up strikes on Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges across the Dnipro in recent days with such drones.
However, Russia may try to field more resilient and more dangerous versions of its strike drones before Ukraine has effective countermeasures in place. Russia could use them to degrade Ukraine's energy infrastructure and logistics ahead of a winter strike campaign that it said will very likely be brutal.

articles.title: Poroshenko: 2027 state budget must show Russia Ukraine can fight, Kremlin's bet on exhausting us will fail
articles.body:
Ukrainian MP and European Solidarity party leader Petro Poroshenko has called for all available resources and efforts to be directed towards strengthening the military capabilities of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), with this priority reflected in the Government Action Program and the draft State Budget for 2027. He expressed confidence that a strong army would enable diplomats to compel the Russian leadership to agree to a ceasefire.
"If we truly want to force Russia to cease fire, this must be reflected in the 2027 state budget. The budget must show Russia that Ukraine is capable of fighting, that our army will have weapons, personnel, ammunition and technologies, and that the Kremlin's bet on exhausting us will definitely fail," Poroshenko said in a video address.
He stressed the importance of a public discussion on ways to achieve peace, while noting that a ceasefire did not mean recognising the occupation or giving up territories.
"First, stop the fighting. Get all our partners on our side. Then negotiate for as long as necessary. But Ukraine must use every day of silence to rearm the army, develop its own defence-industrial complex, produce missiles, drones, air defence systems, technical intelligence countermeasures, electronic warfare systems and ammunition, restore the economy and strengthen our alliances," the politician said.
The party leader said that fulfilling commitments to European partners was a matter of the country's financial resilience during the war.
"European funds support macro-financial stability, the functioning of the state and the fulfilment of its social obligations. And this will allow us to direct more of our own resources towards the main priority – the Armed Forces of Ukraine… For us, European integration, financial support from our partners and strengthening the army are all part of a single strategy – to make Ukraine strong so that Russia understands that continuing the war will not bring it the result it seeks. We need strength not instead of diplomacy, but for diplomacy. Then there will be a result," Poroshenko said.

articles.title: 3 One-Year-Old Boys Among 18 Killed in Russian Strike on Pryluky – Zelensky
articles.body:
Three one-year-old boys, along with two older children, were among 19 people killed when a Russian missile struck a residential building in Pryluky in northern Ukraine during a massive overnight attack, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 7.
The boys – Oleksandr, Kyrylo and Serhii – were killed alongside eight-year-old Maksym, Zelensky said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Another child’s body was pulled from under the rubble in the evening, Ukraine’s interior ministry said, bringing the death toll up to 19.
Pryluky, around 150 kilometers (93 miles) east of Kyiv in the Chernihiv region, was among several Ukrainian cities targeted in Russia’s overnight missile and drone barrage.
The attack killed at least 25 people nationwide, including five children, and damaged residential buildings and civilian infrastructure.
A Russian missile hit a five-story apartment building in Pryluky, causing a large section of the structure to collapse. Emergency crews were deployed to search the rubble for survivors.
The State Emergency Service initially reported four people killed and 20 injured, including three children. The death toll later rose to 19, including five children, while 55 people were injured, including seven children.
Fifteen people were rescued from the site, including one child. Rescue workers continue to clear the destroyed structure and search for anyone who may still be trapped.
The overnight barrage also targeted Kyiv and Kremenchuk.
Ukraine Working on 5 Ceasefire Tracks With Partners, Foreign Ministry Says
In Kyiv, Russian forces launched ballistic missiles in several waves, with the first salvo arriving shortly after 3 a.m. Two people were killed, while impacts and fires were reported in several districts.
In Kremenchuk, Russian missiles and drones damaged apartment buildings and private homes. Two people were killed and seven injured, according to local authorities.
Zelensky said Russia knows it is striking ordinary Ukrainian cities and civilian life, calling the continued missile attacks a deliberate choice of terror.
“This is exactly what Moscow chooses despite all our efforts with our partners to bring peace closer,” he said, calling for increased pressure on Russia and more military aid for Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine says it struck plant making parts for Russian military aircraft engines—a Snizhne factory Russia has used since 2014
articles.body:
Ukraine's 413th Separate Raid Regiment of the Unmanned Systems Forces struck the Snizhne Machine-Building Plant in occupied Donetsk Oblast in September, working with other Defense Forces units, the regiment posted on 6 October, sharing a video of the strike. The General Staff reported the strike on the plant on 11 September, saying that the extent of the damage was being clarified.
The strike adds to Ukraine's campaign of long-range attacks on Russian military targets as Russia has begun its winter campaign of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure. Hitting the suppliers of aircraft parts goes after Russia's ability to keep its attack jets and helicopters flying.
The regiment said the plant works for Russia's military industry, producing engine components for attack aircraft and combat helicopters.
A former Motor Sich plant in occupied Snizhne
The Snizhne plant was a separate division of Motor Sich, a Ukrainian aircraft-engine maker based in Zaporizhzhia, a city that remains under Ukrainian control. Snizhne has been under Russian occupation since 2014. The plant specializes in producing parts for gas-turbine engines, including compressor and turbine discs and blades, the General Staff said. It never built whole engines. In September 2014, months into the occupation, it was machining blanks from Motor Sich's Zaporizhzhia plant into turbine blades and was one of only two plants in the former Soviet Union making such blades for helicopters, a plant worker said.
Motor Sich said in December 2017 that it had lost control of the plant. Weeks later, Viacheslav Bohuslaiev, then Motor Sich's honorary president and a member of parliament, told RFE/RL's Donbas.Realii that Motor Sich still owned the plant and had handed its management to a foreign company, while keeping it under the company's "full control."
In February 2023, Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office served Bohuslaiev a notice of suspicion of aiding a terrorist organization, alleging that Motor Sich shipped blanks to the Snizhne plant and received finished engine parts through foreign-registered companies. The case went to court in October 2023, and Bohuslaiev, who denies the charges, has been in pretrial detention since October 2022 as the trial continues.
Snizhne, which Russia uses as a rear base, has been hit before. In May, Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces and the Security Service of Ukraine struck a Russian training center for drone pilots in the city, and in September, a strike on energy infrastructure cut power across Snizhne.

articles.title: Ozel warns Saudi defence pact could drag Turkey into Yemen war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'Saudis' problem will be ours': Turkish opposition leader warns Ankara over defence pact
Turkish opposition leader Ozgur Ozel has strongly opposed Ankara’s defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, warning against Turkey being drawn into the Saudi-Houthi conflict and criticising Donald Trump.
Speaking at his New Party's parliamentary group meeting on Tuesday, Ozel said the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement amounted to Turkey becoming a party to a war involving Saudi Arabia, while accusing the government of committing to the deployment of Turkish troops before the agreement had been approved by parliament.
"An armed attack against one of the three countries will be considered an attack against all three. In other words, from now on, the Saudis' problem will be our problem," Ozel said.
Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the agreement in Mecca on 7 August. It commits the three countries to mutual defence, with an armed attack against one member treated as an attack against all three.
Ozel also criticised what he described as the government's alignment with US President Donald Trump's regional strategy, saying Turkey should not become part of a new Middle Eastern order dictated from Washington.
"We do not accept being part of Trump's Middle East order," he said.
His strongest criticism came when he warned against Turkey becoming subordinate to Washington's regional policy.
"We do not accept being Trump's soldiers on command," Ozel said.
Turkey could provide drones, intel
The comments reflect broader opposition concerns that the pact could draw Turkey deeper into the Saudi-Houthi conflict, although analysts say a direct Turkish combat role in Yemen is unlikely, at least initially.
"The Mecca pact is quite new, and the Houthis forced an early birth of the defence clause," Omer Ozkizilcik, a political analyst at the Atlantic Council, told The New Arab.
"We should expect the Turkish and Pakistani role in defending Saudi Arabia to increase gradually," he said, adding that Turkey could provide significant support for Saudi Arabia's defence against drones.
However, Ozkizilcik said he did not expect Turkey or Pakistan to take an active and direct combat role in Yemen, at least in the initial stages.
"However, the more important and efficient Turkish role may be on the intelligence level and strategy planning," he said.
Turkey has significant experience operating in civil war environments and engaging with tribes and non-state armed groups, Ozkizilcik said. Ankara also maintains relationships with non-Houthi Yemeni actors that have remained at a distance from Saudi Arabia.
"Turkey could potentially alter Yemeni dynamics against the Houthis," he said, arguing that Turkish intelligence support to Saudi Arabia could ultimately prove more effective than direct airstrikes.
The pact comes as fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and the Houthis has intensified, with the Iran-aligned group carrying out attacks against Saudi targets including the kingdom’s vital oil infrastructure and its capital.
The fighting has shattered years of relative calm in the Saudi-Houthi conflict, which has now become another major front in the broader Middle East war.
'No troops a century later'
Ozel argued that signing a mutual defence pact with a country involved in an ongoing war risked making Turkey a direct party to the conflict.
"Mutual defence pacts are concluded in peacetime. They are established for deterrence," he said. "Signing this agreement with a country that is at war means directly becoming a party to the war."
He also criticised the reported decision to deploy Turkish military personnel to Saudi Arabia, arguing that such a move required parliamentary approval.
"They have decided to deploy troops there," Ozel said, accusing the government of making commitments on behalf of parliament before the agreement had been formally submitted for approval.
He cited Article 92 of Turkey's constitution, which governs the deployment of the country's armed forces abroad, arguing that any decision to send Turkish troops must be approved by parliament.
"Article 92 of the constitution is there. If soldiers are going to be sent, it must go through parliament again," he said.
Ozel also pointed to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's earlier criticism of Saudi Arabia's role in Yemen, noting that Erdogan had previously questioned Riyadh's responsibility for the conflict.
Ozel argued that Ankara had now moved from criticising Saudi Arabia's intervention in Yemen to entering a defence arrangement that could require Turkey to stand alongside Riyadh in the event of an attack.
The Turkish government has said the agreement does not mean Turkey will directly intervene in the Yemen conflict. Ankara is instead expected to focus on defence cooperation, joint planning, military training and intelligence sharing with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
For Ozel, however, the agreement represents a fundamental shift in Turkish foreign policy.
"We do not accept the adventurism that would send our soldiers into the deserts of Yemen 100 years later," he said, in an apparent reference to Ottoman rule.
The comments come as Ankara seeks to deepen defence cooperation with Riyadh and Islamabad under the new pact, which comes more than seven months into regional conflict triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran. Before the Houthi escalation, Saudi Arabia, like the five other Gulf states, had come under repeated attack by Iran and Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
For now, analysts expect Turkey's role to focus more on helping Saudi Arabia defend its territory and on intelligence and strategic support than on sending combat forces into Yemen.

articles.title: Report reveals US aircraft losses in Iran war
articles.body:
Report reveals US aircraft losses in Iran war
At least 81 US aircraft have been lost since Washington and Israel started their war against Iran in late February, a report prepared for US lawmakers concludes.
The cost of destroyed or damaged American warplanes, helicopters, and drones could reach $3.3 billion, according to the paper released by the Congressional Research Service (CRS) on Tuesday.
The figures provided in the document are based on news reports and statements by the US Central Command and officials from the War Department, the CRS said. Congress previously criticized the Pentagon for its reluctance to provide a complete list of aircraft losses in the conflict.
Some of the most advanced US warplanes have suffered hits, including one F-35A Lightning II stealth fighter, which was damaged by Iranian fire on March 19, and 12 F-15E Strike Eagle fighters, the report read.
Three F-15s were shot down by friendly fire in Kuwait’s airspace in early March and another was hit over Iran the next month. Eight more suffered minor damage during Tehran’s missile attack on an airbase in Jordan in September, but have since been fixed and returned to service, the CRS said.
Seven KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling aircraft were also destroyed or damaged, according to the paper. Two were involved in an incident on March 14, with one KC-135 crashing in Iraq, killing all six crew members, and another performing an emergency landing. Six more refueling planes were affected in an Iranian bombardment of a US base in Saudi Arabia a few days later.
Other notable aircraft losses included two A-10 Thunderbolt IIs, two MC-130J special operations aircraft and an E-3 Sentry airborne warning-and-control aircraft, the report added.
Among the helicopters reported destroyed, one AH-64 Apache was shot down over the Strait of Hormuz, four AH-6 Little Birds were lost during rescue operations and an MH-60 Sea Hawk crashed over the Arabian Sea in mid-September.
The heaviest attrition was felt by the US fleet of MQ-9 Reaper drones, with at least 45 lost during the conflict with Iran, the report read.
The CRS said that several issues could benefit from congressional oversight, including whether the Pentagon possesses the funding to replace damaged aircraft and whether the losses of aging platforms, which are in short supply, could create capability gaps for the US military.
Last month, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) said that the conflict with Iran had cost the US approximately $38 billion in its first five months. The bill could increase by another $2 billion to $3 billion for every additional month of fighting, it cautioned.
Iran has increased its capacity to produce arms by 2.5 times compared to its pre-war level, the country’s Defense Ministry spokesman, Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik, said on Tuesday, warning that any further US aggression will be met with a decisive response by Tehran. The Islamic Republic currently manufactures more than 1,000 types of weapons systems and munitions, many of which have undergone technological upgrades during the conflict, he stressed.

articles.title: Putin Tells Tehran Ready to Help Mediate Middle East War: Iran State Media
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian in a phone call that Moscow was ready to help efforts to mediate the Middle East war, Iranian state media reported on Wednesday, with the months-long conflict locked in a stalemate.
Russia and Iran – two of the most sanctioned countries in the world – have significantly deepened their military and trade ties during Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, becoming increasingly reliant on each other.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Russian leader and Pezeshkian in their call spoke of the “positive and expanding trajectory of relations” between the two allies, stressing the need to further deepen ties, state news agency IRNA reported.
On the war, Putin “referred to efforts by some countries to mediate and help reduce tensions, saying that Russia supports” them, the agency added.
Putin said that Iran “can be assured that Moscow is also ready to play a role and provide assistance in this regard”, according to IRNA.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov last month said in a UN speech that Moscow was ready to help stabilise the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region as the war drags on.
The Middle East war began in late February with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Iran has blockaded the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway, which has become the focal point of the conflict, while the US has maintained a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

articles.title: EU idea of defense policy seeking ‘confrontation’ with Russia a ‘dead end’: Kremlin
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
The Kremlin said on Wednesday that the EU’s idea of a defense policy that it argued seeks “confrontation” with Russia is a “dead end.”
In remarks to journalists at a press briefing, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov accused Europe of being “obsessed with plans to militarize the EU” and said the 27-member economic union is moving toward adopting a military-political element.
“This is problematic because they are building their defense and security identity on the basis of confrontation with the Russian Federation – a dead-end path that, as history shows, leads to no good outcome,” Peskov said.
Amid France’s test of a new ballistic missile launched from a nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine a day earlier, Peskov said Russia remains vigilant and is closely monitoring the situation amid Europe’s “aggressive rhetoric” against his country.
Peskov further said that Russia has taken note of French President Emmanuel Macron’s remarks about the test’s “loud and clear” message, which he said in a video of him observing the launch that has been posted on US social media company X.
He added that while Russia is taking security measures in the context of the EU's “militarization,” Moscow remains open to dialogue with Europe.
Peskov also commented on a possible phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, which the latter said Tuesday would take place “very soon,” saying such a call has not yet been specifically agreed on.
“If such an initiative is put forward, I have no doubt that it will be promptly approved,” Peskov added.
On Tuesday, Trump said that he has a call scheduled "very soon" with Putin concerning reports emerging of a pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia’s Siberian region of Irkutsk.
Local authorities in Irkutsk imposed quarantine measures for people and several departments of the district hospital amid reports, which said an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East has been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”
Russia’s consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor announced Monday that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region is “calm,” while the development has raised concerns and public health fears on social media.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday that it is closely monitoring reports in this context, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russia that same day to provide full transparency and share detailed information with the international community regarding the incident.
“The media are reporting a great deal, and the overwhelming majority of what they are reporting regarding this situation is false information,” Peskov said, urging the public to rely on Rospotrebnadzor's statements regarding the situation.
He also said the World Health Organization has been informed of the situation “in accordance with established practice.”

articles.title: Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi Arabia, Yemen's Aden airport
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran-backed Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi Arabia, Yemen's Aden airport
Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Wednesday claimed attacks on military facilities and airports in neighboring Saudi Arabia as the fighting deepened the latest front in the Iran war and threatened a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said on social media that the rebels launched ballistic missiles and drones in the attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, but didn’t provide evidence.
Flights to and from the airport were briefly disrupted, according to Flightradar24, a tracking platform.
Saree said Abha airport, a frequent target of Houthi drones and missiles, was targeted. The rebels also claimed to have hit an air base in the city of Khamis Mushait and two military bases Najran and Asir. All are in southwestern Saudi Arabia and near the border with Yemen.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said they intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile north of Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces in recent days have launched a major ground and air offensive against the Houthis in an attempt to retake territory that the rebels seized about a month ago along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. Those positions gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping as they pursue a blockade of Saudi vessels.
On Monday, officials said forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen recaptured several key areas around the strait.
The fighting has since then centered in and around the crucial town of Dhubab, some 54 kilometers (33.5 miles) south of the port city of Mokha, according to both the Houthis and the Yemeni government.
Clashes were also reported in the district of Waziayah in southwestern Taiz province, which links Yemen’s mountainous highlands to the Red Sea, and overlooks roads to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Houthis target the airport in Aden  
The Houthis also said they launched a missile strike early Wednesday against Yemen’s port city of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government. An Associated Press journalist heard explosions around 2 a.m.
The rebels hit a military camp close to the Aden airport with ballistic missiles, Saree said.
Security authorities in Aden said the Houthis targeted the airport with two missiles, with no casualties. The airport is close to the seat of government.
“The targeting of this vital civilian facility represents a direct threat to the safety of civilians, passengers, employees and flight crews,” the Aden police said in a statement.
The attack on the Aden airport threatened “a humanitarian disaster,” as one missile hit close to the runway just before the scheduled landing of a flight from Cairo, the Human Rights Ministry said.
Flight 603, operated by Yemen’s flagship airline, landed safely in Aden at 3:30 a.m., according to flight tracking platform FlightAware.
The ministry said the missile hit as other passengers were waiting to board their flight to the Saudi coastal city of Jeddah.
“The Houthis believe that they can maximize Saudi economic costs and compel Saudi Arabia to surrender to Houthi demands by striking civilian infrastructure, such as oil facilities and airports,” the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, wrote in an analysis.

articles.title: Ukraine’s drone pilot calls it his proudest strike: cheap FPV drone detonating over two tons of explosives packed inside Russian mine-clearer
articles.body:
"Skipper", an FPV company commander in Ukraine's 413th Raid Unmanned Systems Regiment, has described destroying a Russian UR-77 mine-clearing vehicle with drones during the 2023 counteroffensive as the strike he is proudest of, according to Army TV.
The UR-77, nicknamed "Zmiy Horynych" after a fire-breathing serpent of Slavic folklore, carries a rocket-fired line charge to blow paths through minefields, as per Militarnyi. Each charge carries more than two tons of explosives, which is why a cheap FPV hit can trigger a blast far larger than the drone itself.
"It exploded so hard that I thought it was a small nuclear blast. There are more than two tons of plastic explosive inside, and when it went off after the second hit, it was something unbelievable," Skipper says.
Skipper joined the army at the start of the full-scale invasion and moved from infantry and aerial reconnaissance to commanding an FPV unit. His regiment now operates on the Zaporizhzhia front, where FPV drones conduct combat missions.
From sailing yachts to FPV drones
In civilian life, Skipper was a sailing instructor, and he says the sport partly helps in military work, especially his knowledge of navigation and radio communication. He is convinced that a technological edge can be one of the keys to victory.
He counts the UR-77 strike among his unit's early work, from a time when few Ukrainian units were using FPV drones at all, he says. The hit came during hard fighting in the counteroffensive, when his crews were among the first to work the FPV niche.
Russia turns a mine-clearer into a wrecking tool
The UR-77 was built in the 1970s for a different war, one of fast tank thrusts that needed enemy minefields cleared quickly. Its base rides on the chassis of the 2S1 Gvozdika self-propelled howitzer, and its charge can cut a lane six meters wide, with some anti-personnel mines detonated across a band up to 15 meters wide.
Modern combat changed that role. The classic mine-clearing use remains, but Russia now more often turns these machines on Ukrainian fortifications, using the line charge to flatten defenses rather than open a path.

articles.title: AI is changing Russia’s drone war on Ukrainian cities, deputy air defense commander says
articles.body:
Russian forces appear to use AI to plan air attacks and recognize targets amid raids on Ukrainian cities. This may include recent air attacks on Odesa that have come in waves with short gaps, Deputy Air Force Commander for Air Defense Colonel Yurii Cherevashenko says, Ukrinform reports.
Russia has already equipped its jet-powered Geran-4 drones with machine vision, allowing them to recognize and track targets on their own in the final seconds of flight. Recently, a single jet drone hit a locomotive in Odesa Oblast in late September and killed two railway workers.
The scale of Russia's AI use is hard to measure, Cherevashenko continues, but Ukrainian specialists already see its elements in how attacks are organized. The long, wave-by-wave strikes on Odesa would be far harder to plan and coordinate without it, he believes.
"Russian forces use AI to lay out attack routes and to recognize targets," Cherevashenko says, framing it as his own assessment rather than a confirmed fact.
The sea is harder to defend than land
Odesa Oblast is home to the biggest port in Ukraine, "Southern". Protecting it is a challenging task as guarding the airspace over water is tougher than over land, Cherevashenko says. Some air defense assets do not perform as well at sea, and in some cases, crews can intercept a target only as it approaches.
Weather adds to the problem, with storms and fog, while the open sea gives Russia more freedom to choose drone routes and launch points. To protect ports and the coast, Ukraine uses drone motherships, platforms that carry other drones aloft to extend their flight time and keep watch over set areas.
Ukraine answers AI with AI
Ukraine is also building its own AI for air defense. Automated turrets using machine vision now help counter Russian drones. According to Army Media, the Air Force says such turrets have scored their first shoot-downs, including of Geran-5 jet drones, with one soldier saying 50 rounds were enough to bring down a Geran.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry is going further. In late September, it unveiled an AI system called SPECTR, built by its A1 Artificial Intelligence Center and already in testing with several combat units, to analyze battlefield data, predict Russian moves, and suggest options to commanders.

articles.title: Rubio woos NATO member Iceland after Greenland deal
articles.body:
Rubio woos NATO member Iceland after Greenland deal
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has praised Iceland for allowing Washington to “project power” from the North Atlantic island nation into the Arctic.
Iceland is strategically positioned to help the Pentagon monitor Arctic airspace and conduct missions tracking Russian submarines in the Atlantic, not unlike Denmark’s autonomous territory of Greenland, which US President Donald Trump had notoriously threatened to annex. The US president and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen have signed an agreement to substantially increase Washington’s military presence there.
On Tuesday in Iceland, which joined NATO when it was created in 1949, Rubio praised Rejkyavik for allowing “the US military to project power using your land, your air, your sea, giving us a critical outpost for monitoring clandestine behavior and deterring our adversaries.”
The secretary stressed that Washington would not take action in Iceland without Reykjavik’s consent. Questions about US intentions were renewed last month after Trump posted an image showing North America and nearby islands covered in the Stars and Stripes, including Greenland and Iceland. Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir responded by summoning US Ambassador Billy Long to lodge a protest.
Rubio and Gunnarsdottir both played down the diplomatic incident at their joint press conference.
”We’re not talking about social media posts,” Rubio said, while Gunnarsdottir said the two governments “are looking forward, not backward.”
.@SecRubio on Trump social media post depicting U.S. acquisition of Iceland: "We're not talking about social media posts, I'm here, we're here meeting with a country...everything's very positive in our relationship." https://t.co/ZVA5q5Bjq1
— CSPAN (@cspan) October 6, 2026
Long also apologized last year after joking that Iceland could become the 52nd US state, with himself as governor. A petition urging Gunnarsdottir to reject his posting as US ambassador reportedly gathered around 2,000 signatures.
The US first established a presence in Iceland during World War II, taking over from British forces in 1941. A 1951 defense agreement signed under the banner of the newly created NATO cemented Iceland’s role during the Cold War.
Naval Air Station Keflavik, once the main US military hub in Iceland, was formally handed over to the local authorities in 2006, although the US continues to play a critical role in the country’s national security.
Rubio’s visit was designed to highlight decades of cooperation and the legacy of the Cold War. He and Gunnarsdottir met at the same venue where US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev held talks in 1986 on nuclear arms.
Washington’s ability to project military power worldwide is currently strained, with substantial assets tied down in the Middle East supporting the war with Iran. Rubio said the smaller US role in the joint Northern Viking exercise earlier this year reflected the need to “allocate resources” in response to current events and was not an “enduring decision” to reduce Washington’s attention to Iceland.

articles.title: Massive attack: Air defenses neutralize 117 drones, five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles
articles.body:
Massive attack: Air defenses neutralize 117 drones, five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force said this in a Telegram post.
Starting at 18:00 on Tuesday, October 6, the enemy attacked Ukraine with:
- Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missiles launched from Russia's Rostov region;
- Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles launched from Russia's Bryansk and Voronezh regions;
- 48 air-, land- and sea-launched Kh-101, Iskander-K and Kalibr cruise missiles launched from the Vologda and Kursk regions and the Caspian Sea, respectively;
- 130 Shahed-type attack UAVs (46 of them jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs and Parodiya decoy drones launched from Oryol and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, temporarily occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The main areas targeted were the Kyiv, Kharkiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:00 on Wednesday, October 7, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 161 targets, including:
- five Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Zircon/Oniks ballistic missiles;
- 39 Kh-101, Iskander-K and Kalibr cruise missiles (information on another six cruise missiles is being clarified);
- 117 drones.
Hits by missiles and attack UAVs were recorded at 18 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at five locations.
The attack is ongoing, with up to ten enemy UAVs remaining in Ukrainian airspace.
Earlier reports said that two people were killed in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district during the Russian attack in the early hours of October 7.
In Pryluky, Chernihiv region, two people were killed and seven injured in a Russian missile strike on October 7.
Also on October 7, Russian forces attacked critical infrastructure in Oleksandriia, Kirovohrad region, killing one person and injuring three others.
In Kremenchuk, two people were killed and seven injured in a Russian strike.
