articles.title: Three years after October 7: What changed for Israel, the Middle East and Russia?
articles.body:
Netanyahu’s October 7 response has no endgame. Russia has a stake in what follows
On October 7, 2023, Israel faced a horrific attack when Hamas killed over a thousand of its citizens and took hundreds of hostages. This atrocity can never be justified.
But there is another fact that we cannot ignore: Israel’s overconfidence and conviction of superiority over its adversaries led to the country’s most catastrophic security failure. Three years later, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government still has no convincing answer as to how the ensuing war is supposed to secure a safer future for the country.
More firepower, no endgame
The Israeli leadership’s main takeaway from the October 7 tragedy was the need to strike earlier, harder, and deeper. Deterrence gave way to destruction and elimination – first of the adversaries’ military capabilities, then of their leaders. The war expanded beyond Gaza, engulfed Lebanon, and finally escalated to a direct confrontation with Iran. Aggression became the guiding principle of regional policy. Yet, the tragedy also demanded a reassessment of the adversary, a sober evaluation of the country’s intelligence, and governmental accountability. Force can punish an enemy, but it cannot rectify the errors that made the attack possible in the first place.
Here, we clearly see the main contradiction of Netanyahu’s policy. Israel can destroy command centers, eliminate commanders, demolish infrastructure, and occupy territory. However, it is incomparably more difficult to shape neighboring societies in a way that would prevent the threat from re-emerging. The government expanded its military objectives but never defined a realistic political outcome. Who will govern Gaza? What kind of international recognition will that authority rely on? How can the daily lives of Palestinians be restored? What will ensure the safety of Israelis once the army withdraws? As long as there are no answers to these questions, every victory necessitates yet another military operation.
It would certainly be a mistake to deny the losses inflicted upon Israel’s adversaries. Hamas leaders Ismail Haniyeh and Yahya Sinwar, and Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah have been killed. In February 2026, Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in US-Israeli strikes. This case is distinct because the strike was linked not to the events of October 7 itself, but to the broader confrontation surrounding Iran and its nuclear program – though the events of October 7 had served as the initial catalyst.
It’s true that the loss of leadership disrupts command structures, severs ties, and hinders the restoration of military capabilities; however, the outcome must be judged by the state of the organizations and the country itself following these strikes. Iran retained its operational capacity; on March 8 – barely a week after the assassination – Mojtaba Khamenei, the son of the late Ali Khamenei, was elected as the new Supreme Leader. The death of the leader did not lead to the collapse of Iran, as both Israel and the US had hoped.
Nothing drives people to become militants like the loss of loved ones and the destruction of their homes and lives. Those who have survived deadly attacks on their families have nothing to lose; such people seek protection, revenge, or at least a sense of purpose – and militant organizations step in to provide all this. Moreover, Hamas and Hezbollah are structured not as armies with a vertical chain of command, but as networks comprising a military wing, social services, schools, charitable activities, family and community ties. A slain commander can be replaced, but such an environment cannot be easily destroyed by bombs.
History has already demonstrated this. Hezbollah emerged in response to the 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon; following the 1992 death of its leader, Abbas al-Musawi, Hassan Nasrallah took the helm and strengthened the movement. Hamas lost its founder, Ahmed Yassin, in 2004, yet won the parliamentary elections in Gaza just a couple of years later. Neither Hamas nor Hezbollah may regain their former strength anytime soon: they suffered great losses, and their supply and command capabilities have been crippled. Yet their story does not end with a list of slain commanders; it lives on in those who remain amidst the ruins.
Israel’s victories, the region’s instability
On the third anniversary of October 7, the situation in Gaza reveals the same disconnect between military pressure and political outcomes. The October 2025 agreement secured the return of the surviving hostages, and by January 2026, the bodies of the deceased had also been brought back from Gaza. However, Hamas has not been disarmed (despite Netanyahu describing it as largely disarmed), and the transition to a new governance structure has yet to begin. Israeli strikes continue, and the army reportedly controls about two-thirds of the territory. While Israel retains immense coercive power, it has been unable to establish a sustainable order.
The external aspect proved particularly difficult to handle. In the wake of October 7, Israel was naturally seen as a nation that had endured a horrific attack; everyone sympathized with it. Later, however, the image shifted: the world saw a devastated Gaza, a displaced population driven from place to place, and a humanitarian catastrophe. Now, facing another rainy winter, hundreds of thousands of people in Gaza are living in overcrowded camps where torrential rain floods their tents, or in buildings at risk of collapse. The longer this catastrophe drags on, the less people are willing to believe the explanation offered by Israel – that its actions are merely self-defense.
People all over the world have openly started expressing hostility toward Israel. Such a level of hatred would have been unimaginable just a few years ago. In the spring of 2026, Pew Research Center surveyed residents of 36 countries: on average, 67% held a very negative view of Israel, while only 25% viewed it favorably. Attitudes have deteriorated even in countries that sympathized most with Israel – such as the UK, Italy, Poland, and Australia. While criticism of the government’s actions does not equate to justifying Hamas, global anti-Semitism has risen due to the conduct of Netanyahu and his far-right ministers – Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, who publicly express hateful, dehumanizing statements.
Netanyahu has gradually lost the sympathy of the international community. Public outrage has moved beyond street protests, influencing diplomatic decisions and relations with partners. The stance of Arab states has also shifted. Before the war, they viewed the normalization of relations with Israel as a means of gaining access to technology, investment, and enhanced security guarantees. Now, public fury over the Palestinian tragedy makes direct rapprochement difficult. Saudi Arabia continues to demand irreversible progress toward Palestinian statehood as a condition for normalizing relations with Israel. The assumption that the Palestinian issue could be sidelined by striking deals with Arab governments proved unfounded. The issue could neither be bypassed nor frozen; it has resurfaced in the region in its most destructive form.
The Middle East has become less predictable. The weakening of Iran’s allies has shifted the balance of power but failed to establish recognized rules of coexistence. Regional states are seeking additional external security guarantees and are ramping up their military capabilities. The direct confrontation between Israel and Iran has expanded the scope of potential targets and the number of parties involved in the conflict. Israel’s tactical advantage exists alongside the heightened vulnerability of the entire regional system.
Russia’s stakes in a fractured Middle East
Russia is primarily concerned with Iran’s stability. Tehran is important both as an independent partner and as a participant in Eurasian transport, trade, and energy networks. Strikes on Iranian infrastructure and disruptions to its foreign trade directly affect Russian interests. The North-South Corridor is gaining importance as an alternative transport route, yet it is simultaneously becoming more dependent on Iran’s ability to keep ports, roads, and border crossings operational. Increased demand for the route does not automatically guarantee an increase in its capacity; the war increases the need for connectivity while complicating the task of maintaining it.
The fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in late 2024 significantly expanded Israel’s freedom of action in Syria. Under Assad, Israel had carried out periodic strikes but was compelled to factor in Russia’s presence, leading to a degree of restraint. Following the rise of Ahmed al-Sharaa to power, Israel began acting with far less inhibition: it expanded its military footprint in Syria, continued to dismantle military infrastructure, and began openly dictating terms to Damascus regarding the deployment of its own forces in the country’s south. The weakness of the new government presented Israel with an opportunity to impose limits on its neighbor’s sovereignty. For Russia, this signifies the collapse of the previous regional balance and creates a need to defend its interests in an environment where Israel increasingly seeks to unilaterally define the permissible rules of conduct for its neighbors.
For Moscow, these changes meant that it had to negotiate the terms of its military presence with the new authorities. Agreements reached in August 2026 regarding Russian facilities demonstrate that it is still possible to maintain relations. Exercising regional influence now requires greater flexibility and less reliance on a single political partner.
The economic consequences for Russia are also mixed. Disruptions in Middle Eastern oil supplies could keep global prices high and boost export revenues. However, a protracted war also drives up transport and insurance costs, disrupts payment settlements, and dampens economic activity in countries with which Russia is developing ties. Amidst this turbulence, Moscow’s role is growing. Russia is a major player in the global energy market, a partner in coordinating oil policy, and an independent diplomatic force that maintains contact with opposing sides.
Cooperation with Moscow enables the Persian Gulf states to expand their options and reduce reliance on US security guarantees. Diplomatically, the crisis offers Russia an opportunity to champion a more consistent approach to security. Its support for Palestinian statehood and opposition to strikes against sovereign nations resonate with many non-Western partners. However, political influence is only achieved when a country’s stance is backed by practical action. Moscow needs to maintain channels of communication with Iran, Israel, and Arab nations, facilitate agreements, and safeguard its own projects.
Netanyahu’s policy has failed to ensure long-term security. Despite Israel’s military achievements, the stated objective – long-term security – hasn’t been met, and the costs of the risky venture continue to rise. Three years on, Israel finds itself more capable of delivering strikes, yet less able to convince its neighbors – and even its allies (such as the Trump administration) – that its policies are paving the way to an acceptable future. As long as Israel substitutes these objectives with continued reliance on coercion, the consequences of the war will be felt far beyond its borders.

articles.title: Ex-Google boss warns Ukraine over Russia’s ‘Starlink rival’
articles.body:
Ex-Google boss warns Ukraine over Russia’s ‘Starlink rival’
Russia’s emerging Rassvet satellite network – often described as a “Starlink rival” – could provide Moscow’s military with sustainable communications and data to attack any target in Ukraine at will, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has warned.
Speaking to The Economist last week, Schmidt noted that while Ukraine was initially seen as the main innovator in the conflict, Russia had largely closed that gap while pressing its advantage with far greater resources.
Schmidt noted that one of these domains is Russia’s Rassvet satellite project, which he suggested was about a year from maturity. “Once that network is in place, it is more or less unblockable,” he warned, adding that this could let Russian forces “hunt anywhere” inside Ukraine.
The ex-Google CEO also weighed in on the idea of granting Ukraine access to Starlink over Russia, which could allow Kiev to rely on Elon Musk’s satellites to target oil refineries and civilian infrastructure, calling it “really a political decision.”
“It’s really a government decision. And the US government needs to grapple with this question,” he said.
Developed by private Russian aerospace firm Bureau 1440, part of the IKS Holding conglomerate, Rassvet debuted in 2023 with the launch of three experimental satellites. The network is designed to offer speeds of up to 1Gbps with latency below 70 milliseconds and to operate at an orbit of around 800 km – higher than that of Starlink to balance the number of satellites against an increased coverage area.
This year, the company launched a total of 32 satellites, after six experimental spacecraft sent up in 2023 and 2024, with plans to have 292 satellites by some time in 2027.
On Tuesday, the company also unveiled a line of user terminals, some of which claimed speeds of up to 700 Mbps. The Ukrainian outlet Militarny suggested that some of the showcased terminals could eventually be fitted to strike drones.
Russia’s deployment of Rassvet has sparked major concern in Ukraine across the spectrum. In July, satellite communications expert Vladimir Stepanets told Militarny that the first satellite group provided at least two stable “communication windows” over the country daily, each lasting more than an hour.
Ukraine’s military intelligence separately told Janes it had recorded Russian forces using Rassvet communications over Ukraine for “several hours” by late July and warned the system could support real-time reconnaissance and strike-drone operations.
Vladimir Zelensky’s technology adviser, Sergey Beskrestnov, also warned that a fully deployed Rassvet could become a “small catastrophe” for Kiev as it would provide Russia with online control of strike drones and missiles.
Zelensky himself told the Financial Times last week that he had repeatedly asked US President Donald Trump to sanction companies involved in Rassvet development and production while warning that the network could become operational “by the end of this year or early next year.” Trump has not publicly responded to the request.
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, who now serves as deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said that attempts to “block” Rassvet would amount to destroying it and could trigger “full-scale space warfare.”

articles.title: Russian Attack Leaves Unexploded Ballistic Missile Among Homes in Kyiv, Hits Film Studio and Bird Center
articles.body:
An unexploded Russian ballistic missile was discovered among residential buildings in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district on Wednesday morning, Oct. 7, after a massive overnight attack on the capital and multiple Ukrainian regions.
Bomb disposal experts and State Emergency Service (DSNS) crews were deployed to secure the site, remove the missile’s warhead, and transport it for subsequent neutralization.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Main Directorate of the National Police in Kyiv said the missile had been launched at the capital overnight and was found in a residential area.
“Attention citizens! In the Darnytskyi district, police and the DSNS are conducting a complex demining operation involving an unexploded ballistic missile – launched by the enemy at the capital overnight – that was found amidst residential buildings,” police stated.
Police bomb disposal experts and DSNS units were working at the scene, while access to the area was restricted.
Specialists were tasked with removing the warhead and transporting it to a testing ground for subsequent neutralization. Police urged Kyiv residents not to approach the site of the operation.
The capital was targeted by ballistic missiles several times, with strikes reported at around 3:23 a.m. and again at approximately 5 a.m.
Rescuers extinguished a fire covering 200 square meters (2,153 square feet) at a local garage cooperative, where the bodies of the two victims were discovered during the firefighting operation.
Triumph of Common Sense: Dissecting the Carlson-Rees-Mogg Interview
Dovzhenko National Film Studio hit again
The attack also damaged the Oleksandr Dovzhenko National Film Studio, one of Ukraine’s oldest film studios.
“Another difficult night and a morning of bad news. The film studio’s building housing three soundstages was damaged in a massive missile attack,” the studio said on Facebook.
No one was killed in the strike. Rescue workers, police and emergency medical personnel were operating at the scene.
Russia also attacked the studio in June, destroying Ukraine’s largest and oldest costume collection.
Warehouse destroyed, bird rehabilitation center burned
The overnight strikes also completely destroyed the central warehouse of ATL Autoservice, a major automotive goods chain that stored much of its stock of oils, batteries, and car accessories.
The company confirmed the destruction and said its employees were safe.
“Most importantly, the people are alive. That is the only thing that cannot be replaced. Everything else is a matter of time, resources, and our collective effort,” the company said.
ATL Autoservice said its partners and suppliers had been informed that the company remained financially and operationally stable and would continue to fulfill all its obligations.
In the Kyiv region, the “Sadyba Niushanyk” bird rehabilitation center was also destroyed in the combined overnight attack involving drones and ballistic missiles.
The center’s co-founder, Iryna Snopko, said the strike in the Vyshhorod district completely destroyed the bird infirmary, chicken coop, and quail enclosure.
“We’ve been hit. The bird facility – including the chicken coop and quail house – has burned down. Birds and a cat were inside, along with all the equipment and feed,” Snopko wrote.
“Nyushanik Estate” was a specialized center caring for birds of prey and waterfowl. Its specialists looked after storks, swans, owls, hawks, and kestrels.
Birds that could not return to the wild because of severe injuries remained at the estate permanently. The center’s staff also regularly advised members of the public on how to rescue injured or stranded birds.

articles.title: Massive Russian attack on 7 October: 161 aerial assets brought down, hits at 18 locations
articles.body:
Massive Russian attack on 7 October: 161 aerial assets brought down, hits at 18 locations
The Russians launched a massive attack on Ukraine using various aerial weapons on the night of 6-7 October. The Ukrainian Air Force has said air defence has brought down 161 Russian aerial assets.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force on Facebook
Details: Since 18:00 on 6 October, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with:
- Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missiles from Russia's Rostov Oblast
- Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles from Bryansk and Voronezh oblasts, Russia
- Forty-eight air-, land- and sea-based Kh-101, Iskander-K and Kalibr cruise missiles from Russia's Vologda and Kursk oblasts and the Caspian Sea respectively
- A total of 130 Shahed-type attack drones (46 jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the following areas: Oryol and Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Russia, and occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in occupied Crimea.
The Russian strikes are mainly targeting Kyiv, Kharkiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
The aerial attack is being repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces.
Early reports indicate that as of 09:00, air defence had intercepted 161 assets:
- Five Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400 ballistic missiles and Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missiles
- Thirty-nine Kh-101, Iskander-K and Kalibr cruise missiles (information is being gathered regarding a further six cruise missiles)
- 117 Shahed-type loitering munitions (38 jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs and drones of other types.
Strikes by Russian missiles and attack UAVs have been recorded at 18 locations and the fall of intercepted weapons (debris) at five locations.
Quote: "The attack continues, as up to 10 enemy UAVs are in the airspace. Follow safety rules!"
Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: "Russian army "gave" Putin "gift" of destroying residential building in Pryluky," attacked energy infrastructure - Zelenskyy on Russia's shelling
articles.body:
"Russian army "gave" Putin "gift" of destroying residential building in Pryluky," attacked energy infrastructure - Zelenskyy on Russia's shelling
Kyiv • UNN
At least 11 people were killed and more than 30 wounded as a result of the overnight attack. Russia launched 70 missiles and drones at Kyiv and 12 regions.
Today, on putin’s birthday, the Russian army "gave" him the "gift" of destroying a residential building in Pryluky. Overall, Russia fired 70 missiles at Ukraine overnight on October 7, many of them ballistic; infrastructure in Kyiv and 12 regions came under attack, with the energy sector among the key targets. At least 11 people are known to have been killed and more than 30 wounded. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported this in response to the massive Russian attack, UNN writes.
Today, on putin’s birthday, the Russian army "gave" him the "gift" of destroying a residential building in Pryluky, Chernihiv region. It was an ordinary five-story apartment building. Unfortunately, as of now, five people are known to have been killed and 26 wounded, including five children. People may still be trapped under the rubble. Rescuers have been working continuously at the site, doing everything possible to find everyone. Russian missile strikes also damaged five more apartment buildings in Dnipro and four high-rise buildings in Kremenchuk. Unfortunately, two people were killed and eight wounded. A high-rise building in Zaporizhzhia was damaged by a drone. In Kyiv, the Russians killed two people. Two more people were killed in Oleksandriia. My condolences to all the families and loved ones of those killed. Overall, infrastructure in Kyiv and 12 regions came under attack overnight
As the President reported:
One of the key targets was our energy sector. The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most insidious attacks: 70 missiles in total, many of them ballistic, as well as "Shaheds." Unfortunately, only some of them were shot down. Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge
"And air defense packages are a vital necessity for us right now. That is why every day we are looking for missiles for the "Patriots," which can and must genuinely protect people’s lives here, in the Ukrainian sky. Thank you to everyone who is helping us," the Head of State noted.

articles.title: How NATO Plans to Win: ‘Theory of Victory’ Against Russia to be Unveiled in Poland
articles.body:
NATO’s top military commander in Europe is set to unveil his “Theory of Victory” in Poland, a strategy that reportedly sets out how the alliance could repel and ultimately defeat a Russian attack on its eastern flank.
Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, will publicly present the plan for the first time during a visit to Warsaw next week, Poland’s Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz told Polish state news agency PAP on Tuesday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Bloomberg reported on Monday that the plan draws heavily on lessons from the war in Ukraine, where relatively cheap drones and rapidly evolving technologies have reshaped the battlefield and exposed the limits of forces built around more expensive conventional weapons.
The news outlet, which saw an unclassified version of the document, said NATO would seek to stop a Russian incursion by using ground forces backed by low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-enabled targeting.
Once the alliance had gained freedom of maneuver, its forces would seek to rapidly destroy Russian command-and-control systems and inflict a quick and overwhelming defeat.
Grynkewich is due to present the plan at the Warsaw Security Forum, an annual conference bringing together senior political, military and security officials, that will be held in the Polish capital on October 12-13.
Russia Repeatedly Tests Romanian Air Defense
Organizers said the strategy had until now been discussed only at the highest level of NATO’s military leadership. Kosiniak-Kamysz told PAP that he had seen Grynkewich’s proposals and rated the US general’s preparations “very highly.”
                                                                                                                                                                         The plan reportedly covers how NATO would respond to a potential Russian incursion into the alliance’s territory. Photo: Andrzej Iwanczuk/NurPhoto/Getty Images                              
‘Maintain NATO’s advantage’
Grynkewich’s spokesman, Col. Martin O’Donnell, told Bloomberg: “The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage.”
“Given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked,” he said.
According to Bloomberg, the strategy also covers hybrid attacks that fall below the threshold of open warfare, with NATO seeking to demonstrate sufficient readiness to convince a potential adversary that aggression would fail.
Poland is a significant setting for the unveiling. The NATO eastern-flank state borders Ukraine and Belarus and shares a 210-kilometer land frontier with Russia’s heavily militarized Kaliningrad exclave, leaving it exposed in the event of any aggression by Moscow.
Tensions on eastern flank
The plan comes amid heightened tensions between Moscow and the NATO alliance more than four years into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
NATO says hostile Russian activity against its members and partners, including airspace violations, cyberattacks and acts of sabotage, has increased in frequency.
But NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said last week there was “no imminent threat” to alliance territory, adding that NATO would detect and respond to any Russian military buildup.
The alliance has nevertheless steadily reinforced its eastern defenses since Russia invaded Ukraine, with Poland among nine countries now hosting multinational battlegroups.
NATO has also adopted what it describes as its most comprehensive and detailed defense plans since the Cold War.

articles.title: Denmark says Russia has conducted sabotage attacks against its defense firms
articles.body:
Denmark says Russia has conducted sabotage attacks against its defense firms
COPENHAGEN, Oct 7 - Russia has begun sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying Ukraine after concluding that broader disruption efforts failed to curb Western military support for the country, a Danish intelligence official said on Wednesday.
The shift reflects a significant escalation in Moscow's hybrid warfare campaign, the official, from the Danish national security and intelligence service (PET), told a homeland security conference in Copenhagen.
"What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more," the official said.
Russia concluded that its previous broad-spectrum targeting "did not have the effect of deterring the Western (military alliance) NATO from supporting Ukraine," the official added, and while Moscow maintains political control over operations, its operational boldness is growing and Russia is now "trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line. That means weapons production."
Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen rejected the allegations on Wednesday, accusing Danish authorities of making unfounded accusations against Russia.
The official cited a Russian defence ministry list of alleged European drone and drone component manufacturers that Moscow said in April amounted to potential military targets, without elaborating further.
Russia is increasingly using untrained proxies — including homeless people and people addicted to drugs — recruited via Telegram and other social media platforms. Recruitment typically starts with low-threshold tasks such as reconnaissance or photography, then escalates toward actual sabotage operations, PET has said.
"It could be anyone just looking for quick money," the official said. "If the first person isn't successful, they'll throw another one at the problem until they succeed."
Denmark's defence intelligence service last month said Russia is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against the West in coming months, after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
In September 2025, before Denmark hosted an EU summit, drones disrupted air traffic at six Danish airports, including Copenhagen, the Nordic region's busiest, in what Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called a hybrid attack on her nation. REUTERS

articles.title: Yemen conflict escalates as Houthis hit Aden airport, target Riyadh
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthi rebels targeted Aden International Airport with ballistic missiles and explosive drones early Wednesday, the Transport Ministry said, amid intensifying combat between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed forces.
The Saudi-led coalition, pushing to retake strategic territory seized by the Houthis, said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh.
The escalation came after Yemeni government forces, with Saudi-led coalition air support, launched a lightning counteroffensive this week to capture the Red Sea coast around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait shipping route and the city of Mokha.
Yemen's government said that forced the Houthis out of areas they had captured last month, reviving a complex 12-year war, which led to one of the world's worst humanitarian crises and fragmented the Arab world's most impoverished country.
One missile landed near the runway at Aden International Airport minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the ministry said. Authorities cancelled the landing and diverted the aircraft to Jeddah, while two planes on the runway were moved away from the area over fears of further strikes, it added. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control.
The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of Riyadh.
It said it was tracking the launch platform over Houthi-controlled Sanaa and would destroy it, but gave no details of casualties or damage.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on the airport.
The Houthis, which control much of Yemen's north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran's influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene. A U.N.-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted heavy fighting, but it did not lead to a lasting settlement, with a spillover from the Iran conflict triggering the latest fighting.
The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the Houthis. The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran's Middle East proxy network and says it develops its own weapons. Tehran also rejects the allegations.
Earlier Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported.
In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had attacked Abha International Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones. It was not immediately clear whether this was linked to the missile the coalition said it had intercepted near Khamis Mushait. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha airport.

articles.title: October 7 and the forever war it unleashed, from Gaza to Yemen
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
October 7 and the forever war it unleashed, from Gaza to Yemen
The war triggered by the events of 7 October 2023 will drag on for years to come. What began that day quickly revealed much broader objectives, many of which had been taking shape well before the fighting erupted.
Just a month earlier, in September 2023, the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, or IMEC, was announced in New Delhi. The project, backed by the United States, India, the European Union, France, Germany, Italy, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, was designed to connect Asia with Europe through the Middle East.
IMEC was conceived as an integrated network spanning energy, oil, telecommunications, technological infrastructure, subsea cables, ports and railways. The aim was to bind these countries together economically and strategically, partly as a counterweight to China’s Belt and Road Initiative.
In political terms, the corridor would connect South Asia to the Middle East and Europe, while helping contain China and its allies. It would also create a framework for deeper integration between Israel and regional states, reinforcing the path towards normalisation and the Abraham Accords.
Then came 7 October.
Israel soon made clear that it saw the war as part of a much broader regional project. It openly spoke of reshaping the Middle East and began pursuing geographic and demographic changes in the arenas where it was fighting, particularly Gaza and Lebanon. It has continued along the same path in both, while extending its military operations into Syria.
With firm US backing, Israel remains committed to that wider project. The war eventually led to direct confrontation with Iran, a conflict Israel still appears keen to revive, with preparations seemingly continuing in coordination with Washington.
Iran is no minor regional actor. It has built a project of its own and, for years, wielded considerable influence across the Middle East. Israel wants to dismantle that influence and replace it, particularly in Lebanon, while consolidating its position in Syria, pushing the Palestinian issue out of the regional equation, and forcing other states towards peace agreements and normalisation.
Washington has its own objectives. It wants to bring Iran to heel while opening the country to Western investment and economic influence, including in its oil sector. The broader aim is to loosen Tehran’s ties with China and pull it closer to the West. If that effort fails, Washington may once again turn to war.
But the conflict is about more than the Middle East. At stake is the wider balance of power that will emerge globally.
The United States wants to preserve a world in which it remains the dominant power, without a serious rival. To achieve that, Washington is willing to pressure allies and adversaries alike, and at times even exploit the pressure exerted by its rivals to keep its own partners in line.
Donald Trump’s approach to the Russia-Ukraine war offers one example. His strategy towards Europe is based on extracting concessions, reminding European states of their military and political dependence on Washington, and reinforcing the idea that they remain vulnerable without US support.
A similar logic is at work in the Gulf, where regional states are now confronting a major war in Yemen.
At the start of the latest fighting, Trump signalled that he was unwilling to enter the war directly on Saudi Arabia’s side. At the same time, contacts between Washington and the Houthis came to light. Rather than shutting down that channel, Trump appears content to keep it in play, allowing pressure on Riyadh to build while steering events towards the political outcome he wants.
None of this means the United States has abandoned Saudi Arabia. Security, military and intelligence coordination continues, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio has publicly insisted that Washington will stand by the kingdom.
But for Trump, support is never free. Every war, intervention or security guarantee comes with a political price. In this case, that price is to draw the Gulf states, much like Europe, more firmly into Washington’s confrontation with Iran.
Some now see the war in Yemen as preparation for another strike on Iran and for the formation of a new coalition built around that objective, just as the wars in Gaza and Lebanon preceded the direct confrontation with Tehran.
There is no consensus, however, on how the Yemen war will unfold.
Some expect a prolonged war of attrition that drains all sides. Others believe it could be decided far more quickly, pointing to changes in military tactics since Operation Decisive Storm, shifts in the regional balance of power, the emergence of the Mecca Alliance, and US support for Saudi Arabia against the Houthis at a time of continuing US-Iranian hostility and renewed fears of war.
What is clear is that this is no longer simply a war over Palestine. It has become a struggle over the regional order itself, with consequences for the balance of power both in the Middle East and beyond.
Israel sees the Yemen war as another opportunity to expand its influence. It has little interest in seeing large, powerful states emerge around it and will continue trying to weaken those it regards as potential rivals.
Netanyahu has hinted at this logic before. After Israel struck Iran and its regional allies, he spoke of turning next to what he described as an emerging “radical Sunni axis”. The author understood this as a reference to the growing alignment between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.
The Yemen war gives Netanyahu an opening to offer Israel’s services to Riyadh, while trying to pull Saudi Arabia away from Turkey and Pakistan and towards an agreement under the Abraham Accords framework.
Trump is likely to push in the same direction, while also seeking to recalibrate relations between Turkey and Israel.
The war therefore presents a major test for the states of the region, particularly the members of the Mecca Alliance and, above all, Turkey and Saudi Arabia.
The interests of Ankara and Riyadh have already converged in Syria. There, both have faced serious challenges but have so far managed to avoid the worst outcomes, while helping preserve Syria’s territorial unity against Israeli efforts to fragment the country. That has also been aided by a degree of strategic overlap with the United States.
Yet the Israeli threat has not disappeared.
Israel has little interest in seeing Syria re-emerge as a unified, strong state with the ability to rebuild economically. Its incursions and attacks continue, as does the seizure of additional Syrian territory.
The latest war in Yemen has added another layer to this competition.
As the fighting began, the members of the Mecca Alliance quickly convened and announced the activation of its collective defence mechanisms. In practical terms, that means greater Turkish and Pakistani support for Saudi Arabia through military technology, weapons and intelligence, while also limiting the space for Israel to exploit the war or insert itself into the conflict.
Only hours after the meeting, Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa arrived in Riyadh for talks with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, raising the prospect that Syria could also move closer to the Mecca Alliance.
Such a development would deepen security and military cooperation and help fortify other regional fronts, particularly if the Yemen war intensifies, if Iran and its allies retaliate elsewhere, or if Israel decides to expand its military operations in southern Syria.
Damascus is already preparing for such possibilities. It has reinforced its military presence along the borders with Iraq and Lebanon in anticipation of further escalation.
Israel, meanwhile, could look for other ways to increase pressure on the Mecca Alliance. That could mean further action against Syria, or moves elsewhere, including in Somaliland and the wider Horn of Africa.
Lebanon is also firmly in the eye of the storm.
The war there has not ended. Israel continues its military operations and territorial encroachments while maintaining intense political pressure.
Lebanon says it wants to be the last Arab state to sign a peace agreement with Israel. Israel, by contrast, wants to pull Beirut into such an agreement far sooner.
Its strategy is to isolate Lebanon through political, military and economic pressure, force it to the negotiating table, and prevent it from remaining part of a broader Arab bargaining position.
If Israel succeeds in drawing Lebanon into this framework, the consequences would extend beyond Beirut. It would increase pressure on Arab states more broadly, place Syria under even greater strain, and help constrain Turkey’s position in the Mediterranean.
The war, then, did not truly begin on 7 October, and it will not end any time soon.
When it does, the regional order that emerges will bear little resemblance to the one that existed before it.
Mounir al-Rabih is editor in chief of Beirut-based Al-Modon
This is an edited translation from Arabic
Have questions or comments? Email us at: editorial-english@newarab.com

articles.title: Naval drone hits oil tanker off Russian resort city Sochi, triggering massive blaze
articles.body:
An oil tanker off Russia’s Black Sea coast was struck by a naval drone, triggering a huge fire and black smoke cloud that blanketed parts of the resort city of Sochi, Russia’s transport ministry has said.
The transport ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked and that “crude oil is burning openly in the waters of the Black Sea”.
“Firefighting efforts will begin once the fire’s intensity has subsided and rescue vessels can safely approach the tanker,” the ministry said.
A crew of 23 – all Indian citizens – had been rescued, it added.
Russia and Ukraine have targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since the conflict began, and Russia has recently attacked grain vessels carrying Ukrainian goods near the coast of Romania.
There was no comment from Kyiv on the attack.
Videos and photos circulated on social media from Sochi – a popular Black Sea resort city of almost 500,000 people – showed bright orange flames out at sea and a thick column of black smoke billowing into the sky.
Local officials restricted access to the coast and beaches.
Elsewhere on Tuesday, Bulgaria’s prime minister said that two commercial vessels had been struck by drones in the first attack on shipping in the Nato member’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
Bulgarian authorities said that the origin of the drones was under investigation, but Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the drone strikes. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev condemned the attack.
After an emergency government meeting, Radev said: “This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law.”
Sea and aerial drones attacked the ships about 80 miles (128km) off Bulgaria’s coast, he said.
Zelenskyy warned in his nightly address on Tuesday that a “massive strike” from Russia was likely to come, and in the early hours of Wednesday Kyiv was attacked.
Russian strikes damaged buildings and warehouses across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram.
Agence France-Presse reported multiple explosions in Kyiv, and Reuters reported two people were killed by Russian strikes.
A separate Russian strike on Ukraine’s south-eastern city of Dnipro damaged an industrial facility, officials said, without giving details.
Kyiv has been under increased attack as winter approaches, with Russian airstrikes targeting energy infrastructure, rail and road transport, including bridges that connect the city over the Dnipro river. Air raid sirens have sounded almost constantly day and night, urging residents to take cover in basements, shelters and subway stations.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: "Gryphon": Ukrainian forces combine robots with drones to strike Russians deep in the rear. Interview with the commander of "NC13"
articles.body:
"Gryphon": Ukrainian forces combine robots with drones to strike Russians deep in the rear. Interview with the commander of "NC13"
In January of this year, the "NC13" strike UGV unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade tested a new tactic deep behind Russian lines. Since then, the unit has successfully carried out more than 100 similar operations, turning what began as an experiment into a proven combat system.
The new tactic was named "Gryphon" in honor of a service member from the unit who went missing in action in 2023 while carrying out a combat mission near Andriivka in the Donetsk region. It was in this area, near Bakhmut, that Oscar-winning Ukrainian director Mstyslav Chernov filmed the documentary "2000 Meters to Andriivka" during a different Ukrainian counteroffensive.
The concept behind the new tactic involves deploying kamikaze UGVs, essentially ground robots, deep behind enemy lines using heavy bomber drones. After landing, the robotic systems continue moving toward their targets and can be used to strike key positions, logistics, and personnel while also creating disruption in the enemy rear.
The "NC13" unit was also behind an operation that drew significant international attention about a year ago, when Ukrainian forces captured Russian positions without deploying infantry, using only UGVs and drones.
As a result, two Russian service members surrendered to the robotic systems, after which the machines escorted them to Ukrainian positions as prisoners of war.
Today, the new tactic is part of the Third Army Corps' large-scale operation known as "Vivaldi." Since the start of the offensive, Ukrainian forces have liberated 176 square kilometers of territory (68 square miles).
According to the Office of the President of Ukraine, Russian forces suffered more than 5,000 casualties, including those killed, wounded, and captured, during the first three stages of the operation. It is currently known that Ukrainian forces have taken 250 Russian service members as prisoners of war (POWs). The Third Army Corps separately reported 2,000 Russian personnel casualties during the latest stage alone.
Approximately 80% of logistics and 90% of wounded evacuation for Ukrainian troops during all three stages of the operation were carried out by unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs.
"NC13" commander Mykola Zinkevych, call sign "Makar," explains how the new "Gryphon" tactic works, how the idea of air-dropping ground robots emerged, what happened during the first operations, how Russian forces are reacting to the technology, and why he believes Ukraine is shaping the future of technological warfare.
He also discusses how Western partners are becoming less able to understand Ukrainian military technologies and, more broadly, the needs of modern warfare.
Can you please explain, in general, what this new tactic involves?
In general, this is a sabotage-operation tactic that was fully planned, developed, and implemented by the "NC13" strike unmanned ground systems unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade.
The tactic is genuinely new and has no equivalent anywhere in the world because no one had previously deployed unmanned ground vehicles from unmanned aerial vehicles.
The concept itself is that, using heavy bombers, we drop small ground-based kamikaze systems deep into enemy territory, at a distance of 5 to 15 kilometers (3 to 9.3 miles). From there, we carry out different sabotage operations: eliminating enemy personnel, destroying logistics, and so on.
When did you begin using this tactic? Any first operation is essentially a test. How confident were you that it would work?
We carried out the first operation about eight months ago (in January 2026- UP).
We spent quite a long time developing the tactic itself and modifying the equipment because standard ground-based kamikaze systems are not designed for this kind of use.
The engineers spent a great deal of time making it work. The pilots also had to learn how to operate with these systems and deploy them correctly. The planning department, accordingly, spent a lot of time preparing the operation.
But when it worked for the first time, the excitement was incredible. Our first operation went 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) deep behind enemy lines. We deployed two ground-based kamikaze systems near the target, and from there, the systems themselves moved into the shelter.
It was an enemy staging point where personnel were brought in. They would stop there to rest before moving on to carry out their missions. We eliminated that staging point using two ground-based kamikaze systems.
What was the enemy's reaction? What did it look like from their side?
In fact, the enemy did not understand what had happened, what system had been used, what had struck them, or what tactic we were employing.
Even now, it remains a major surprise for them because we operate in different sectors within the Third Army Corps' area of responsibility.
We combine different technologies in order to change the rules on the battlefield.
We have been able to strike the enemy from the air at significant depth for quite some time. We have also been using unmanned ground vehicles to strike enemy forces for a while.
But this combination (UGV + UAV) allows us to operate at greater depth, in areas where the enemy does not expect to be reached and where they feel relatively safe. So we are going to take that freedom away from them.
How many such operations have been carried out so far?
More than one hundred. We always work systematically. If something works once, twice, or three times, we still do not consider it a fully established capability because it could be accidental.
But when something is carried out more than ten times, it becomes a systematic approach. We have SOPs, standard operating procedures, in place for this tactic: how to use it, where it can be implemented, and what its capabilities are.
It can be used for reconnaissance, mining deep behind enemy lines, striking targets, hunting moving enemy personnel, disrupting logistics, and more. We have fully developed this tactic, identified all of its capabilities, and now use it as a full-fledged tool on the battlefield.
War in general, and especially Russia's war against Ukraine, is a war of speed. Everything depends on who can come up with something new and adapt faster. Are the Russians already trying to do something similar?
I am confident that we are far ahead of the enemy. Even when it comes to the systematic use of strike unmanned ground vehicles on the battlefield, which we have been doing for about a year, the enemy is still far behind.
So when it comes to tactics like "Gryphon," which we are discussing today, there is still a very large gap between us and them.
But I would not rule out the possibility that, over time, the enemy will begin copying this approach and using similar methods.
In fact, during more than 100 successful missions, there have been many almost meme-like moments when the enemy had no idea what they were looking at and would actually approach the robots to inspect them.
There was one occasion when we managed to completely disrupt a Russian mechanized assault that had been planned for foggy weather conditions. At the time, we were actively targeting one of the enemy's logistics routes. We eliminated several personnel over the course of the day.
They started to panic because they did not understand what was happening. They thought a sabotage and reconnaissance group, or SRG, had broken through into their rear. As a result, they canceled the mechanized assault they had planned for that day.
So these small robots can create very significant disruption.
In general, there was serious panic among enemy forces at the depth where we were operating. And panic is actually very important because if we create panic within enemy ranks, they begin to have problems controlling their personnel. Soldiers start refusing to carry out missions, which then creates panic at the command level because commanders do not understand what is happening in their rear, and so on.
That creates destabilization, and all of that works in our favor.
Why exactly do they panic?
Even when you know what it is, you can become even more afraid. You do not know where it might be waiting for you, where it might drive, where it might catch up with you, and so on. So in some ways, it is even better when they know.
You know, now you have to watch not only the sky, but also the ground beneath your feet. Not just for mines, but because something might come after you.
There was one interesting intercepted communication where an enemy soldier reported to his commander that a "Baba Yaga" (russian military slang for heavy bomber drones - UP) had flown in, landed, then started driving and chasing them.
It was pretty funny to listen to.
But it did catch them in the end.
This tactic seems to have many advantages. Which one do you consider the most important?
- The absolute advantage of using any technology is that, first and foremost, we do not have to put people at risk. We preserve human lives.
For me, as the commander of a strike UGV unit and as a former infantryman, it is actually more important to preserve our own personnel, to protect Ukrainian infantrymen, assault troops, and soldiers, than it is to destroy the enemy. Destroying the enemy comes second.
And in fact, by destroying the enemy, we prevent them from advancing toward our forces and make life easier for our infantry. So above all, any technology helps us protect human life. Robots do not bleed, and human life is priceless. That is essentially our guiding principle throughout everything we do.
The next advantage, of course, is depth. The depth at which we can operate with these systems.
Yes, 10 to 15 kilometers (6.2 to 9.3 miles) is not the maximum range. Unfortunately, I cannot disclose the exact figures. But we are deployed and then continue moving very, very deep into enemy territory. The deeper we go, the more valuable, so to speak, the resources and targets we can destroy.
You touched a little on the future. Is there already a vision for how this technology could develop? I will not ask exactly how, but should we expect it to be scaled up further?
Yes. By the end of 2026, there will be many large-scale, exciting, and interesting stories, announcements, and new tactics from our unit.
We already have a number of newly implemented applications and tactics involving unmanned ground vehicles, (including the use of UGVs equipped with grenade launchers, which is also a new and unique tactic -UP).
It is simply not yet the right time to talk about them. And we have many more things planned. So we just need to wait a little longer.
Western countries have traditionally been considered leaders in military technology. You speak with foreign military officials. How well do they understand the technological breakthrough currently taking place in Ukraine?
I attended the Munich Security Conference in February and had the opportunity to speak with many foreign military officials, various partners, and government representatives.
In reality, they are very far behind. Absolutely.
They understand what we are talking about, what we are deploying, what we are using, and how it works. But they do not fully understand its importance and value on the battlefield, or just how much the battlefield itself has changed.
And I am more than certain that the rest of the world is lagging very, very far behind.
Even the technologies I see being introduced into militaries around the world are still quite far removed from what is actually being used on the battlefield between Ukraine and Russia.
Looking specifically at unmanned ground vehicles, I have seen their entire evolution on the front line, from 2024 until today.
We work, interact, and collaborate with many manufacturers. A great deal of equipment has been developed because we provided our expertise and doctrine.
I also have a certain number of systems produced by foreign manufacturers, and there is a very significant difference between them (Ukrainian and Western UGVs - UP).
We are not even talking about price, although the prices are extremely high. But in terms of actual battlefield use, Western systems still fall far short of the needs of the modern battlefield.
Are foreign partners reaching out to Ukrainian military personnel often enough for this kind of expertise? Is there interest in contributing to the development of these innovations?
I would say they do reach out, but not nearly as actively as they should. In my opinion, this is the kind of expertise people should be actively pursuing, not just occasionally asking, "So, what are you working on?"
No one knows what will happen in the world tomorrow. We live in a time when you never know what to expect.
If Ukraine can offer something to its partners, what can it receive from them in return?
Ukraine is the sword and shield of Europe. It is defending not only itself and its own future, but the future of the entire continent.
So every time other countries help us, they should understand that they are not only helping Ukrainians. They are also helping themselves.
Right now, Ukraine especially needs effective and timely weapons deliveries from its partners. First and foremost, this means air defense systems capable of protecting Ukrainian cities from attacks, as well as heavy weapons, including artillery and armored vehicles, that can help Ukraine regain the initiative on the battlefield.
Of course, this support must always be justified. Because Ukraine is doing everything possible to defend its territory, - liberate occupied land, and protect the future of the country and the nation, - that is why all of these processes and technologies have emerged.
The battlefield has effectively become a testing ground for innovation. On the one hand, that is a positive thing.
But on the other hand, it is deeply tragic, because every such achievement comes at a price. And that price is not paid in money. It is paid with the lives of Ukrainian service members and people who should have been the future of the Ukrainian nation.
History has seen many cases where a promising technology or a major breakthrough emerged, but it was overlooked, underfunded, or never scaled up...
This is not something that appeared only today. It is something that has been developed and planned over a period of time, has already been implemented for quite a while, and is constantly being modernized.
It will continue to evolve and eventually grow into something new.
Because there are technologies that work today. There are technologies that will work tomorrow. And there are technologies that worked yesterday but no longer work today.
But each of them becomes a driving force behind the next one.
Kateryna Lisunova, Ukrainska Pravda

articles.title: Russia's Deadly Attacks Damage Homes Across Ukraine On Putin's Birthday, Zelenskyy Says
articles.body:
PRYLUKY, Ukraine -- Rescuers frantically picked through rubble and debris of a destroyed apartment building in northern Ukraine as they search for survivors of a Russian missile attack that killed at least 18 people.
At least 20 people nationwide, including two in the capital Kyiv, were killed in the October 7 barrage.
The bombardment was part of near-daily attacks that have steadily increased in frequency and ferocity, as the Kremlin struggles on the battlefield front line.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it one of the "most vile" attacks in recent memory, and he noted they occurred on the birthday of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Russian forces "destroyed" a residential building "as a birthday 'gift' to Putin," Zelenskyy said in a post to X.
At least 10 other such buildings were damaged elsewhere, along with Ukraine's energy infrastructure, one of Moscow's other "key targets," he said.
In Pryluky, which is about 150 kilometers east of Kyiv, firefighters, emergency workers, and local volunteers dug through bricks and building debris searching for survivors of the attack. The five-story building was mostly torn apart by the Russian strike with its roof destroyed, windows blown out.
"The fire was right in front of my eyes. There were explosions. I was screaming in my apartment. Extremely scary. I can't describe it," one woman, who gave her name as Lidiya, told Current Time.
"So many people have died. I knew everyone here," she added, holding back tears.
With a fifth wartime winter approaching, Russian strikes on Ukraine have become a daily occurrence.
Moscow has previously sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by attacking the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures.
Since this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia and middle-range strikes targeting its key logistics in Ukraine's occupied eastern and southern regions.
Tanker Hit In Black Sea
Following the latest Russian attacks, Zelenskyy later reported on what he called Kyiv's "just responses." He said Ukrainian forces had targeted two of Russia's oil facilities and a military training ground overnight on October 7, adding, "There was also a response in the Black Sea."
Hours earlier, Russia's Transport Ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked by "naval drones" near the Black Sea resort city of Sochi.
The ministry reported an intense fire following the attack, saying that "crude oil is burning openly" on the surface of the Black Sea. It later added that the crew of 23, all Indian citizens, had been rescued and the fire had been extinguished.
According to the Ukrainian monitoring site BlackSeaNews, the vessel was used by Russia as part of its so-called shadow fleet, a network of vessels used to transport Russian fuel and evade sanctions.
Sochi's local authorities said access to the city's coast and beaches was being restricted. Previous Ukrainian strikes on energy targets in southern Russia have caused oil slicks, prompted beach closures, and led to toxic black rainfall.
The developments came amid renewed US interest in negotiating a diplomatic settlement to the long-running war.
While US President Donald Trump has long said it is one of the key goals of his presidency, Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions.
Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the Kremlin has shown no willingness to compromise on its key demands, including full control over Ukraine's key eastern Donetsk region, a stronghold Russian forces have not yet been able to capture.

articles.title: Denmark accuses Russia of sabotage against defence companies
articles.body:
Denmark accuses Russia of sabotage against defence companies
According to Danish intelligence, Russia has launched sabotage operations against Danish companies that supply goods to Ukraine, having concluded that broader destabilisation attempts failed to curb military support.
Source: Reuters
Details: This shift indicates a significant escalation in the hybrid warfare waged by Moscow, said Josefine Christensen, lead analyst at the Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET), during a homeland security conference in Copenhagen.
Quote from Christensen: "What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more."
She noted that Russia had concluded that its previous broad-spectrum attacks "did not have the effect of deterring the Western NATO from supporting Ukraine".
Christensen added that Moscow maintains political control over the operations, while operational boldness is growing. Russia is now "trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line. That means weapons production".
Without providing further details, Christensen cited a Russian Ministry of Defence list naming European manufacturers of drones and their components, which Moscow said in April had been designated as potential military targets.
Background: A shipment of Russian sunflower oil bound for India was cancelled and other cargoes were delayed after attacks on Black Sea ports disrupted exports from India's top supplier, an industry official and trade sources reported.

articles.title: Kyiv region was struck by Russian drones and ballistic missiles: warehouses damaged and fires broke out
articles.body:
Kyiv region was struck by Russian drones and ballistic missiles: warehouses damaged and fires broke out
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked the Kyiv region with drones and ballistic missiles, damaging warehouses and causing fires. Two men were killed in Kyiv.
On the night of October 7, Russia attacked the Kyiv region with drones and ballistic missiles; production and warehouse premises were damaged. This was reported by Kyiv Regional Military Administration head Tymur Tkachenko on social media, UNN writes.
The enemy continues its attacks on the Kyiv region. At night, the region came under a combined attack by enemy drones and ballistic missiles. Three production and warehouse premises were damaged in Obukhiv district. Fires broke out and have now been contained. A truck and trailer were also damaged. Fortunately, there were no casualties
Update
The enemy also attacked Kyiv.
According to the Kyiv City Military Administration regarding Russia's attack on the city's civilian infrastructure on the night of October 7, as of 08:00 the following is known: "At night, the enemy attacked the capital with ballistic missiles. As a result of the terrorist attacks by the Russian Federation, the consequences were recorded in two districts of the city of Kyiv":
-  in Podilskyi district, a missile fell in a non-residential area, causing a fire; 
-  in Darnytskyi district, a missile strike caused a fire at a garage cooperative. The fire was extinguished; there is destruction. At another address, debris was also recorded falling in an open area. 
"Unfortunately, two men were killed in the enemy shelling," the Kyiv City Military Administration reported.

articles.title: Russian missile and drone strikes across Ukraine kill six and injure more than 20
articles.body:
Russian missile and drone strikes across Ukraine kill six and injure more than 20
Russian forces attacked Ukraine overnight on October 7 with missiles, including ballistic missiles, and drones.
In Kyiv, a Russian strike damaged nonresidential buildings, offices, and warehouses in the Obolonskyi, Shevchenkivskyi, and Podil’skyi districts, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. In the Darnytskyi district, a Russian strike caused a fire at a garage cooperative, killing two people. Two others were rescued.
Russian forces also struck other regions of Ukraine.
In the Chernihiv region, a missile strike damaged a five-story residential building in the city of Pryluky. The State Emergency Service reported that four people were killed in Pryluky and 20 were injured, including three children.
A Russian strike also damaged residential buildings in Kremenchuk. Local authorities did not report any casualties.
Russian forces also attacked a transportation infrastructure facility in Zaporizhzhia and an industrial facility in Dnipro.

articles.title: German court orders detention of former intelligence chief after spying arrest
articles.body:
A formal arrest warrant has been issued against Germany’s former top spy, with a judge ordering him to be held in pre-trial detention, a day after he was arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency.
August Hanning, 80, is accused of buying secret documents from a former colleague and using them to advise a foreign intelligence service, according to the office of the federal prosecutor.
Hanning’s arrest on Tuesday, along with that of his former office head, referred to as Manfred D. It has sent shock waves through Germany’s political and intelligence community, with analysts calling it potentially the country’s biggest espionage scandal since the end of the cold war.
It has raised questions in Berlin over how Germany’s foreign intelligence service can uphold its reputation internationally, particularly at a time of heightened security concerns. Also under scrutiny is the sustainability of rules governing the conduct of retired senior officials and their ability to earn extra income based on their insider knowledge and professional networks.
Hanning was head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service (BND) between 1998 and 2005.
A lawyer for Hanning denied he had been involved in any wrongdoing on Wednesday, telling the conservative daily newspaper Die Welt: “While it is true that he was in possession of confidential documents, the allegation that he passed on information contained therein to the detriment of Germany, let alone for payment, is incorrect.”
Manfred D, who was also placed under formal arrest on Wednesday by the judge in Karlsruhe, has yet to respond to questions via his lawyer.
Hanning is alleged to have agreed in 2010 to pay for information from Manfred D, who allegedly then smuggled it out of the BND. Manfred D, 64, had worked under Hanning and went on to serve subsequent BND bosses after Hanning, before retiring in March this year.
Hanning is believed to have received about 2,000 documents from Manfred D until June 2022, some of which were classified, according to prosecutors. He is alleged to have used the information in his papers for his private consulting work.
Prosecutors were alerted to Hanning’s alleged criminal activities by investigators gathering evidence in a separate child kidnapping case involving a steakhouse restaurant dynasty, which the former spy chief is accused of participating in using his former contacts with Israeli intelligence. Christina Block, an heiress to the business, allegedly paid Hanning and a retired police officer more than €100,000 (£85,000) for their roles in the alleged abduction of her two children from her ex-husband.
A report in Der Spiegel on Wednesday said investigators were looking into a possible connection to the foreign intelligence service of Azerbaijan as one of the agencies Hanning may have been passing information to.
Azerbaijan’s media and broadcasting council denied any connection to Hanning or the investigation. “The malicious intent of the forces behind this disinformation operation is to damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations,” the council said in a statement.
The scandal has awakened memories of the Günter Guillaume affair, when an East German Stasi spy and his wife posing as refugees infiltrated the government of the then chancellor Willy Brandt, leading to Brandt’s resignation in 1974.
Marc Henrichmann, the head of the parliamentary committee overseeing the intelligence services, which has repeatedly raised questions about the post-career consulting activities of intelligence agency employees but has been told legal obstacles stood in the way of challenging them, said he was “fairly flabbergasted” by the affair, but stressed it was as yet unclear the breadth and extent of the alleged wrongdoing.
“As yet we don’t know exactly what happened,” he told the public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk, while acknowledging the need to “restore broken trust” in the BND.
On Wednesday, politicians and intelligence analysts called for stricter regulation around allowing former security employees to make use of their influence and knowledge after retiring.
The scandal comes at a time when Germany is attempting to make its intelligence agencies, including the BND and its domestic sibling, the BfV, more robust, efficient and independent from those of its allies, in particular boosting their powers of surveillance to more effectively tackle sabotage and hacking attacks, amid rising threats from external powers such as Russia and Iran.
The scandal is yet another blow to the BND’s reputation. Not only is it notoriously dependent on information from foreign agencies to foil terror attacks on German soil, but it has faced other cases of its staff allegedly spying for other countries.
It has also been reeling from the case of a department head, Carsten L, who was accused in December 2022 of spying for Russia. His trial is now being heard by Berlin’s higher regional court.
Sensitivities over the country’s past, when dictatorships misused their powers of surveillance to spy on their own people, have made reform of the agencies hard to pursue.
Hanning, the son of a brickyard owner, rose through the ranks of the intelligence service to become its head. After the attacks of 11 September 2001, he oversaw the investigation into some of the terrorists who had studied in Hamburg. He initiated wide-reaching reforms of the BND including bringing it closer to politics, becoming a close adviser to the then interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble. He spoke out against a “culture of leaks” and was deeply critical of the NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden, calling him an “internal offender”.
Once his civil service career was over, Hanning continued to hold a role as a respected behind-the-scenes negotiator, and frequently intervened in government security policy debates. At the same time he built up his consultant business, founding an agency with his wife, Ruth, called Hanning Consult, and worked for various other global consulting agencies. He even produced a “spy cookbook” with his wife, called “Top(f) Secret” (Topf being the German word for saucepan).

articles.title: 81 US aircraft lost or damaged during Iran war, congressional document shows
articles.body:
Yasin Gungor
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
At least 81 US fixed-wing, rotary-wing, and uncrewed aircraft were lost or damaged during military operations against Iran, according to a recent report prepared by the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service.
The figures compile operational incidents recorded since Feb. 28 across Pentagon records, US Central Command (CENTCOM) statements, military inspector general findings, and press accounts.
The compilation shows extensive losses across uncrewed platforms, led by 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones and three MQ-1 multi-role craft downed during operations, along with one MQ-4C Triton that crashed in a flight mishap.
Manned combat airframes also sustained substantial hits.
Twelve F-15E Strike Eagle fighters were affected, including three destroyed by friendly fire over Kuwait, one downed over Iran, and eight that suffered light damage during an Iranian missile strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan before returning to service.
Iranian ground fire damaged an advanced F-35A Lightning II, while two A-10 Thunderbolt II ground-attack jets were lost or heavily damaged.
Support fleets suffered major attrition as well.
Seven KC-135 Stratotanker refueling craft were affected, including one fatal crash in Iraq that killed six crew members and five reportedly damaged on the ground in Saudi Arabia.
One E-3 Sentry early warning plane took a direct hit, two MC-130J special operations transports were intentionally destroyed during a rescue mission, and seven military helicopters, including AH-64 Apache and AH-6 Little Bird models, were lost or damaged.
The disclosures arrive amid soaring financial tolls in the Iran war, which began Feb. 28 with coordinated US-Israeli strikes.
A Lead Inspector General report in September estimated total campaign expenses at $33.4 billion through late June, including $3.7 billion in equipment losses, while the Congressional Budget Office projected hardware replacement costs at up to $3.3 billion.
The Congressional Research Service noted that the number of aircraft may remain subject to revision due to classification, ongoing combat activity, and attribution.

articles.title: Taliban and North Korea Hold Talks During Military Exercises in Russia
articles.body:
The Taliban and North Korea held talks during Russia’s Center-2026 strategic military exercises.
Afghanistan’s Ministry of Defense reported the talks on October 3.
The exercises were held from September 28 to October 3. Representatives from Afghanistan and North Korea attended the drills as observers.
Nasibullah Madani, commander of the Joint Combat Training Command, led the Afghan delegation. He met with North Korean military attaché Ro Ki Chol. A photo released by the Afghan ministry shows the two together at an arms exhibition.
According to Safir TV, during the visit, Taliban representatives also held talks with military officials from China, India, Vietnam, Colombia, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and other countries.
The ministry said the discussions covered bilateral relations, the exchange of military experience, professional training, and opportunities for cooperation.
These topics referred to the Afghan delegation’s meetings in general. The statement did not provide any specific details about the talks with North Korean representatives or mention any concrete agreements with Pyongyang.
In addition to observing the exercises, the delegation visited a military equipment exhibition. The exhibition featured heavy weapons, drones, long-range missiles, and robotic systems.
The Taliban is also strengthening its military ties with Russia. As Militarnyi previously reported, on May 27, 2026, the two sides signed an agreement on military-technical cooperation.
The agreement’s text was not made public. According to Zamir Kabulov, Russia’s special envoy for Afghanistan, the agreement primarily provides for the restoration of military equipment already in the Taliban’s possession.
The Russian side has also said it could establish training centers to maintain the equipment.
Meanwhile, Russia is expanding its military partnership with North Korea. In June 2024, Moscow and Pyongyang signed a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty.
