articles.title: Russian forces destroy central warehouse of the ATL auto service network in Kyiv
articles.body:
Russian forces destroy car parts retailer ATL's main warehouse in Kyiv
A Russian attack on Kyiv has completely destroyed the central warehouse of the ATL car parts retailer and servicing chain. As a result, its shops and service stations will have to rely on existing stock in the coming days, limiting the range of products available.
Source: ATL on Facebook
Details: Most of the engine oils, batteries and other automotive products supplied by the company were stored and distributed through the warehouse. No employees were injured.
Their car parts retail outlets and service centres are continuing to operate as usual. ATL said it had prepared for such a disruption by distributing supplies across its facilities and building up stocks in advance.
Meanwhile, the loss of the central warehouse will disrupt logistics. In the coming days, customers will only have access to products already in stock at the network's shops and service centres.
The company says it is continuing to meet its commitments to partners and suppliers. The extent of the damage is still being assessed, and no figure has been given for the losses.
Background:
- On the night of 6-7 October, Russian forces conducted a large-scale combined attack on Ukraine, using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and attack drones simultaneously.
- The Russians launched the massive attack using various air attack weapons. According to the Air Force, air defence brought down 161 aerial assets.

articles.title: National Security Council condemns strikes on ships in the Black Sea
articles.body:
News
National Security Council condemns strikes on ships in the Black Sea
President Iotova: Russia’s War in Ukraine has significantly deteriorated the security environment in the region
Wednesday 7 October 2026 19:36
Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 19:36
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The Consultative Council on National Security (CCNS), convened by Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova, strongly condemns the attacks on merchant ships in the Black Sea, calling them a gross violation of international maritime law, and calls for an immediate investigation to establish those responsible for the attacks, Bulgaria’s head of state Iliana Iotova said following a five-hour meeting of CCNS. The meeting discussed security risks in the Black Sea and potential threats to the country’s critical infrastructure arising from the ongoing war in Ukraine.
The head of state convened the first Consultative Council on National Security of her term following an incident in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, where two merchant ships flying foreign flags were hit by military drones on October 6.
President Iotova said that Russia’s war in Ukraine has significantly worsened the security environment in the Black Sea region:
President Iliana Iotova
PHOTO BGNES
“Given the incidents, it was acknowledged that there are serious challenges to protecting critical infrastructure. These threats are a direct consequence of the lack of prospects for a peaceful resolution to the military conflict''.
Iliana Iotova said CCNS members had also agreed to continue implementing the measures adopted by the Council of Ministers to counter risks and threats. ''The Consultative Council on National Security agreed on proposals to the executive and legislative branches, with the proposals being adopted by a three-quarters majority. Three parliamentary groups voted against. We condemn the attacks on merchant ships and call for an investigation to establish those responsible for the attacks”, Iliana Iotova added.
“An immediate ceasefire is the strongest guarantee of our security. Bulgaria must play an active role in this process,” the president also said.
“Bulgaria should urgently hold consultations with Romania and Türkiye on joint action to halt attacks on merchant ships in the Black Sea and ensure the safety of navigation. Bulgaria should take an active role in negotiations and in finding consensus among the countries bordering the Black Sea: Russia, Ukraine, Bulgaria, Romania, Georgia and Türkiye”, Iliana Iotova added.
PHOTO BGNES
It is also necessary to strengthen maritime situational awareness through the use of unmanned aerial systems for reconnaissance and surveillance, as well as to accelerate the modernization of the armed forces with the aim of acquiring counter-drone systems with kinetic capabilities, in close cooperation with NATO and the European Union.
According to the participants in the meeting, Russia’s war against Ukraine has led to a significant deterioration in the security environment in the Black Sea region.
Premier Rumen Radev
PHOTO BGNES
Following the meeting, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said that, at this point, there are no grounds for Bulgaria to categorically say that Russia was responsible for the strikes on vessels in the country’s exclusive economic zone. According to him, determining the origin of the drones used in the attacks should be based on concrete evidence rather than hypotheses.
Ivaylo Mirchev
PHOTO BTA
“What became clear from the Consultative Council on National Security is that there are sufficient indications of clear Russian involvement in the sinking of one of the vessels”, said Ivaylo Mirchev, co-chairman of Democratic Bulgaria. He added: “I don’t remember anyone at the table having doubts that Russia was behind the attack.”
The MP also said that the text adopted by the Consultative Council on National Security was not supported by four parliamentary groups - Democratic Bulgaria (DB), We Continue the Change (PP), Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS) and Vazrazhdane.
The meeting was attended by the Speaker of Parliament, the prime minister, the ministers of defence and interior, the heads of the security services, and representatives of the parliamentary groups.
Edited by Diana Tsankova
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov

articles.title: Former German intelligence chief August Hanning may have passed secret documents to Azerbaijan, Der Spiegel reports
articles.body:
August Hanning, the former head of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND) whose arrest was announced on Oct. 6, may have passed classified documents to an agent from Azerbaijan, according to an investigation by Der Spiegel. Hanning, who was detained on suspicion of espionage and disclosure of state secrets, allegedly prepared an analytical report for Azerbaijani intelligence. Manfred D., the former head of Hanning’s office, was also detained.
According to investigators cited by Der Spiegel, the former BND head unlawfully obtained 2,000 classified documents and may have shared them while communicating with a foreign agent, though it remains unknown whether Hanning’s analysis reached the recipient, and German authorities have not officially confirmed that they suspect the former intelligence chief of working for Baku. His connection to Azerbaijan, however, is beyond doubt: he was officially a member of the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum.
Hanning headed the BND from December 1998 to November 2005. According to prosecutors, in 2010 Hanning made an arrangement with Manfred D. to receive information from the BND in exchange for payment. Hanning intended to use the documents he received in his private consulting business. According to the German outlets Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR, the documents included materials from foreign partner agencies, documents on Iran’s nuclear program, and documents on the Russian military.
In at least one instance, Hanning is known to have prepared a security report for an unnamed foreign intelligence service (not a Russian one, according to media reports). Meanwhile, after leaving the BND, Hanning made at least seven trips to Russia, The Insider found — all of them within the period from 2015 to 2019.
Often, Hanning would fly into Moscow in the evening and fly out the next day. In the summer of 2016 he flew from Munich to Moscow on the evening of July 6 and flew out to Berlin on the afternoon of July 7. A similar trip between Berlin and Moscow took place in May 2019.
The investigation into Hanning has continued for several months. He came to the attention of law enforcement last year in connection with his possible involvement in the abduction of the children of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block. As part of that case, Hanning’s home was searched in September 2025; some of the BND documents were found during those searches.

articles.title: Russian barrage hits Kyiv hours after Zelensky warns of impending attack
articles.body:
Russian strikes kill 24 across Ukraine after Zelensky warning
Russian missiles and drones hit residential and civilian sites in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities
At least 24 people were killed in Russian strikes across Ukraine on Wednesday, including four young children who died when a missile slammed into a residential block in the north of the country as they slept.
Windows shattered in the powerful blast in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region, reducing one half of the five-storey building into a smoking pile of charred concrete and twisted metal.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said three of the 18 victims of the strike were just 12 months old while another was aged eight.
Seven other children were among dozens wounded and one child was among 15 rescued, he wrote on social media, accusing Russia of knowingly striking “ordinary cities, ordinary life”.

articles.title: Sharaa visits Riyadh amid speculation about Syrian role in Yemen
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Sharaa visit to Riyadh fuels speculation about possible Syrian role in Yemen war
Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa met Saudi Crown Prince and de facto leader Mohammed Bin Salman on Tuesday in Riyadh amid speculation about a possible Syrian role in Yemen.
A statement from the Syrian presidency said that Al-Sharaa and bin Salman discussed relations between the two countries and ways to develop them, as well as the latest developments in the region.
Al-Sharaa was accompanied on the visit by Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani.
The statement made no mention of Yemen or the Houthi rebels, which Saudi Arabia has been fighting since September.
However, the visit took place amid intense fighting in Yemen between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis, with attempts by government forces to take control of the Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb waterway.
Saudi Arabia is also attempting to activate its Mecca defence agreement with Pakistan and Turkey amid reports that the latter two countries could offer military support to Riyadh in the war, but without directly fighting the Houthis.
Syria has close relations with both Saudi Arabia and Turkey, with the latter in particular seen as having influence on Sharaa’s government, due to its support for rebel forces prior to former dictator Bashar al-Assad’s fall in December 2024.
Saudi Arabia has previously called on a number of countries for help in the campaign against the Houthis, including the United States and Egypt as well as its Mecca Agreement allies. The US, however, has declined to become involved directly.
Earlier in the current flare-up of fighting in Yemen, a social media campaign, promoted by some figures close to the Syrian government, drew parallels between the Yemen war and the 2024 rebel victory over Assad.
The campaign supported alleged Yemeni government victories over the Houthis and featured AI-altered images of Syrian activists in traditional Yemeni dress.
There have been some unverified reports that Syrian fighters may be present in Yemen, assisting government forces.
Hiba Nasr, the US correspondent for Asharq Bloomberg, said in a post on X on Wednesday that “Syria may join the war in Yemen. No final decision has been made, but the idea is under discussion, according to multiple sources.”
During the Syrian civil war, Syrian fighters reportedly assisted forces of the Turkish-backed Government National Accord against Khalifa Haftar’s forces in Libya.
There are reports that Saudi Arabia may be interested in deploying Syrian fighters to Yemen because of their previous experience operating Turkish-made drones and weapons.
In addition, Saudi Arabia may view them as more reliable amid reports of internal divisions among Yemeni government forces.
"There are no Syrian troops in Yemen, and the Syrian government has not sent any. However, Sharaa’s visit to Saudi Arabia may have been to study possible arrangements regarding Yemen, including the sending of troops," the New Arab’s correspondent in Syria said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia marks Putin's birthday with one of its most vile attacks, killing 11 Ukrainians
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Russia marks Putin's birthday with one of its most vile attacks, killing 11 Ukrainians
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Russian attacks killed 11 Ukrainians and injured more than 30 others on the night of 6-7 October.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote: "Today, as a birthday 'gift' to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in Chernihiv Oblast. It was an ordinary five-storey apartment building. Tragically, as of now, five people have been reported killed and 26 injured, including five children. There may still be people under the rubble."
Details: Zelenskyy noted that rescue workers are continuing to work at the sites of the attacks.
Russian missile strikes damaged another five apartment buildings in the city of Dnipro and four high-rise buildings in Kremenchuk, Poltava Oblast. Two people were killed and eight others injured.
A drone damaged a high-rise building in Zaporizhzhia.
Russian attacks killed two people in Kyiv and another two in Oleksandriia, Kirovohrad Oblast. Overall, infrastructure in Kyiv and 12 oblasts came under attack overnight.
One of Russia's key targets was Ukraine's energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy stressed that the Russians had sought to inflict maximum damage and make a show of it. The president described it as one of the most vile attacks, without providing further details.
Russian forces used 70 missiles, including a large number of ballistic missiles, as well as Shahed drones. Ukrainian air defence was able to shoot down only some of the Russian assets. Zelenskyy stressed that Russian ballistic missiles remain the biggest challenge.
Quote: "And air defence packages for us right now are a vital necessity. That is why every day we are looking for missiles for Patriot systems that can and must actually protect people's lives here, in Ukrainian skies. Thank you to everyone who is helping us."

articles.title: Unexploded Russian ballistic missile being made safe in Kyiv residential area – photos
articles.body:
Unexploded Russian ballistic missile being made safe in Kyiv residential area – photos
The National Police and the State Emergency Service are carrying out a complex operation to defuse an unexploded Russian ballistic missile found among residential buildings in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district. The missile was launched towards Kyiv by Russian forces overnight.
Source: National Police of Ukraine in Kyiv
Quote: "Bomb disposal experts from the National Police in Kyiv and crews from the State Emergency Service are currently working at the scene. The experts will remove the warhead and then transport it to a designated disposal site to be made safe."
Details: Access to the area in question has been restricted.
Residents are urged not to approach the site and, if they find any other suspicious objects, to immediately call the emergency numbers 101 or 102.
Background:
- Russia launched a large-scale attack on Ukraine on the night of 6-7 October. Ukraine's Air Force reported that air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 161 aerial assets.
- Kyiv, Kharkiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts were the main targets of the attack.

articles.title: Ukraine Spoofs Two Russian Ballistic Missiles Mid-Flight, Sending Them Into Dnipro River
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Spoofs Two Russian Ballistic Missiles Mid-Flight, Sending Them Into Dnipro River
Earlier this year, Ukraine used an electronic warfare system to divert two Russian ballistic missiles from a key government site in Kyiv, causing them to crash into the Dnipro River, according to The Wall Street Journal on October 7.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The missiles were traveling toward the Ukrainian capital at hypersonic speeds when they were disrupted by radio signals generated by the Ukrainian electronic warfare unit Night Watch, which operates the domestically developed Lima system.
Around the same time, navigation applications on phones across Kyiv began showing users as being located in Peru—an effect linked to the false positioning signals generated during the operation, according to WSJ.
Night Watch uses Lima to interfere with satellite navigation relied on by Russian drones, guided bombs, and missiles. The system can transmit signals across a range of roughly 120 miles, or 193 kilometers, according to a member of the unit who uses the call sign Alchemist.
Rather than physically destroying an incoming weapon, electronic warfare can jam its navigation or use spoofing to feed its guidance system false positioning information, potentially forcing it away from its intended target.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Night Watch also says it used a similar method against a Russian Kinzhal hypersonic missile in November 2025. The system reportedly transmitted false navigation data that caused the missile to change course and ultimately fail while traveling at high speed.
Lima systems are deployed across Ukraine as part of a wider electronic warfare network designed to disrupt Russian precision-guided weapons. Ukrainian personnel told WSJ that the equipment can also interfere with friendly drones, requiring coordination between electronic warfare teams and Ukrainian UAV operators.
An officer with Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said electronic warfare suppresses between 70% and 95% of radio-controlled Russian drones detected in the sector where his team operates, according to the newspaper.
Russia has meanwhile been modifying its weapons in an effort to overcome Ukrainian electronic countermeasures. According to WSJ, Night Watch discovered in late 2024 that Russian missiles and drones were being equipped with Chinese-made antennas capable of identifying sources of interference and rapidly adjusting to avoid them.
Night Watch and Lima developer Cascade subsequently spent about three months developing an updated version of the system known as Lima Quant.
Earlier, Ukraine reported that the Lima electronic warfare system had neutralized 26 Russian Kh-47M2 Kinzhal missiles in the first three months of 2026, bringing the total to 58 since the system entered service. Lima uses a combination of jamming, spoofing, and cyber interference to disrupt the navigation of incoming missiles and drones.

articles.title: Kalashnikov, Russia’s biggest small-arms maker, says it fills its entire 2026 arms contract on time with batch of 7.62mm Dragunov sniper rifle
articles.body:
Russia's Kalashnikov concern has met its annual arms contract. The top producer of small arms has announced it delivered a batch of classic 7.62mm Dragunov sniper rifles to a Russian Security Forces customer and fully met its 2026 contract on time
The delivery shows how little the sanctions regime slows Russia's arms maker. In February 2026, Ukraine's Defense Intelligence said that nearly half of Kalashnikov's plants were still not subject to sanctions by any coalition country. Eight months later, the concern reports a full year's order delivered on schedule.
"The items were shipped on the set deadline, the obligations under the 2026 contract fully met," the manufacturer said.
A rifle in service for six decades
The weapon in that batch is not new. Designed by Yevgeny Dragunov between 1958 and 1963, the Dragunov sniper rifle entered serial production at the Izhevsk machine-building plant in 1963, so in 2026, it has remained in serial production for more than 60 years.
The self-loading 7.62mm rifle is meant to hit personnel and unarmored targets at ranges up to 800 meters, the concern said. It uses gas-operated automatics with a short-stroke piston and a gas regulator, and can fire any 7.62x54R round, though sniper ammunition yields the best grouping, according to the maker.
Sanctions chase a moving network
The sniper rifles are only one line in Kalashnikov's output. Russia's defense industry has leaned heavily on refurbishing Soviet-era armor as newer reserves run low, with Ukraine's intelligence reporting in June 2025 that Russia had begun deploying 1960s-era T-62 tanks.
The restoration work was centered primarily at the 103rd Armored Repair Plant in Atamanovka, Trans-Baikal Territory of Siberia. Ukrainian intelligence documented the transfer of 21 T-62 tanks from the eastern region to the western part.
Small arms are a different line of production, built new rather than pulled from storage. That is why a 1963 design keeps rolling off the line while the sanctions net, as Ukraine's intelligence describes it, still has holes.

articles.title: Lithuanian firm brings Ukraine-proven drones to London
articles.body:
A Lithuanian manufacturer whose loitering munitions and reconnaissance drones are in Ukrainian service is bringing its full range to London this week, including a counter-drone interceptor built to shoot down Shahed and Lancet types, according to Granta Autonomy.
The company began supplying uncrewed aircraft to the Ukrainian front immediately after the full-scale invasion and says it is one of only a handful of suppliers to have remained continuously active since, changing its equipment to keep pace with the battlefield. Ukrainian forces now operate a full battery of its systems funded by European defence ministries, among them the X-Wing loitering munition and the Hornet XR reconnaissance drone.
The newest product is the Black Wasp, a vertical take-off interceptor engineered to counter Shahed, Geran and Lancet drones. It reaches 320 kilometres an hour with a climb rate of 30 metres a second, uses the company’s machine learning flight control system for automated flight, precision tracking and terminal guidance, and integrates with radar networks for three-dimensional targeting telemetry.
The X-Wing combines vertical take-off with fixed-wing efficiency to reach 70 kilometres with more than 45 minutes of loiter, carrying a four-kilogram anti-armour or fragmentation warhead and using machine targeting for navigation and strike where satellite signals are denied. The Hornet XR is a hand-launched reconnaissance aircraft weighing 3.2 kilograms, with more than three hours of endurance, a 70-kilometre control link and a deep-stall recovery for landing.
Gediminas Guoba, chief executive and founder, said: “Our team regularly tests our solutions on the frontlines alongside military operators. The new Black Wasp and X-Wing demonstrate our commitment to scalable, EW-resistant architecture. Paired with our Hornet XR, the X-Wing allows a single ground station to control a pair of ‘sensor’ Hornets alongside up to 30 ‘shooter’ X-Wings, creating a complete, highly effective kill chain that outpaces complex and costly alternatives.”
That last claim is the one to examine closely on the stand. One operator running two reconnaissance aircraft and thirty strike aircraft from a single ground station describes a quite different arithmetic from the one Western forces are used to, where each airframe generally requires its own crew, and it is the arithmetic that has made Ukrainian drone units effective against far better equipped formations.
The company also builds two-axis stabilised micro-gimbals in Lithuania to European standards, with dual electro-optical cameras offering up to 40 times zoom. The 180-gram NightScout carries a thermal camera for surveillance work, while the 135-gram SOLO is built for loitering munitions, and three-axis gimbals are due in the first quarter of next year.
Granta is exhibiting at Apex Europe at The Magazine in London on Wednesday and Thursday.

articles.title: Ukraine adds Kyiv trains, prepares pontoon crossings after Russian bridge attacks
articles.body:
Ukraine's state railway, Ukrzaliznytsia, has added 18 Kyiv City Express shuttle runs between Vydubychi and Darnytsia for 5–9 October, while the government has begun preparatory work on temporary crossings over the Dnipro River after Russian strikes disrupted bridge traffic. Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk outlined the backup plan in an interview with Suspilne on 3 October.
About 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro in Kyiv each day, making the river crossings critical to movement across the capital, Kalashnyk said. Russia's attacks on the Southern and Northern bridges have disrupted traffic, with the Southern Bridge fully closed to cars and metro on 2 October and restrictions introduced on other crossings. The risk of further damage is heightened by Russia's upgraded jet-powered Geran-4, which now carries a specialized warhead designed to cut through bridge structures and power-line supports, according to presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov.
Jams, restrictions, and extra trains
On 6 October, large traffic jams formed between Kyiv's left and right banks, with the heaviest queues on approaches to the Southern Bridge, Obozrevatel reported. The jams followed Russian strikes that cratered the Northern Bridge.
Green-line metro trains resumed carrying passengers between the banks during the yellow threat level on 4 October, Radio Svoboda reported. Under the current restrictions, traffic on the Southern and Podilskyi bridges is stopped in certain directions for at most the first 15 minutes after an air alert begins.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
The additional Kyiv City Express shuttles run during the busiest hours, 06:00–09:00 and 16:00–21:00. Together with scheduled suburban and regional trains, they bring the number of peak-hour runs between the banks to up to six, Ukrzaliznytsia said.
Pontoons first, tunnel later
Kalashnyk said the government plans to build several backup crossings over the Dnipro. The sites have already been chosen, and he named a combination of earth embankments and pontoon crossings as measures that can be built quickly. He said construction could take up to three months and that the backup crossings should provide at least 50% of the capacity of the existing bridges. The government is also considering quick-build concrete structures and, in the longer term, a tunnel under the Dnipro, he told Suspilne.
Volodymyr Kreidenko, deputy head of the parliamentary committee on transport and infrastructure and an MP from the Servant of the People party, proposed reversible traffic across the bridges: "in the morning from the left bank to the right, in the evening from the right to the left." He also suggested hubs near the bridges where people could take a bicycle or e-scooter, and passenger ferry crossings, Radio Svoboda reported.
Andrii Koretskyi, an associate professor in the department of bridges, tunnels and hydraulic structures at the National Transport University, cautioned that temporary crossings cannot substitute for a permanent bridge.
"The only alternative to a bridge is a bridge as a permanent structure," he told Radio Svoboda.
He said a tunnel under the Dnipro is technically possible but "not a quick solution at all." He pointed to the scale involved: where the Irpin River requires spanning a few dozen or, in places, a few hundred meters, the Dnipro within Kyiv is "roughly 400 to 1,500 meters" wide.

articles.title: Iran threatens to block ‘illegal’ routes through Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Iran threatens to block ‘illegal’ routes through Strait of Hormuz
Iran has threatened to block what it calls “illegal” traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, saying it retains full control of the passage despite US claims to the contrary.
The waterway is one of the world’s most important energy routes, normally carrying around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Traffic through the strait has been severely disrupted since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February, driving up energy prices. Brent crude was trading at around $101 a barrel on Wednesday, compared with roughly $72 before the conflict.
Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander and adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader, said on Wednesday that several transit routes through the strait along Oman’s coast would soon be closed.
Naqdi said the routes had been created by blasting and damaging rocky passages and were being used by small boats to carry oil through the waterway before transferring it to tankers. He described the shipments as “smuggling” and argued that they were too limited to show that traffic through Hormuz was returning to normal.
”The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Naqdi said, adding that the restrictions would remain until Tehran’s “legitimate demands” were met.
Iran has previously offered to reopen the strait if Washington eases military pressure and lifts its blockade of Iranian ports.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered a sharply different assessment on Wednesday, saying the strait is “open” and that Iran had “lost complete control” of Hormuz.
”There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” Rubio told reporters.
President Donald Trump has also said the US military is helping oil shipments pass through the strait, claiming that daily flows have risen above 20 million barrels. He has blamed the global diesel shortage primarily on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries rather than the Middle East conflict and has urged Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt the attacks.
Regional crude exports have rebounded significantly. A seven-day moving average reached 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, according to provisional Kpler data cited by Reuters. The figure includes oil shipped through routes other than Hormuz.
Security risks in the strait remain high. The Panamanian-flagged tanker On Peace was hit by a projectile near Oman on Tuesday, injuring 12 crew members, according to the Indian authorities. No group has claimed responsibility.

articles.title: Ukraine's General Staff: over 200 combat clashes recorded on battlefield over past day
articles.body:
Ukraine's General Staff: over 200 combat clashes recorded on battlefield over past day
A total of 202 combat clashes have occurred on the battlefield over the past day, with Ukraine's defence forces repelling Russian attacks on nine fronts.

On the North Slobozhanshchyna front, the Russians conducted three attacks near the settlements of Bachivsk, Rivne and Volfyne.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian units repelled 11 Russian attacks. The Russians attempted to advance near the settlements of Volokhivka, Starytsia, Izbytske, Zakharivka, Mala Vovcha and Varvarivka.
On the Kupiansk front, the Russians conducted one attack near the village of Kivsharivka.
On the Lyman front, Russian attempts to advance were stopped. Ukrainian forces repelled eight Russian attacks near the settlements of Novomykhailivka, Nadiia, Stavky, Novoselivka and Lyman.
On the Kramatorsk front, Ukrainian forces repelled two Russian attacks near the village of Minkivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 14 Russian attacks were recorded. The Russians conducted assaults near the settlements of Kostiantynivka, Novoselivka, Mykolaipillia and Osykove.
On the Pokrovsk front, Ukrainian defenders stopped 27 Russian attacks. The Russians concentrated their main efforts near the settlements of Serhiivka and Molodetske and also conducted assaults towards Kucheriv Yar, Vilne, Bilytske, Vodianske, Dobropillia and Novohryshyne.
On the Huliaipole front, Ukrainian forces repelled 13 Russian attacks near the settlements of Hirke, Rybne, Vozdvyzhivka, Dolynka, Rivne, Kopani, Yehorivka, Novoselivka and Charivne.

articles.title: Ukraine built a $9K drone to hunt a $10M Russian jammer
articles.body:
- Ukraine's Brave1 Market has listed the SHOT-L1, a strike drone that automatically homes in on radio emissions from Russian electronic warfare systems.
- The drone has a range of up to 80 km, carries a 4 kg payload and costs UAH 416,000 (about $9,300).
A Ukrainian fixed-wing strike drone built to find Russian electronic warfare systems by their own radio signals and dive onto them has been listed on Brave1 Market, the government-run online store where Ukrainian military units order weapons, Ukrainian outlet Defender Media reported.
The drone, called SHOT-L1, can strike targets up to 80 km (50 miles) away and is priced at UAH 416,000 (about $9,300) per unit on the platform. The manufacturer has not been named, and there is no information yet on whether the drone has been codified, the formal approval that admits a product into service with the Ukrainian military.
An operator sends the SHOT-L1 toward the area where a target is believed to be, and once the drone reaches the assigned zone, an onboard system scans it for radio emissions, works out the direction of a detected source and steers the drone onto it automatically. If it picks up several emitters at once, the drone goes for the strongest one, the manufacturer says.
If no active signal turns up within a set time, the drone switches to a backup mission and attacks a fixed ground target chosen before launch.
The SHOT-L1 carries a 4 kg (8.8-pound) payload and cruises at 100 km/h (62 mph) with up to 60 minutes of flight time. It has a thermal camera, an analog video link and a terminal guidance system for the final approach.
The manufacturer lists three Russian jamming systems as typical targets: the R-340RP Pole-21, the R-330Zh Zhitel and the Mgla. Pole-21 is designed to jam satellite navigation signals such as GPS, while the truck-mounted Zhitel is built to jam satellite phones, cellular networks and navigation signals. Ukrainian estimates put the cost of a single Zhitel at around $10 million. Russian forces have used both systems widely in the war in Ukraine, where jamming is a constant problem for Ukrainian drone units that depend on radio control links and satellite navigation.
Brave1 Market launched in 2025 and lets Ukrainian units buy drones, ground robots and electronic warfare equipment with their own budgets or with points earned for confirmed combat results. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said troops ordered more than 590,000 drones through the platform in the first nine months of 2026, with interceptor drones the most popular category.

articles.title: Pentagon chief awards Presidential Unit Citation to USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group
articles.body:
Diyar Guldogan
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth praised the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group on Wednesday for a "historic" combat deployment, as the aircraft carrier headed to San Diego following an extended mission in the Middle East.
"What the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group did, no other carrier strike group has ever done," Hegseth told the crew.
Hegseth cited 10,000 sorties, 23,000 combat flight hours and nearly 4,000 combat sorties during the deployment. He said the group dropped 1.5 million pounds of ordnance on enemy targets.
The secretary said President Donald Trump asked him to personally thank the sailors and other personnel involved in the mission, including their role in the Epic Fury operation aimed at preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
He also praised the carrier strike group's role in a subsequent blockade, describing it as “impenetrable since day one.”
Hegseth highlighted the length and demands of the deployment, saying the crew spent 265 consecutive days without a port call. He said the deployment was extended twice after personnel believed they would be returning home.
“Two times extended when you thought you were going home, and we asked you to do more,” he said. “And you know what you did? You did more, and it wasn't easy.”
Hegseth said the carrier strike group played a central role in the administration's effort to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
“I couldn't be more proud of what you executed in this historic mission to ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon,” he said. Iran “will never get a nuclear weapon.”
Hegseth announced that the carrier strike group would receive the Presidential Unit Citation, one of the military's highest unit awards.
“It is with great pride today that I would like to award to you the Presidential Unit Citation,” he said.

articles.title: Newsom Calls for 25th Amendment After Trump Imagines Iran Attacking California
articles.body:
“Donald Trump is mentally ill,” California Gov. Gavin Newsom told TIME and other media outlets in a statement after the President made remarks Monday suggesting an attack by Iran on the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego would be “a small price to pay.”
“TIME FOR THE 25TH!” Newsom added, in apparent reference to the 25th Amendment, a constitutional provision that establishes procedures for presidential succession and for replacing or declaring a President unable to perform their duties. Newsom has referred to the 25th Amendment before, alongside other lawmakers and critics, who have suggested that, among other things, Trump’s struggle to find an off-ramp for the war he started with Iran in February—and his expressions of willingness to let civilians in Iran and the U.S. die en masse—suggest that he is unfit to hold office.
The California politician, serving his last term as governor, is widely seen as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in the 2028 election. Newsom and Trump have clashed over a host of issues, including immigration enforcement, environmental and climate policy, and state funding.
Trump made his recent scrutinized remarks at a rally in Nebraska, as he sought understanding from voters grumbling about the costs of the war. Trump initially promised to end it in weeks, and Democrats, including Newsom, have criticized him for prolonging the conflict.
“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” Trump said of letting the conflict rage a few more weeks until after the U.S. midterms, after which he has vowed the war will come to an end. “They can take out a city. Let them take—let it—let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s—this is a very small price to pay.”
In separate posts across multiple social media accounts following Trump’s Monday remark, Newsom warned that the President’s comment was not only “madness” but also “dangerous” and “deranged.” Speaking to journalist Jim Acosta, Newsom argued that the statement puts over 130,000 active-duty military personnel stationed in San Diego at risk: “Don’t think for a second our adversaries aren’t listening to that.”
Newsom also claimed that Trump’s remark could be “treasonous.” He posted that the President’s statements make one of the U.S.’s largest naval hubs a potential target and that he directed California’s State Threat Assessment Center “to actively monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the President’s remarks as an invitation to target” the state.
The White House has defended Trump’s remark on the California cities and claimed that it’s being misinterpreted.
“The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,” White House Communications Director Steven Cheung posted on social media. “He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”
Other California politicians hit back
Trump’s statement on Los Angeles and San Diego has since become fodder for California’s Democratic politicians ahead of the November general elections.
“Thirteen million Californians call LA and San Diego counties home,” Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra posted on social media. “Their lives are not a ‘small price to pay’ or a punchline for Donald Trump.”
The Democratic mayors of those cities also rebuked Trump. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass called the President’s remark “completely irresponsible,” adding that the “role of a President is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives.” Todd Gloria, San Diego’s mayor, posted that his city was “not collateral damage” in the war with Iran, and exclaimed: “Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”
More than 40 Democratic members of U.S. Congress representing California, including Sens. Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, also signed a statement demanding that Trump apologize to more than 16 million Americans living in the cities.
And it’s not just Democrats.
Jim Desmond, a Republican candidate for a U.S. House seat in the state’s 48th congressional district, disagreed with Trump’s remark. “As a Navy veteran, I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war,” Desmond posted on X. “Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality. No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”
Speaking to a local Fox affiliate, Rep. Kevin Kiley, a former Republican running for reelection as an independent in California’s 6th congressional district, said that while there is “no evidence” Iran could strike a city in the state, “such rhetoric is unhelpful.”
Is Trump becoming incoherent?
Trump’s “small price to pay” phrasing isn’t new—he made a similar comment about fuel costs during a rally in Mobile, Ala., last week: “Remember about the oil: You’re paying a price, but boy, is that a small price than what it would be if these lunatics were allowed to have a nuclear weapon and used it on Mobile, Alabama.”
Observers, however, say his comment on the California cities may not be malicious but does signal increasing incoherence, adding to questions that have swirled for years about Trump’s mental acuity and fitness for the presidency.
Those concerns gained renewed attention following Trump’s recent interview with TIME. The interview showed “moments of confusion, incoherence, and paranoia that look like windows into Trump’s mental state,” a politics writer for Slate summarized. “Suffice it to say that if any other president—or person—spoke the way Trump does, you’d probably worry about their psychological and perhaps medical well-being.”
Read More: What Trump Has Built
Critics have long questioned Trump’s mental and cognitive health, though his Administration has repeatedly argued that the President remains fit to carry out presidential duties, citing regular checkups.
Lawyer George Conway, a Republican-turned-Democrat and a vocal Trump critic who has called for his removal from office since 2019, posted on X: “You can reasonably dispute the meaning of a lot Trump says because he’s so incoherent and inarticulate. But what you can’t reasonably dispute is that he is a sadistic and delusional narcissistic sociopath, at once both psychopathic and psychotic, who is lacking in morality, conscience, empathy, remorse, and impulse control, and whose only concern if a city (in any country, including ours) were to be wiped off the face of the Earth, would be how it affects him.”

articles.title: Mali reclaims rebel stronghold with Russian support (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Mali reclaims rebel stronghold with Russian support (VIDEO)
Malian troops backed by Russian forces have retaken the northern separatist stronghold of Kidal, the government has announced, reversing the loss of the strategic town during a coordinated rebel and jihadist offensive in April.
The transitional authorities said troops consolidated their positions in the regional capital on Tuesday following intensive air and ground operations. Their return would enable the gradual restoration of public administration and basic services, according to the government statement.
The Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) acknowledged leaving Kidal and claimed there had been “disproportionate” airstrikes by Mali’s military and the Russian Defense Ministry-run Africa Corps. Its spokesperson, Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane, described the move as a “controlled withdrawal” to preserve personnel and equipment, saying its forces had pulled out without direct combat and that the retreat was temporary.
Kidal has long been a center of separatist demands for an independent state in northern Mali. Malian troops and fighters from the Russian private military company Wagner recaptured it in November 2023, before losing control following a nationwide offensive in April by the FLA and the Al-Qaeda-linked Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) that also killed Defense Minister Sadio Camara.
The West African nation has been gripped since 2012 by a jihadist insurgency that has spread to neighboring Burkina Faso and Niger despite years of French military intervention. Nearly 49,000 people have been killed in violence linked to militant Islamist groups across the Sahel since 2022, the Africa Center for Strategic Studies said in August.
Bamako and its Sahel allies have accused foreign powers of supporting the armed groups. Addressing the UN General Assembly on September 28, Malian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop accused Ukraine of aiding jihadists and separatists, citing coordinated attacks in April and July. Mali severed diplomatic ties with Kiev in August 2024 after Ukrainian military intelligence spokesman Andrey Yusov said rebels received information enabling an ambush on Malian and Wagner forces.
Last month, CNN reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were assisting the FLA with drone training and operations, citing Ukrainian personnel. Kiev has rejected allegations that it supports terrorist groups in the Sahel.
Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger have also accused France of supporting terrorist groups in the Sahel. All three former French colonies have ended defense cooperation with Paris and strengthened security ties with Moscow. Personnel from the Africa Corps, which replaced Wagner in Mali by 2025, have since supported Malian troops in operations against jihadists and separatist armed groups.
Since 2020, a wave of military coups has reshaped politics across the Sahel region in Africa, toppling civilian governments in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.
France, once the region’s dominant external power, has steadily lost influence amid rising anti-French sentiment and deep frustration over insecurity, economic stagnation, and foreign interference. The former colonial power was forced to withdraw troops from Mali in 2022, Burkina Faso in 2023, Niger later that year, and Chad in early 2025.
About 4,500 soldiers had been deployed under Operation Barkhane, France’s largest overseas mission, across Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, and Chad – a campaign that the military governments in Bamako, Niamey, and Ouagadougou have said only permitted Islamist insurgents to expand their activities.
The three West African states have established the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and withdrawn from the International Organization of Francophone Nations (OIF) operating in Francophone countries, many of them former French colonies. The AES has forged new alliances, including with Russia, which its leaders hail as a more reliable economic and security partner.
In July, the joint forces recaptured Anefis, a strategic town about 100 km south of Kidal, after more than a week of fighting. Mali’s military said operations there and in two nearby localities killed nearly 100 militants and destroyed 12 combat vehicles.
